Diagnosed by a supervised fast showing INAPPROPRIATELY HIGH INSULIN AND C-PEPTIDE with a low glucose. A HIGH insulin with a LOW C-peptide means EXOGENOUS insulin — factitious or malicious administration — which is a completely different problem, and screen for sulfonylureas too.
the_functioning_pancreatic_tumours.gastrinoma_zollinger_ellison: Gastrin excess causing MULTIPLE, RECURRENT, ATYPICALLY SITED peptic ulcers (including distal duodenum and jejunum) that resist standard treatment, plus DIARRHOEA and steatorrhoea from acid inactivation of pancreatic enzymes. Suspect it in ulcers that recur despite eradication and adequate acid suppression, or ulcers with diarrhoea. Fasting gastrin must be measured OFF proton pump inhibitors — PPIs raise gastrin and cause a false positive.
the_functioning_pancreatic_tumours.vipoma: WDHA — Watery Diarrhoea, Hypokalaemia, Achlorhydria. Profuse secretory diarrhoea that persists during fasting.
the_functioning_pancreatic_tumours.glucagonoma: NECROLYTIC MIGRATORY ERYTHEMA — a distinctive rash — with diabetes, weight loss, anaemia and venous thrombosis. The rash is frequently treated as eczema for months.
the_functioning_pancreatic_tumours.somatostatinoma: Diabetes, gallstones and steatorrhoea — the classic triad from inhibition of insulin, gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzymes.

warnings: In MEN 2, exclude and treat the phaeochromocytoma BEFORE any other surgery — otherwise a fatal intraoperative crisis.
MEN 2B has no parathyroid disease; that is what separates it from 2A.
Medullary thyroid carcinoma does not take up radioiodine. Surgery is the only cure.
Carcinoid SYNDROME usually implies liver metastases or an extra-portal primary — the liver inactivates mediators from a gut primary.
Carcinoid heart disease is RIGHT-sided, because the lungs inactivate the mediators.
Give octreotide before any procedure in carcinoid to prevent crisis.
High insulin with LOW C-peptide is exogenous insulin, not an insulinoma. Screen for sulfonylureas too.
Measure fasting gastrin OFF proton pump inhibitors — PPIs cause false positives.
Primary hyperparathyroidism under 40, or multi-gland, should raise MEN 1.
limitations: Genetic testing pathways, prophylactic surgery timing by codon, and tumour marker cut-offs are specialist- and protocol-directed.

flashcards.q: The three Ps of MEN 1?
flashcards.a: Parathyroid, pancreas, pituitary.

flashcards.q: MEN 2A vs 2B?
flashcards.a: Both: medullary thyroid carcinoma + phaeochromocytoma. 2A adds parathyroid; 2B adds mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus and has NO parathyroid disease.

flashcards.q: What must be treated first in MEN 2 surgery?
flashcards.a: The phaeochromocytoma — otherwise a fatal intraoperative crisis.

flashcards.q: Why does a gut carcinoid usually cause no syndrome?
flashcards.a: It drains into the portal vein and the liver inactivates the mediators.

flashcards.q: Why is carcinoid heart disease right-sided?
flashcards.a: The lungs inactivate the mediators before they reach the left heart.

flashcards.q: Whipple triad?
flashcards.a: Hypoglycaemic symptoms, documented low glucose, relief with glucose.

flashcards.q: High insulin, low C-peptide?
flashcards.a: Exogenous insulin administration, not an insulinoma.

flashcards.q: Why stop PPIs before measuring gastrin?
flashcards.a: They raise gastrin and cause a false positive for Zollinger-Ellison.

flashcards.q: Which rash suggests glucagonoma?
flashcards.a: Necrolytic migratory erythema — often misdiagnosed as eczema.

checkboxes: Phaeochromocytoma excluded before surgery in MEN 2
Octreotide cover arranged before carcinoid procedures

entries.title: Adrenal Disorders — Cushing, Conn and Addison
entries.summary: Too much cortisol, too much aldosterone, too little of everything. Each has one diagnostic trap: in Cushing confirm the excess before hunting the source; in Conn the clue is hypertension WITH hypokalaemia; in Addison the crisis is treated on suspicion, never after the result.

terms: adrenal disorders — cushing, conn and addison

cushing_syndrome.the_features_that_actually_discriminate: Obesity, hypertension and diabetes are common in the general population and do NOT discriminate. The features with real discriminating value are PROXIMAL MYOPATHY (cannot rise from a chair without using the arms), EASY BRUISING, THIN SKIN, and WIDE (>1 cm) PURPLE STRIAE. Look for these specifically.
cushing_syndrome.other: Moon face, interscapular and supraclavicular fat pads, facial plethora, hirsutism, osteoporosis and fragility fracture, psychiatric change, poor wound healing, immunosuppression, and growth arrest in children — a child who is gaining weight but NOT growing is a red flag.
cushing_syndrome.the_commonest_cause: EXOGENOUS CORTICOSTEROIDS, by a wide margin. Always take a full drug history including inhaled, topical, intra-articular and over-the-counter preparations — and traditional or unregulated remedies, which are a genuine and under-recognised source of potent steroid.

the_diagnostic_sequence.step_1_confirm_excess: Overnight or low-dose DEXAMETHASONE SUPPRESSION, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, or late-night salivary cortisol. Two abnormal tests are usually required. Loss of the normal DIURNAL RHYTHM is the fundamental abnormality.
the_diagnostic_sequence.step_2_acth: Measure ACTH. SUPPRESSED ACTH means an ADRENAL source (adenoma, carcinoma). NORMAL or HIGH ACTH means pituitary (Cushing DISEASE) or ectopic.
the_diagnostic_sequence.step_3_localise: High-dose dexamethasone suppression, CRH testing, inferior petrosal sinus sampling, and imaging. Ectopic ACTH — classically small cell lung cancer — tends to present rapidly with severe HYPOKALAEMIA, marked pigmentation and weight LOSS rather than the classic body habitus.
the_diagnostic_sequence.the_error: Imaging before confirming biochemical excess. Adrenal and pituitary incidentalomas are common, and finding one in a patient who does not have Cushing leads to unnecessary surgery.

cushing_syndrome.pseudo_cushing: Alcohol excess, severe depression, obesity and poorly controlled diabetes can all produce abnormal cortisol dynamics. This is why confirmation requires more than one test.

conn_syndrome.what: PRIMARY hyperaldosteronism — autonomous aldosterone from a unilateral adenoma or, more commonly, bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.
conn_syndrome.why_it_matters: It is far commoner than historically taught — a meaningful proportion of resistant hypertension — and it is potentially CURABLE. It also causes cardiovascular and renal damage out of proportion to the blood pressure, so finding it changes outcome, not just tablets.
conn_syndrome.the_clue: HYPERTENSION WITH HYPOKALAEMIA, especially if the potassium falls easily on a thiazide. But note that many patients are NORMOkalaemic — normal potassium does not exclude it. Also: metabolic alkalosis, and hypertension resistant to three or more agents.
conn_syndrome.who_to_screen: Resistant hypertension, hypertension with hypokalaemia, hypertension with an adrenal incidentaloma, hypertension under 40 or with a family history of early stroke, and hypertension with sleep apnoea.
conn_syndrome.diagnosis: ALDOSTERONE:RENIN RATIO — high aldosterone with SUPPRESSED renin. Many antihypertensives interfere (especially spironolactone, which must be stopped well in advance, and beta-blockers) — follow the local protocol for which drugs to withdraw. Then confirmatory suppression testing, then CT and ADRENAL VEIN SAMPLING to determine whether disease is unilateral (surgery) or bilateral (mineralocorticoid antagonist).
conn_syndrome.the_contrast: SECONDARY hyperaldosteronism has HIGH renin — renal artery stenosis, heart failure, cirrhosis, diuretics. The renin is what separates them.

addison_disease.what: PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency — the adrenal cortex itself fails, so BOTH cortisol AND aldosterone are lost. Autoimmune in most of the developed world; TUBERCULOSIS remains a leading cause worldwide and must be considered. Also adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen in meningococcal sepsis), metastases, HIV, and drugs.
addison_disease.the_distinguishing_sign: HYPERPIGMENTATION — in palmar creases, buccal mucosa, scars and pressure areas. It occurs because ACTH is high and its precursor peptide stimulates melanocytes. It is present in PRIMARY insufficiency only.
addison_disease.secondary_insufficiency: Pituitary failure or, far more commonly, SUPPRESSION BY EXOGENOUS STEROIDS. Here ACTH is LOW, so there is NO pigmentation, and ALDOSTERONE IS PRESERVED because it is driven by renin, not ACTH. So secondary insufficiency does not cause the hyperkalaemia and severe salt wasting of Addison.
addison_disease.biochemistry: HYPONATRAEMIA and HYPERKALAEMIA (the combination should always prompt the thought), hypoglycaemia, mild hypercalcaemia, eosinophilia, and a metabolic acidosis.
addison_disease.diagnosis: 9 a.m. cortisol and ACTH, then a SHORT SYNACTHEN test. Adrenal autoantibodies. Imaging if a non-autoimmune cause is suspected.

adrenal_crisis.presentation: Shock disproportionate to the apparent illness, vomiting, abdominal pain that can mimic an acute abdomen, fever, confusion, hypoglycaemia.
adrenal_crisis.the_rule: TREAT ON SUSPICION. Give hydrocortisone and fluid IMMEDIATELY — take the cortisol sample if convenient, but NEVER wait for the result. Hydrocortisone does not interfere with a subsequently performed Synacthen test if dexamethasone is used instead. Delay kills; a dose of steroid in someone who turns out not to need it harms almost nobody.
adrenal_crisis.precipitants: Infection, surgery, trauma, vomiting, and — most commonly and most preventably — failure to increase the dose during illness.

addison_disease.the_education_that_prevents_deaths: SICK DAY RULES — double the oral dose during febrile illness; if vomiting, use the emergency INTRAMUSCULAR hydrocortisone. Every patient must have an emergency injection kit, be trained to use it, carry a steroid card or bracelet, and have a family member trained too. This is the single highest-value intervention in the whole condition.

warnings: Adrenal crisis is treated on SUSPICION. Give hydrocortisone and fluids immediately — never wait for cortisol results.
The commonest cause of Cushing syndrome is exogenous steroid. Ask about inhaled, topical, injected and unregulated preparations.
Confirm cortisol excess biochemically BEFORE imaging. Incidentalomas are common and lead to unnecessary surgery.
Hypertension WITH hypokalaemia should prompt an aldosterone:renin ratio — but normal potassium does NOT exclude Conn.
Stop interfering antihypertensives, especially spironolactone, before measuring the aldosterone:renin ratio.
Hyperpigmentation occurs in PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency only. Secondary has low ACTH, no pigmentation and preserved aldosterone.
Hyponatraemia WITH hyperkalaemia should always raise Addison disease.
Every patient on long-term steroid needs sick day rules, an emergency injection kit and a steroid card. Failure to increase the dose during illness is the commonest precipitant of crisis.
A child gaining weight but not growing is a red flag for Cushing.
Consider tuberculosis as a cause of Addison disease — it remains a leading cause worldwide.
limitations: Test protocols, drug withdrawal periods and replacement regimens are protocol-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Which Cushing features actually discriminate?
flashcards.a: Proximal myopathy, easy bruising, thin skin, wide purple striae. Not obesity or hypertension.

flashcards.q: What does a suppressed ACTH indicate in Cushing?
flashcards.a: An adrenal source. Normal or high ACTH means pituitary or ectopic.

flashcards.q: What is the classic Conn clue?
flashcards.a: Hypertension with hypokalaemia — though many are normokalaemic.

flashcards.q: Primary vs secondary hyperaldosteronism?
flashcards.a: Renin. Suppressed in primary (Conn), high in secondary.

flashcards.q: Why is there pigmentation in Addison but not secondary insufficiency?
flashcards.a: ACTH is high in primary and stimulates melanocytes; it is low in secondary.

flashcards.q: Why is aldosterone preserved in secondary insufficiency?
flashcards.a: It is driven by renin, not ACTH.

flashcards.q: Biochemical hallmark of Addison?
flashcards.a: Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, plus hypoglycaemia.

flashcards.q: What is the rule in adrenal crisis?
flashcards.a: Treat on suspicion — hydrocortisone and fluids before any result.

flashcards.q: Commonest precipitant of adrenal crisis?
flashcards.a: Failure to increase the steroid dose during illness.

checkboxes: Full steroid history including topical and unregulated sources
Biochemical confirmation before imaging in Cushing
Hydrocortisone given on suspicion in crisis
Sick day rules taught and emergency kit issued

entries.title: Pituitary Tumours and the Sella Turcica
entries.summary: A mass in a bony box beneath the optic chiasm. It causes trouble three ways: by SECRETING, by COMPRESSING (bitemporal hemianopia), or by DESTROYING. Apoplexy is the emergency, and prolactinoma is the one treated medically rather than surgically.

terms: pituitary tumours and the sella turcica

the_three_mechanisms.secretion: A functioning adenoma over-produces one hormone.
the_three_mechanisms.compression: Upward growth compresses the OPTIC CHIASM, classically producing a BITEMPORAL HEMIANOPIA, because the crossing nasal retinal fibres — which carry the temporal fields — are hit first. Lateral extension into the cavernous sinus affects cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI.
the_three_mechanisms.destruction: A large mass destroys normal pituitary tissue causing HYPOPITUITARISM. The classic order of loss is GROWTH HORMONE and GONADOTROPHINS FIRST, then TSH and ACTH, with prolactin often preserved or raised.

prolactinoma.why_it_is_special: It is the commonest functioning pituitary tumour and — uniquely — it is treated MEDICALLY first. DOPAMINE AGONISTS (cabergoline, bromocriptine) both suppress prolactin AND shrink the tumour, often dramatically. Operating first on a prolactinoma is a recognised error.
prolactinoma.features: Women: amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, infertility — usually presents early and small. Men: erectile dysfunction, reduced libido, gynaecomastia, infertility — usually presents LATE and large, because the symptoms are attributed to other things or not reported.

two_traps.stalk_effect: ANY sellar mass can compress the pituitary stalk and interrupt the tonic dopamine inhibition of prolactin, producing a MODESTLY raised prolactin. That is NOT a prolactinoma — it is a non-functioning mass. A modest elevation with a large tumour suggests stalk effect; a very high prolactin with a large tumour suggests a true prolactinoma. Getting this wrong means treating a non-functioning macroadenoma with cabergoline and watching it grow.
two_traps.hook_effect: A MASSIVELY raised prolactin can saturate the assay and produce a FALSELY LOW or normal result. If a large tumour has an unexpectedly modest prolactin, ask the laboratory for a DILUTED sample.

prolactinoma.other_causes_of_hyperprolactinaemia: Pregnancy and breastfeeding, primary HYPOTHYROIDISM (raised TRH stimulates prolactin — always check the thyroid), chronic kidney disease, chest wall lesions, stress and venepuncture, and DRUGS — antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone, and some antidepressants. Drugs are the commonest cause overall.

acromegaly.features: Growth of hands, feet and jaw (prognathism), coarsening of features, interdental spacing, macroglossia, carpal tunnel syndrome, sweating, skin tags, arthropathy. Onset is insidious — compare OLD PHOTOGRAPHS, which is the single most useful bedside investigation, and ask about ring and shoe size changes.
acromegaly.why_it_matters: The morbidity is cardiovascular (cardiomyopathy, hypertension), metabolic (diabetes), and oncological (increased colorectal cancer risk, so colonoscopic surveillance). Untreated it shortens life substantially.
acromegaly.diagnosis: IGF-1 as the screening test (GH is pulsatile and a random level is useless). Confirm with an ORAL GLUCOSE TOLERANCE TEST showing FAILURE OF GH SUPPRESSION. Then MRI.
acromegaly.gigantism: If it occurs before epiphyseal fusion, the result is gigantism rather than acromegaly.

the_functioning_tumours.cushing_disease: ACTH-secreting adenoma — usually a microadenoma that can be hard to find on imaging, which is why inferior petrosal sinus sampling exists.
the_functioning_tumours.tsh_oma: Rare. Produces thyrotoxicosis with an INAPPROPRIATELY NORMAL OR RAISED TSH — the pattern that should never be dismissed as an assay error without thought.

pituitary_apoplexy.what: Sudden haemorrhage or infarction into a pituitary tumour. A neurosurgical and endocrine EMERGENCY.
pituitary_apoplexy.presentation: SUDDEN severe headache, VOMITING, VISUAL LOSS or field defect, OPHTHALMOPLEGIA, reduced consciousness, and meningism. It is frequently mistaken for subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis.
pituitary_apoplexy.the_thing_that_kills: ACUTE ADRENAL INSUFFICIENCY from sudden ACTH loss. GIVE HYDROCORTISONE IMMEDIATELY on suspicion — before imaging, before endocrine results. That single action is what saves the patient; the surgery can follow.
pituitary_apoplexy.management: Steroids first, urgent MRI, urgent neurosurgical and endocrine involvement, formal visual field assessment. Some patients are managed conservatively; those with significant visual compromise usually need decompression.

the_other_sellar_masses.craniopharyngioma: Arises from Rathke pouch remnants. Bimodal age distribution — children and older adults. CALCIFICATION on imaging is characteristic. Commonly causes DIABETES INSIPIDUS and growth failure in children, and it damages the hypothalamus, producing obesity and behavioural change that persist even after successful surgery.
the_other_sellar_masses.meningioma_germinoma_metastasis_lymphocy: Hypophysitis is increasingly seen with immune CHECKPOINT INHIBITORS and is an important modern cause of hypopituitarism — any patient on immunotherapy with fatigue and hyponatraemia needs pituitary function checked.
the_other_sellar_masses.empty_sella: Herniation of the subarachnoid space into the sella flattening the gland. Usually benign and incidental, but check pituitary function.
the_other_sellar_masses.sheehan_syndrome: Pituitary infarction from severe POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE. The classic first sign is FAILURE OF LACTATION, followed by amenorrhoea and the features of panhypopituitarism. It remains an important diagnosis wherever obstetric haemorrhage is common, and it is often diagnosed years late.

body.the_replacement_rule: When replacing multiple hormones, GIVE HYDROCORTISONE BEFORE LEVOTHYROXINE. Starting thyroxine first increases metabolic demand and can precipitate an adrenal crisis in someone with unrecognised ACTH deficiency. This ordering is essential and frequently got wrong.

warnings: In pituitary apoplexy, give hydrocortisone IMMEDIATELY on suspicion — before imaging and before results.
Give hydrocortisone BEFORE levothyroxine when replacing multiple hormones, or you may precipitate adrenal crisis.
A modestly raised prolactin with a large tumour is usually STALK EFFECT, not a prolactinoma. Treating it with cabergoline lets a non-functioning tumour grow.
A large tumour with an unexpectedly low prolactin may be the HOOK EFFECT — request a diluted sample.
Prolactinoma is treated MEDICALLY first. Operating first is an error.
Always check thyroid function in hyperprolactinaemia — primary hypothyroidism raises prolactin.
Drugs are the commonest cause of hyperprolactinaemia. Review antipsychotics, metoclopramide and domperidone.
Random growth hormone is useless — screen acromegaly with IGF-1 and confirm with an OGTT.
Failure of lactation after postpartum haemorrhage is Sheehan syndrome until proven otherwise.
Check pituitary function in any patient on checkpoint inhibitors with fatigue or hyponatraemia.
Formally assess visual fields in any sellar mass — bitemporal hemianopia is missed on casual confrontation.
limitations: Imaging protocols, surgical indications, dopamine agonist regimens and replacement doses are specialist-directed. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Why bitemporal hemianopia?
flashcards.a: The chiasm carries crossing nasal retinal fibres, which serve the temporal fields, and they are compressed first.

flashcards.q: Which pituitary tumour is treated medically first?
flashcards.a: Prolactinoma — dopamine agonists both suppress prolactin and shrink it.

flashcards.q: What is the stalk effect?
flashcards.a: Any sellar mass compressing the stalk interrupts dopamine inhibition, modestly raising prolactin. Not a prolactinoma.

flashcards.q: What is the hook effect?
flashcards.a: A very high prolactin saturates the assay and reads falsely low — request a dilution.

flashcards.q: How is acromegaly screened and confirmed?
flashcards.a: IGF-1 to screen; failure of GH suppression on OGTT to confirm.

flashcards.q: What kills in pituitary apoplexy?
flashcards.a: Acute adrenal insufficiency — give hydrocortisone on suspicion.

flashcards.q: Hydrocortisone or levothyroxine first?
flashcards.a: Hydrocortisone. Thyroxine first can precipitate adrenal crisis.

flashcards.q: First sign of Sheehan syndrome?
flashcards.a: Failure of lactation after postpartum haemorrhage.

flashcards.q: Which sellar mass classically calcifies?
flashcards.a: Craniopharyngioma.

checkboxes: Thyroid function and drug history checked in hyperprolactinaemia
Dilution requested if hook effect suspected
Hydrocortisone given on suspicion of apoplexy
Old photographs reviewed if acromegaly suspected

entries.title: Advanced Glycation End Products — How Sugar Damages Tissue
entries.summary: Glucose binds irreversibly to long-lived proteins, cross-links them, and makes tissue stiff and leaky. This is the mechanism behind diabetic microvascular disease — and it explains why damage continues even after glucose is controlled.

terms: advanced glycation end products — how sugar damages tissue

body.the_core_chemistry: Glucose reacts NON-ENZYMATICALLY with amino groups on proteins — no enzyme controls it, so the rate depends only on how much glucose is present and for how long. A reversible Schiff base forms, rearranges to a more stable Amadori product (HbA1c is exactly this, which is why HbA1c works as a measure), and over time undergoes irreversible reactions to form ADVANCED GLYCATION END PRODUCTS. This is the same Maillard reaction that browns food.
body.why_the_damage_is_selective: AGEs accumulate on LONG-LIVED proteins — collagen, elastin, crystallin, myelin, basement membrane. Short-lived proteins are replaced before significant glycation occurs. This is why diabetes damages the tissues it does: the retina, the glomerulus, peripheral nerves, arterial walls, the lens and skin all depend on proteins that last years.

the_two_ways_ages_cause_harm.direct_cross_linking: AGEs form covalent cross-links between collagen molecules. Cross-linked collagen is STIFFER and less able to be remodelled. Consequences: stiff arteries with widened pulse pressure and isolated systolic hypertension; thickened, leaky basement membranes; reduced myocardial compliance (diastolic dysfunction); stiff joints and limited joint mobility; and lens crystallin cross-linking contributing to cataract.
the_two_ways_ages_cause_harm.receptor_mediated: AGEs bind a receptor called RAGE on endothelium, macrophages and mesangial cells. This activates NF-κB and drives sustained INFLAMMATION, oxidative stress, adhesion molecule expression and growth factor release. This is the inflammatory, not merely mechanical, half of the story — and it is why diabetes is a pro-inflammatory vascular state.

the_companion_pathways.polyol: Excess glucose is shunted through ALDOSE REDUCTASE to SORBITOL. Sorbitol is osmotically active and poorly permeable, so it accumulates — this contributes to the osmotic swelling of the LENS (and the transient blurred vision when a patient with very high glucose is rapidly corrected) and to Schwann cell injury. The pathway also consumes NADPH, depleting glutathione and reducing antioxidant defence.
the_companion_pathways.hexosamine_and_pkc: Additional flux through the hexosamine pathway and activation of protein kinase C alter gene expression, increase VEGF (contributing to retinal neovascularisation) and endothelin, and reduce nitric oxide.

metabolic_memory.the_observation: A period of poor glycaemic control produces harm that persists for YEARS even after control is achieved — and, conversely, early good control confers protection that persists. This is called metabolic memory or the legacy effect.
metabolic_memory.the_explanation: AGE cross-links are essentially IRREVERSIBLE and turn over over years, and AGE-driven signalling produces lasting epigenetic changes. The damage does not reset when the HbA1c does.
metabolic_memory.why_this_changes_practice: It makes the case for EARLY and sustained control far stronger than a simple "current glucose" model would suggest. It also explains, without blaming the patient, why complications can still progress after control improves — a conversation that matters enormously for adherence and for trust.

body.the_clinical_correlates: Retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy are all microvascular consequences of this process. Poor wound healing, susceptibility to infection, tendon and joint stiffness (including the "prayer sign" of limited joint mobility), cataract, and accelerated atherosclerosis all follow from the same chemistry.
body.other_sources_of_ages: Not all AGEs are made internally. DIETARY AGEs are formed by high-temperature dry cooking — grilling, frying, roasting, browning. Boiling, steaming and stewing generate far fewer. SMOKING is also a significant exogenous source. These are modifiable and are rarely mentioned to patients.
body.why_this_belongs_in_a_clinical_reference: Because it converts a list of complications into a single mechanism a patient can understand: "sugar sticks to the long-lasting proteins in your eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels and makes them stiff, and that damage is slow to undo — which is why control now matters for years to come."

warnings: AGE cross-links are essentially irreversible. Damage accrued during poor control persists after control improves — this is metabolic memory, not patient failure.
Early sustained control matters disproportionately because of the legacy effect.
Rapid correction of very high glucose causes transient blurred vision through lens osmotic change — warn the patient, and do not prescribe new glasses until control is stable.
HbA1c is itself an Amadori product, so anything altering red cell lifespan invalidates it.
Diet and smoking are exogenous AGE sources. High-temperature dry cooking generates far more than boiling or steaming.
Screening for retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy is required regardless of current glucose, because the damage is cumulative.
limitations: Anti-AGE and aldose reductase inhibitor therapies remain largely investigational; no such treatment is standard care.

flashcards.q: What is an AGE?
flashcards.a: An advanced glycation end product — glucose irreversibly bound and cross-linked to long-lived proteins.

flashcards.q: Why are only some tissues damaged?
flashcards.a: AGEs accumulate on LONG-LIVED proteins — collagen, basement membrane, myelin, crystallin.

flashcards.q: What is HbA1c chemically?
flashcards.a: An Amadori product — the stable intermediate on the way to an AGE.

flashcards.q: Two mechanisms of AGE harm?
flashcards.a: Direct collagen cross-linking (stiffness), and RAGE receptor signalling driving inflammation.

flashcards.q: What does the polyol pathway produce, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: Sorbitol — osmotically active, causing lens swelling and Schwann cell injury, and it depletes NADPH.

flashcards.q: What is metabolic memory?
flashcards.a: Damage from past poor control persisting for years, because AGE cross-links are irreversible.

flashcards.q: Why does vision blur when high glucose is corrected quickly?
flashcards.a: Osmotic change in the lens from sorbitol accumulation and shift.

flashcards.q: Which cooking methods generate most dietary AGEs?
flashcards.a: High-temperature dry methods — grilling, frying, roasting. Boiling and steaming generate far fewer.

checkboxes: Mechanism explained to the patient in plain terms
Retinal, renal and neuropathy screening arranged regardless of current control
Patient warned about transient blurring on rapid correction

entries.title: Inflammatory Myopathies — Polymyositis and Dermatomyositis
entries.summary: PROXIMAL, symmetrical, PAINLESS weakness with a raised CK. Dermatomyositis adds pathognomonic skin signs — and, critically, carries a real underlying MALIGNANCY risk in adults, so the diagnosis obliges a cancer search.

the_core_picture.weakness: PROXIMAL and SYMMETRICAL — difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, lifting arms overhead, washing hair. It develops over WEEKS TO MONTHS. It is characteristically PAINLESS or only mildly achy; prominent pain should make you doubt the diagnosis and consider polymyalgia rheumatica, fibromyalgia or a drug cause.
the_core_picture.what_is_spared: Facial and ocular muscles are spared — involvement there suggests myasthenia instead. Sensation is normal and reflexes are preserved until late.
the_core_picture.the_dangerous_involvement: PHARYNGEAL and OESOPHAGEAL muscle weakness causes DYSPHAGIA and aspiration risk. RESPIRATORY muscle weakness causes ventilatory failure. Both are under-recognised and both change the urgency completely — ask about swallowing and monitor respiratory function.

the_skin_signs_of_dermatomyositis.pathognomonic: GOTTRON PAPULES — violaceous scaly papules over the EXTENSOR surfaces of the knuckles (MCPs, PIPs). HELIOTROPE RASH — violaceous discolouration of the upper eyelids with periorbital oedema.
the_skin_signs_of_dermatomyositis.the_discriminating_detail: Gottron papules sit OVER the knuckles. In lupus, the rash spares the knuckles and affects the skin BETWEEN them. That single distinction separates two conditions that otherwise overlap considerably, and it is checked by looking at the dorsum of the hand.
the_skin_signs_of_dermatomyositis.others: SHAWL SIGN and V-SIGN — photodistributed violaceous rash over the upper back/shoulders and anterior chest. MECHANIC HANDS — hyperkeratotic, cracked, fissured skin on the radial fingers, associated with antisynthetase syndrome. Nailfold capillary changes with dilated loops and dropout, and ragged cuticles. Calcinosis, especially in juvenile disease.
the_skin_signs_of_dermatomyositis.amyopathic_dermatomyositis: The rash occurs WITHOUT clinically apparent muscle disease. It still carries the malignancy and lung disease risk, so it must not be dismissed as a dermatological curiosity.

investigation.muscle_enzymes: CK is usually markedly raised — often in the thousands. It correlates roughly with activity but not reliably, and a normal CK does not exclude disease (particularly amyopathic dermatomyositis and late burnt-out disease). Aldolase, AST, ALT and LDH also rise from muscle; a raised "liver" transaminase from muscle is a classic misattribution.
investigation.antibodies: ANA is often positive. Myositis-specific antibodies carry real prognostic information: ANTI-JO-1 and the other antisynthetases predict INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE, arthritis, Raynaud and mechanic hands. ANTI-MDA5 predicts rapidly progressive, often amyopathic, ILD with a high mortality. ANTI-TIF1-γ and ANTI-NXP2 predict MALIGNANCY. ANTI-MI-2 predicts classic skin disease and a good response to treatment.
investigation.other: EMG shows a myopathic pattern with spontaneous activity. MRI identifies muscle oedema and guides biopsy. MUSCLE BIOPSY remains the definitive test — perimysial and perivascular inflammation with perifascicular atrophy in dermatomyositis; endomysial infiltrate invading non-necrotic fibres in polymyositis.

the_malignancy_association.the_rule: ADULT DERMATOMYOSITIS carries a substantially increased risk of underlying malignancy, greatest in the first few years after diagnosis. Polymyositis carries a smaller but real increase. This obliges an age- and sex-appropriate cancer search AT DIAGNOSIS and continued vigilance.
the_malignancy_association.which_cancers: Ovarian, lung, pancreatic, gastric, colorectal and lymphoma — and NASOPHARYNGEAL carcinoma is notably over-represented in South-East Asian and North African populations, which changes what should be examined.
the_malignancy_association.what_the_search_involves: Thorough history and examination including breast, pelvic, testicular and rectal; CT chest, abdomen and pelvis; age-appropriate screening; and specific consideration of ovarian malignancy in women. Anti-TIF1-γ positivity substantially raises the pre-test probability and should intensify the search.
the_malignancy_association.the_practical_point: Do not treat the muscle disease and forget the tumour. Treating the malignancy often improves the myositis.

the_impostors.inclusion_body_myositis: The great mimic in older patients — but it is ASYMMETRIC, involves DISTAL muscles (notably finger flexors and quadriceps), progresses SLOWLY over years, has a lower CK, and — importantly — RESPONDS POORLY OR NOT AT ALL to immunosuppression. A patient "failing" treatment for polymyositis should prompt reconsideration of IBM.
the_impostors.statin_myopathy: Common. Usually resolves on stopping. A small subset have an immune-mediated NECROTISING myopathy with anti-HMGCR antibodies that PERSISTS and worsens after the statin is stopped and needs immunosuppression.
the_impostors.others: Hypothyroidism (check TSH in every proximal myopathy — it is trivially treatable), Cushing syndrome and steroid myopathy, alcohol, hypokalaemia and hypophosphataemia, vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia, muscular dystrophies, polymyalgia rheumatica (pain and stiffness with a NORMAL CK), and viral myositis.

body.treatment_principles: Corticosteroids are first line, with a steroid-sparing agent introduced early. IVIG has a role, particularly with dysphagia. Rituximab and other agents for refractory disease. Physiotherapy is important, not optional. Skin disease needs photoprotection and topical therapy. Screen and monitor for interstitial lung disease with pulmonary function tests and high-resolution CT — the lungs, not the muscles, are often what determines prognosis.

warnings: Adult dermatomyositis obliges an age- and sex-appropriate malignancy search at diagnosis, with ongoing vigilance.
Gottron papules sit OVER the knuckles; lupus spares the knuckles and affects the skin between them.
Ask about swallowing and monitor respiratory function — dysphagia and ventilatory weakness are under-recognised and change urgency.
A normal CK does not exclude myositis, particularly amyopathic dermatomyositis.
Raised AST and ALT may come from MUSCLE, not liver. Check CK before investigating the liver.
Prominent PAIN argues against inflammatory myopathy — reconsider polymyalgia rheumatica, fibromyalgia or drugs.
Asymmetric, distal, slowly progressive weakness that fails immunosuppression is inclusion body myositis.
Anti-MDA5 predicts rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease with high mortality — treat as urgent.
Statin myopathy that persists after stopping the drug may be immune-mediated necrotising myopathy — check anti-HMGCR.
Check TSH in every proximal myopathy.
limitations: Immunosuppressive regimens, malignancy screening protocols and antibody panel availability are service-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Typical weakness pattern?
flashcards.a: Proximal, symmetrical, painless, developing over weeks to months.

flashcards.q: How do Gottron papules differ from lupus rash on the hand?
flashcards.a: Gottron sits OVER the knuckles; lupus spares knuckles and affects skin between them.

flashcards.q: What must be done at diagnosis in adult dermatomyositis?
flashcards.a: An age- and sex-appropriate malignancy search.

flashcards.q: Which antibody predicts malignancy?
flashcards.a: Anti-TIF1-γ (and anti-NXP2).

flashcards.q: Which antibody predicts rapidly progressive ILD?
flashcards.a: Anti-MDA5.

flashcards.q: Which antibodies predict interstitial lung disease and mechanic hands?
flashcards.a: Anti-Jo-1 and the other antisynthetases.

flashcards.q: Which mimic fails immunosuppression?
flashcards.a: Inclusion body myositis — asymmetric, distal, slow, lower CK.

flashcards.q: Which two functional questions change urgency?
flashcards.a: Swallowing (aspiration) and breathing (ventilatory failure).

checkboxes: ILD screened with PFTs and HRCT

entries.title: Systemic Sclerosis, Sjögren and the Connective Tissue Overlap
entries.summary: In systemic sclerosis the two things that kill are RENAL CRISIS and PULMONARY disease, and the antibody predicts which. In Sjögren the diagnosis is easy and the thing that gets missed is the lifelong LYMPHOMA risk.

terms: systemic sclerosis, sjögren and the connective tissue overlap

the_two_subsets.limited_cutaneous: Skin involvement DISTAL to elbows and knees, plus the face. Formerly CREST — Calcinosis, Raynaud, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia. Raynaud often precedes other features by YEARS. Associated with ANTI-CENTROMERE antibody. The major late risk is PULMONARY ARTERIAL HYPERTENSION.
the_two_subsets.diffuse_cutaneous: Skin involvement PROXIMAL to elbows and knees and on the trunk. Raynaud appears close to disease onset rather than years before. Associated with ANTI-SCL-70 (topoisomerase I) and ANTI-RNA POLYMERASE III. The major risks are INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE (Scl-70) and SCLERODERMA RENAL CRISIS (RNA polymerase III).
the_two_subsets.why_the_split_matters: It tells you what to screen for and how often. The antibody is not academic — it predicts the organ that will threaten the patient.

scleroderma_renal_crisis.what: Abrupt severe hypertension with rapidly progressive renal failure, and often microangiopathic haemolysis with fragmented red cells and thrombocytopenia.
scleroderma_renal_crisis.risk_factors: Early DIFFUSE disease, anti-RNA polymerase III, and — critically — CORTICOSTEROIDS. High-dose steroids PRECIPITATE renal crisis, which is why steroids are used cautiously and at the lowest possible dose in systemic sclerosis. This is a genuine and frequently forgotten prescribing hazard.
scleroderma_renal_crisis.treatment: ACE INHIBITORS, urgently and aggressively — this is the treatment that transformed the prognosis. Notably, ACE inhibitors are given even as creatinine rises, which is counterintuitive but correct here.
scleroderma_renal_crisis.the_paradox_worth_knowing: ACE inhibitors treat renal crisis but do NOT prevent it, and prophylactic use is not indicated.
scleroderma_renal_crisis.normotensive_crisis: A minority present without marked hypertension — do not exclude it on blood pressure alone if renal function is falling with haemolysis.

the_other_organ_involvement.lung: Interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension are now the leading causes of death. Screen with pulmonary function tests including transfer factor, HRCT, and echocardiography — annually, and regardless of symptoms, because breathlessness is attributed to deconditioning until late.
the_other_organ_involvement.gastrointestinal: Oesophageal dysmotility with severe reflux (and a real risk of Barrett oesophagus), gastroparesis, small bowel bacterial overgrowth causing bloating and malabsorption, and GAVE — "watermelon stomach" — causing iron deficiency anaemia.
the_other_organ_involvement.digital: Digital ulcers, pitting scars and critical ischaemia from Raynaud. These are painful, disabling and often under-treated.

systemic_sclerosis.raynaud_with_red_flags: Raynaud beginning after age 30, asymmetric, with digital ulcers, abnormal NAILFOLD CAPILLAROSCOPY (dilated loops and dropout) or a positive ANA is SECONDARY Raynaud and warrants a connective tissue disease workup. Nailfold capillaroscopy is cheap, quick and badly underused.

sjogren_syndrome.what: Autoimmune destruction of exocrine glands — chiefly lacrimal and salivary. Primary, or secondary to another connective tissue disease.
sjogren_syndrome.the_sicca_features: DRY EYES (gritty, foreign body sensation) and DRY MOUTH (difficulty swallowing dry food, needing water to speak, rapidly progressive DENTAL CARIES, oral candidiasis, parotid swelling). The dental destruction is often the most disabling consequence and is preventable with early dental involvement.
sjogren_syndrome.the_systemic_features_that_get_missed: Profound FATIGUE and arthralgia — often the dominant complaint. Also interstitial lung disease, RENAL TUBULAR ACIDOSIS type 1 (presenting as hypokalaemia, and sometimes as hypokalaemic paralysis), peripheral neuropathy including a small fibre and sensory ganglionopathy form, cutaneous vasculitis, and CONGENITAL HEART BLOCK in babies of anti-Ro positive mothers.
sjogren_syndrome.the_pregnancy_point: ANTI-RO and ANTI-LA cross the placenta and can cause NEONATAL LUPUS and irreversible CONGENITAL COMPLETE HEART BLOCK. Any anti-Ro positive woman planning pregnancy needs specialist obstetric input and fetal cardiac monitoring. This applies whether or not she has symptoms.
sjogren_syndrome.the_thing_that_must_not_be_missed: LYMPHOMA. Sjögren carries the highest lymphoma risk of any autoimmune disease — most commonly MALT lymphoma of the parotid. Warning signs: PERSISTENT or asymmetric parotid enlargement, new lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, a FALLING complement C4, a new or rising monoclonal band, and cryoglobulinaemia. Persistent unilateral parotid swelling in Sjögren must be imaged and biopsied, not observed.
sjogren_syndrome.diagnosis: ANTI-RO (SSA) and ANTI-LA (SSB), ANA, rheumatoid factor. SCHIRMER test for tear production, ocular staining score, unstimulated salivary flow, and labial salivary gland biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain.
sjogren_syndrome.management: Symptomatic — artificial tears, saliva substitutes, pilocarpine, meticulous DENTAL care and fluoride, and treating candidiasis. Hydroxychloroquine for fatigue and arthralgia. Immunosuppression for systemic involvement. Vigilance for lymphoma indefinitely.

body.mixed_connective_tissue_disease: Features of systemic sclerosis, lupus and myositis together with a HIGH-TITRE ANTI-U1-RNP antibody. Raynaud and puffy hands are typical early features. Pulmonary hypertension is the main cause of death, so it needs the same screening discipline as systemic sclerosis.

warnings: CORTICOSTEROIDS precipitate scleroderma renal crisis. Use the lowest possible dose in systemic sclerosis and consider the risk before prescribing.
Treat scleroderma renal crisis with ACE inhibitors urgently — even as creatinine rises. They do not prevent it, so prophylaxis is not indicated.
A minority of renal crises are normotensive. Do not exclude it on blood pressure alone.
Screen systemic sclerosis annually for ILD and pulmonary hypertension regardless of symptoms — they are now the leading causes of death.
Persistent or asymmetric parotid swelling in Sjögren needs imaging and biopsy — lymphoma risk is the highest of any autoimmune disease.
A falling C4 or a new monoclonal band in Sjögren is a lymphoma warning sign.
Anti-Ro crosses the placenta and can cause irreversible congenital complete heart block. Any anti-Ro positive woman planning pregnancy needs specialist input.
Sjögren causes type 1 renal tubular acidosis — think of it in unexplained hypokalaemia.
Raynaud starting after 30, asymmetric, or with ulcers or abnormal nailfold capillaries is SECONDARY — investigate.
Dental destruction in Sjögren is preventable. Refer early for dental care and fluoride.
limitations: Antibody availability, screening intervals and immunosuppressive regimens are service-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Limited vs diffuse systemic sclerosis?
flashcards.a: Limited: distal to elbows/knees, anti-centromere, pulmonary hypertension. Diffuse: proximal/trunk, Scl-70 or RNA pol III, ILD and renal crisis.

flashcards.q: Which drug class precipitates scleroderma renal crisis?
flashcards.a: Corticosteroids.

flashcards.q: Treatment of scleroderma renal crisis?
flashcards.a: ACE inhibitors urgently, continued even as creatinine rises.

flashcards.q: Which antibody predicts renal crisis?
flashcards.a: Anti-RNA polymerase III.

flashcards.q: What is the highest-stakes complication of Sjögren?
flashcards.a: Lymphoma — usually parotid MALT.

flashcards.q: Warning signs of lymphoma in Sjögren?
flashcards.a: Persistent or asymmetric parotid swelling, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, falling C4, new monoclonal band.

flashcards.q: Why does anti-Ro matter in pregnancy?
flashcards.a: It crosses the placenta and can cause irreversible congenital complete heart block.

flashcards.q: Which renal lesion does Sjögren cause?
flashcards.a: Type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis — presenting with hypokalaemia.

flashcards.q: Antibody in mixed connective tissue disease?
flashcards.a: High-titre anti-U1-RNP.

checkboxes: Annual PFTs with transfer factor and echocardiogram
Blood pressure monitored and renal crisis risk discussed
Steroid exposure minimised in systemic sclerosis

entries.title: Spondyloarthritis — Ankylosing Spondylitis, Reactive Arthritis and Takayasu
entries.summary: INFLAMMATORY back pain is the opposite of mechanical: it is worse with REST, better with movement, wakes the patient in the second half of the night, and comes with over 30 minutes of morning stiffness. That single history separates a treatable disease from years of dismissal.

terms: spondyloarthritis — ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis and takayasu

inflammatory_versus_mechanical_back_pain.why_this_is_the_whole_diagnosis: Ankylosing spondylitis is typically diagnosed YEARS after symptom onset, because the pain is dismissed as mechanical. The history distinguishes them reliably and costs nothing.
inflammatory_versus_mechanical_back_pain.inflammatory: Onset before age 45 · INSIDIOUS onset · lasts more than 3 months · MORNING STIFFNESS over 30 minutes · IMPROVES WITH EXERCISE and NOT with rest · WAKES the patient in the second half of the night · ALTERNATING buttock pain · dramatic response to NSAIDs.
inflammatory_versus_mechanical_back_pain.mechanical: Any age, often sudden onset, worse with activity, BETTER with rest, minimal morning stiffness, does not wake from sleep.
inflammatory_versus_mechanical_back_pain.the_single_most_useful_question: "Does it get better or worse when you rest?" Better with rest is mechanical. Worse with rest, better when moving, is inflammatory.

ankylosing_spondylitis.examination: Reduced lumbar flexion (SCHOBER TEST — mark 10 cm above and 5 cm below the posterior superior iliac spines; on full flexion the distance should increase by more than 5 cm). Reduced chest expansion from costovertebral involvement. Increased occiput-to-wall distance. Sacroiliac tenderness.
ankylosing_spondylitis.the_a_words_extra_articular: ANTERIOR UVEITIS (acute, unilateral, painful, photophobic red eye — a same-day ophthalmology referral, and it recurs) · AORTIC regurgitation and conduction block · APICAL pulmonary fibrosis · Amyloidosis (AA) · Achilles enthesitis · Atlantoaxial subluxation · IBD (about 5–10% overt, and subclinical gut inflammation in far more).
ankylosing_spondylitis.imaging: Plain films show sacroiliitis LATE — sclerosis, erosion, then fusion, and eventually the "BAMBOO SPINE" with syndesmophytes. MRI with STIR shows BONE MARROW OEDEMA at the sacroiliac joints EARLY, and is what allows diagnosis before irreversible change. Non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis is the same disease before the X-ray changes appear, and it is not a lesser disease.
ankylosing_spondylitis.hla_b27: Strongly associated but NOT diagnostic — it is common in the healthy population and many carriers never develop disease. It raises or lowers probability; it does not decide.
ankylosing_spondylitis.the_fracture_hazard: An ankylosed spine behaves like a LONG BONE. Even minor trauma can cause an unstable, often three-column, fracture — most commonly cervical — with a high risk of spinal cord injury. Any new neck or back pain after even trivial injury in an ankylosed patient needs CT, not reassurance and not plain films. This is one of the most consequential and most missed points in the condition.
ankylosing_spondylitis.management: EXERCISE and physiotherapy are foundational and disease-modifying in effect, not adjunctive. NSAIDs first line. Biologics (TNF and IL-17 inhibitors) for those failing NSAIDs. Conventional DMARDs such as methotrexate do NOT work for axial disease, though they may help peripheral arthritis. Smoking cessation, osteoporosis assessment and cardiovascular risk management.

reactive_arthritis.what: A sterile inflammatory arthritis 1–4 weeks AFTER an infection elsewhere. The joint is NOT infected — synovial fluid is sterile, which is the crucial distinction from septic arthritis.
reactive_arthritis.the_triggers: UROGENITAL — Chlamydia trachomatis. GASTROINTESTINAL — Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia.
reactive_arthritis.the_triad: Arthritis + urethritis + conjunctivitis — "cannot see, cannot pee, cannot climb a tree". The full triad occurs in a MINORITY; the absence of the triad does not exclude the diagnosis.
reactive_arthritis.other_features: Asymmetric oligoarthritis of the LOWER limbs, ENTHESITIS (especially Achilles and plantar fascia), DACTYLITIS ("sausage digit"), KERATODERMA BLENNORRHAGICUM on the soles, and CIRCINATE BALANITIS.
reactive_arthritis.the_essential_step: ALWAYS EXCLUDE SEPTIC ARTHRITIS FIRST by aspirating the joint. A hot swollen joint is septic until proven otherwise; getting this wrong destroys the joint within days.
reactive_arthritis.management: NSAIDs, intra-articular steroids once sepsis is excluded, treat any persisting chlamydial infection and trace contacts, and DMARDs for persistent disease. Most resolve within 6–12 months; a minority become chronic.
reactive_arthritis.the_name: Formerly Reiter syndrome; the eponym is now generally avoided because of the history of the person it honoured.

takayasu_arteritis.what: A LARGE-VESSEL granulomatous vasculitis of the AORTA and its major branches. Classically young ASIAN women under 40 — although it occurs in all populations, and that stereotype causes delayed diagnosis elsewhere.
takayasu_arteritis.why_it_is_called_pulseless_disease: Stenosis of the subclavian and other branches causes ABSENT or ASYMMETRIC pulses, BLOOD PRESSURE DIFFERENCES between arms, and BRUITS over the subclavian and carotid arteries.
takayasu_arteritis.the_two_phases: An early SYSTEMIC phase — fever, weight loss, fatigue, arthralgia, raised inflammatory markers — that is regularly mistaken for infection or malignancy. Then an OCCLUSIVE phase with limb claudication, dizziness, visual disturbance, stroke, renovascular hypertension and aortic regurgitation.
takayasu_arteritis.the_critical_measurement_error: If the subclavian artery is stenosed, the cuff blood pressure in that arm is FALSELY LOW. A patient can have severe hypertension recorded as normal. ALWAYS measure blood pressure in BOTH ARMS AND THE LEGS in suspected Takayasu — otherwise renovascular hypertension is missed and treated as normotension.
takayasu_arteritis.diagnosis: Imaging is the diagnosis — CT or MR angiography, and PET for disease activity. Inflammatory markers support but do not exclude; disease can progress with normal ESR and CRP, so imaging surveillance is needed.
takayasu_arteritis.management: Corticosteroids with steroid-sparing agents and biologics. Revascularisation only when inflammation is controlled, because intervening on an actively inflamed vessel has poor results.
takayasu_arteritis.the_contrast_with_giant_cell_arteritis: GCA affects the OVER-50s and involves cranial branches — headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual loss. Takayasu affects the UNDER-40s and involves the aorta and its proximal branches. Both are large-vessel granulomatous vasculitides and they overlap considerably in the middle.

warnings: A fused, ankylosed spine fractures like a long bone. Any new spinal pain after even minor trauma needs CT — not plain films, not reassurance.
Acute anterior uveitis needs same-day ophthalmology. It is painful, unilateral and recurrent.
Exclude SEPTIC arthritis by aspiration before diagnosing reactive arthritis. A hot joint is septic until proven otherwise.
Methotrexate does not work for AXIAL spondyloarthritis, though it may help peripheral joints.
HLA-B27 is not diagnostic — it is common in healthy people and many carriers never develop disease.
MRI shows sacroiliac marrow oedema years before plain films change. A normal X-ray does not exclude axial spondyloarthritis.
In Takayasu, measure blood pressure in BOTH arms and the legs — subclavian stenosis makes the cuff reading falsely low and hides severe hypertension.
Takayasu can progress with normal inflammatory markers. Use imaging surveillance, not ESR alone.
Ask the single question: is the back pain better or worse with rest? Worse with rest is inflammatory.
Screen spondyloarthritis patients for cardiovascular risk and osteoporosis — both are increased.
limitations: Classification criteria, biologic eligibility and imaging protocols are guideline- and service-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: How does inflammatory back pain differ from mechanical?
flashcards.a: Worse with rest, better with movement, wakes in the second half of the night, over 30 minutes of morning stiffness.

flashcards.q: What is the Schober test?
flashcards.a: Marks 10 cm above and 5 cm below the PSIS; flexion should increase the distance by more than 5 cm.

flashcards.q: Name the extra-articular "A"s of ankylosing spondylitis.
flashcards.a: Anterior uveitis, aortic regurgitation, apical fibrosis, amyloidosis, Achilles enthesitis, atlantoaxial subluxation.

flashcards.q: Why is minor trauma dangerous in ankylosing spondylitis?
flashcards.a: The fused spine acts like a long bone — unstable fractures with cord injury risk. CT, not plain films.

flashcards.q: What must be excluded before diagnosing reactive arthritis?
flashcards.a: Septic arthritis — aspirate the joint.

flashcards.q: Triggers for reactive arthritis?
flashcards.a: Chlamydia urogenitally; Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia enterically.

flashcards.q: Why is Takayasu called pulseless disease?
flashcards.a: Subclavian and branch stenosis causes absent or asymmetric pulses and BP differences.

flashcards.q: What measurement error hides hypertension in Takayasu?
flashcards.a: Subclavian stenosis makes the arm cuff read falsely low — measure both arms and the legs.

flashcards.q: Takayasu vs giant cell arteritis?
flashcards.a: Takayasu under 40, aorta and proximal branches. GCA over 50, cranial branches.

checkboxes: MRI sacroiliac joints if films normal
Joint aspirated before diagnosing reactive arthritis
Blood pressure in both arms and legs if Takayasu suspected
CT for any new spinal pain in an ankylosed spine
Cardiovascular risk and bone health assessed

entries.title: ADPKD, HIV Kidney Disease and Dialysis
entries.summary: ADPKD is not just a kidney disease — the BERRY ANEURYSMS are what kill unexpectedly. HIVAN presents with heavy proteinuria and is treated with antiretrovirals, not immunosuppression. And in dialysis the emergency is always potassium.

terms: adpkd, hiv kidney disease and dialysis

adpkd.genetics: Autosomal dominant. PKD1 (about 85%) causes earlier and more severe disease with end-stage failure typically in the 50s. PKD2 is milder with failure in the 70s. A negative family history does NOT exclude it — de novo mutations and mild parental disease are both common.
adpkd.presentation: Often silent for decades. HYPERTENSION frequently appears BEFORE any fall in renal function and is the earliest treatable finding. Then FLANK or abdominal PAIN, HAEMATURIA (from cyst haemorrhage), recurrent urinary and cyst INFECTIONS, NEPHROLITHIASIS, palpable enlarged kidneys, and progressive renal failure.

the_extra_renal_disease_that_matters_mos.intracranial_aneurysms: Berry aneurysms occur in roughly 5–10%, higher with a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid haemorrhage. RUPTURE IS THE FEARED EVENT and it can be the presenting feature. SCREENING with MR angiography is offered to those with a FAMILY HISTORY of aneurysm or haemorrhage, those in high-risk occupations, and before major elective surgery — not universally. Any ADPKD patient with a thunderclap headache must be treated as subarachnoid haemorrhage until excluded.
the_extra_renal_disease_that_matters_mos.others: Hepatic cysts (very common, rarely cause dysfunction, but can cause massive painful hepatomegaly especially in women and with oestrogen exposure), pancreatic and seminal vesicle cysts, MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE and other valve disease, colonic diverticulosis, and abdominal wall and inguinal hernias.

adpkd.management: Rigorous BLOOD PRESSURE control (the single most effective intervention), generous fluid intake to suppress vasopressin, avoiding nephrotoxics, treating infections with LIPID-SOLUBLE antibiotics that penetrate cysts (fluoroquinolones, co-trimoxazole — many antibiotics do not enter cysts and treatment fails for that reason), and TOLVAPTAN to slow progression in selected patients with rapidly progressive disease. Genetic counselling for the family.
adpkd.the_counselling_point: Children of an affected parent have a 50% risk. Testing before adulthood is generally avoided because there is no intervention in childhood and it affects insurance and psychology — but hypertension screening should still happen.

hivan.what: HIV-associated nephropathy — a COLLAPSING form of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.
hivan.who: Strongly associated with APOL1 risk variants, so it occurs overwhelmingly in people of West African ancestry. It is a disease of ADVANCED, untreated HIV with a low CD4 count.
hivan.presentation: HEAVY, often nephrotic-range PROTEINURIA with rapidly progressive renal failure. Distinctively, the kidneys are often LARGE and ECHOGENIC on ultrasound and the patient is frequently NORMOTENSIVE despite severe renal impairment — both unusual for advanced kidney disease and both useful clues.
hivan.treatment: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY is the treatment — it is the intervention that changes outcome. Add ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria. This is a case where the "kidney" answer is to treat the virus.

hiv_and_the_kidney.the_other_hiv_kidney_problems: Drug nephrotoxicity — TENOFOVIR disoproxil causing proximal tubulopathy and a Fanconi picture (check phosphate and glycosuria with a normal blood glucose), and crystal nephropathy with some agents. Immune complex disease, thrombotic microangiopathy, and the high burden of conventional diabetic and hypertensive kidney disease in an ageing HIV-positive population.

iris.what: IMMUNE RECONSTITUTION INFLAMMATORY SYNDROME — a paradoxical clinical DETERIORATION after starting antiretroviral therapy, as the recovering immune system mounts a response against an existing (often subclinical) infection.
iris.when: Typically within weeks to a few months of starting ART, in those with a LOW baseline CD4 and a high viral load.
iris.the_classic_scenarios: Worsening TUBERCULOSIS with enlarging nodes and fever, CRYPTOCOCCAL meningitis with rising intracranial pressure, worsening PML, CMV retinitis, and hepatitis flares.
iris.the_critical_management_principle: IRIS is NOT treatment failure and is NOT usually a reason to stop antiretroviral therapy. Treat the underlying opportunistic infection, add corticosteroids where indicated (notably in TB-IRIS), and continue ART. Stopping ART because the patient got worse is the intuitive response and it is generally wrong.
iris.prevention: Treat the opportunistic infection FIRST and time ART initiation appropriately — this matters especially in cryptococcal meningitis, where starting ART too early increases mortality.

dialysis.indications_aeiou: ACIDOSIS (severe, refractory) · ELECTROLYTES (refractory HYPERKALAEMIA — the commonest true emergency indication) · INTOXICATION (dialysable poisons: salicylate, lithium, toxic alcohols, metformin) · OVERLOAD (refractory pulmonary oedema) · URAEMIA (pericarditis, encephalopathy, unexplained bleeding from platelet dysfunction). Uraemic PERICARDITIS and ENCEPHALOPATHY are absolute indications and are frequently under-recognised.

haemodialysis.access: An ARTERIOVENOUS FISTULA is the best long-term access — lowest infection and thrombosis rates — but needs weeks to months to mature, so it must be planned ahead. Tunnelled catheters carry high infection risk.
haemodialysis.the_arm_rule: PROTECT THE NON-DOMINANT ARM (or the planned fistula arm) in anyone with advancing chronic kidney disease — no cannulas, no venepuncture, no blood pressure cuffs, no PICC lines. Damaging those veins destroys future access. Ward staff do this routinely without knowing, and it has lifelong consequences.
haemodialysis.complications: Intradialytic HYPOTENSION (commonest), cramps, arrhythmia, DISEQUILIBRIUM SYNDROME (cerebral oedema from too-rapid urea clearance in a first session — prevented by short gentle initial sessions), access infection and thrombosis, steal syndrome, and amyloidosis long term.

peritoneal_dialysis.advantages: Home-based, preserves residual renal function longer, avoids needling, gentler haemodynamically, and does not require reliable electricity or a dialysis unit — a genuine practical advantage in many settings.
peritoneal_dialysis.the_defining_complication: PERITONITIS. A CLOUDY BAG is peritonitis until proven otherwise — send the fluid for cell count and culture and start intraperitoneal antibiotics. Abdominal pain may be mild and fever may be absent, so the bag appearance is the trigger, not the symptoms. Recurrent peritonitis leads to membrane failure and loss of the modality.
peritoneal_dialysis.others: Exit-site infection, hernias, fluid leaks, encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis (rare, late, serious), and glucose absorption worsening diabetic control and causing weight gain.

dialysis.what_dialysis_does_not_do: It replaces only the clearance and fluid functions. It does NOT replace erythropoietin (hence anaemia needing ESAs and iron), vitamin D activation (hence renal bone disease), or the endocrine functions. Patients need those managed separately, and their cardiovascular mortality remains very high.
dialysis.transplantation: The best treatment for suitable patients — better survival and quality of life than dialysis. PRE-EMPTIVE transplantation before dialysis starts has the best outcomes, which is another reason to plan early. Live donation and the immunosuppression burden need frank discussion.
dialysis.conservative_management: A legitimate, actively chosen pathway — not "no treatment". In frail elderly patients with multiple comorbidities, dialysis may not extend life and may reduce its quality. This conversation should happen early, honestly, and repeatedly.

warnings: A thunderclap headache in ADPKD is subarachnoid haemorrhage until excluded — berry aneurysms are the feared complication.
Screen for intracranial aneurysms in ADPKD with a family history of aneurysm or haemorrhage — not universally.
Many antibiotics do not penetrate cysts. Use lipid-soluble agents for cyst infection or treatment fails.
A negative family history does not exclude ADPKD.
PROTECT the fistula arm in advancing CKD — no cannulas, cuffs or venepuncture. Damage there costs future access.
A CLOUDY peritoneal dialysis bag is peritonitis until proven otherwise, even without pain or fever.
HIVAN is treated with ANTIRETROVIRALS. Suspect it with heavy proteinuria, large echogenic kidneys and a normal blood pressure.
IRIS is not treatment failure. Do not stop antiretroviral therapy — treat the opportunistic infection and add steroids where indicated.
Starting ART too early in cryptococcal meningitis increases mortality — treat the infection first.
Uraemic pericarditis and encephalopathy are absolute dialysis indications and are frequently under-recognised.
Avoid rapid urea clearance in a first dialysis session — disequilibrium syndrome causes cerebral oedema.
Check phosphate and for glycosuria with normal blood glucose in patients on tenofovir — proximal tubulopathy.
limitations: Dialysis prescriptions, tolvaptan eligibility, aneurysm screening intervals and ART timing are protocol-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Which extra-renal ADPKD feature is most feared?
flashcards.a: Intracranial berry aneurysm rupture.

flashcards.q: Who is screened for aneurysms in ADPKD?
flashcards.a: Those with a family history of aneurysm or SAH, high-risk occupations, or before major elective surgery.

flashcards.q: Why do cyst infections fail standard antibiotics?
flashcards.a: Most antibiotics do not penetrate cysts — lipid-soluble agents are needed.

flashcards.q: What clues suggest HIVAN?
flashcards.a: Heavy proteinuria, LARGE echogenic kidneys, often normotensive, advanced untreated HIV, West African ancestry.

flashcards.q: Treatment of HIVAN?
flashcards.a: Antiretroviral therapy, plus ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria.

flashcards.q: What is IRIS and what should you NOT do?
flashcards.a: Paradoxical worsening after starting ART. Do not stop ART — treat the infection.

flashcards.q: Recite AEIOU.
flashcards.a: Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalaemia), Intoxication, Overload, Uraemia.

flashcards.q: What does a cloudy PD bag mean?
flashcards.a: Peritonitis until proven otherwise — send for cell count and culture.

flashcards.q: Why protect the non-dominant arm in CKD?
flashcards.a: To preserve veins for a future arteriovenous fistula.

flashcards.q: What does dialysis NOT replace?
flashcards.a: Erythropoietin and vitamin D activation — anaemia and renal bone disease need separate management.

checkboxes: Family history and blood pressure recorded in ADPKD
Fistula arm protected and documented at the bedside
PD bag clarity checked at every exchange
HIV status and CD4 known in unexplained heavy proteinuria
Transplant and conservative pathways discussed early

entries.title: Describing a Skin Lesion — The Vocabulary That Makes a Referral Useful
entries.summary: Dermatology is unusable without the nouns. A macule is FLAT, a papule is RAISED and small, a plaque is RAISED and broad, a vesicle holds clear fluid. Get the noun right and the differential writes itself; get it wrong and no referral can help you.

terms: describing a skin lesion — the vocabulary that makes a referral useful

primary_lesions_flat.macule: FLAT, impalpable, colour change, LESS than about 1 cm. Examples: freckle, early viral exanthem, vitiligo (depigmented macule).
primary_lesions_flat.patch: The same but LARGER than about 1 cm.

primary_lesions_raised_solid.papule: RAISED, solid, LESS than about 1 cm. Examples: acne, molluscum, lichen planus.
primary_lesions_raised_solid.plaque: RAISED, solid, FLAT-TOPPED, BROADER than about 1 cm — often described as a papule that has spread laterally. The classic example is psoriasis.
primary_lesions_raised_solid.nodule: RAISED, solid, DEEPER and larger than a papule, involving dermis or subcutis. Examples: basal cell carcinoma, erythema nodosum.
primary_lesions_raised_solid.wheal: A transient, oedematous, raised lesion with a pale centre and red flare. The defining feature is that an individual wheal lasts LESS THAN 24 HOURS and leaves no mark. If individual lesions persist beyond a day or bruise as they fade, that is URTICARIAL VASCULITIS, not urticaria, and it needs investigation.

primary_lesions_fluid_filled.vesicle: Raised, containing CLEAR fluid, LESS than about 0.5 cm. Herpes simplex, chickenpox, acute eczema.
primary_lesions_fluid_filled.bulla: The same but LARGER — a blister. Bullous pemphigoid, burns, bullous impetigo.
primary_lesions_fluid_filled.pustule: Contains PUS. Not necessarily infected — pustular psoriasis and acne are sterile.
primary_lesions_fluid_filled.cyst: A closed sac with a lining, containing fluid or semisolid material.

secondary_lesions.scale: Accumulation of stratum corneum. Psoriasis (thick, silvery), fungal infection, eczema.
secondary_lesions.crust: DRIED EXUDATE — serum, pus or blood. Impetigo classically gives a golden crust. Crust is not scale, and confusing them changes the differential entirely.
secondary_lesions.erosion: Loss of EPIDERMIS ONLY. Heals WITHOUT scarring.
secondary_lesions.ulcer: Loss extending into DERMIS or deeper. Heals WITH a scar. This distinction determines prognosis and is the reason the words are not interchangeable.
secondary_lesions.fissure: A linear split through the epidermis into the dermis.
secondary_lesions.lichenification: THICKENED skin with EXAGGERATED skin markings, from chronic rubbing. It is evidence of chronicity and of scratching.
secondary_lesions.excoriation: A scratch mark — evidence that the lesion itches, which is diagnostic information in itself.
secondary_lesions.atrophy: Thinning. Commonly from potent topical steroid — look for it wherever steroids have been used long term, especially on the face and flexures.

vascular_lesions_and_the_single_most_imp.blanching: PRESS A GLASS OR FINGER OVER IT. Erythema from vasodilatation BLANCHES. Blood OUTSIDE the vessels does NOT.
vascular_lesions_and_the_single_most_imp.petechiae: NON-blanching, less than about 3 mm. Pinpoint.
vascular_lesions_and_the_single_most_imp.why_this_matters_more_than_anything_else: A NON-BLANCHING rash in an unwell, febrile patient is MENINGOCOCCAL SEPSIS until proven otherwise, and demands immediate antibiotics — not a dermatological opinion. The glass test is the highest-value two-second examination in medicine. It also separates vasculitis and thrombocytopenia from simple erythema.
vascular_lesions_and_the_single_most_imp.telangiectasia: Visible dilated small vessels — these DO blanch. Seen in rosacea, systemic sclerosis, basal cell carcinoma and after topical steroid.

configuration_and_distribution.why_it_matters: The SHAPE and the SITE often narrow the diagnosis faster than the lesion type.
configuration_and_distribution.patterns: ANNULAR (ring — tinea, granuloma annulare) · TARGET/iris (erythema multiforme) · LINEAR (contact, Koebner, Blaschko lines) · GROUPED/herpetiform (herpes simplex) · DERMATOMAL (shingles — and it does NOT cross the midline) · RETICULATE/net-like (livedo) · SERPIGINOUS (larva migrans).
configuration_and_distribution.distribution: EXTENSOR surfaces (psoriasis) versus FLEXURAL (atopic eczema) is a classic discriminator. PHOTODISTRIBUTED — face, V of neck, dorsum of hands, sparing under the chin and behind the ears — points to a photosensitive cause and is easily missed if you do not look at the spared areas.
configuration_and_distribution.koebner_phenomenon: New lesions appearing in a line of TRAUMA — a scratch, a scar. Occurs in psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo and viral warts.
configuration_and_distribution.nikolsky_sign: Gentle lateral pressure on apparently normal skin causes the epidermis to SHEAR OFF. Positive in pemphigus, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis — all of which are serious.

describing_across_skin_tones.the_essential_correction: Almost all classic descriptions were written for pale skin, and "erythema" is the least reliable sign on darker skin. Redness may be invisible, or appear VIOLACEOUS, GREY, or simply DARKER than surrounding skin.
describing_across_skin_tones.what_to_rely_on_instead: TEXTURE and PALPATION — warmth, induration, scale, swelling. Compare with the patient own uninvolved skin rather than with an expected colour. Use oblique/raking light to reveal texture. Look at mucosae, palms, soles and nail beds.
describing_across_skin_tones.the_common_consequences_of_getting_this_: Cellulitis, and the severity of erythroderma, drug eruptions and burns, are all systematically UNDER-diagnosed on darker skin. POST-INFLAMMATORY HYPER- and HYPOpigmentation are far more prominent and more distressing on darker skin and should be discussed and treated as part of the condition, not dismissed.

body.what_a_useful_description_contains: Site and distribution · number · size · morphology (the correct noun) · colour · border (well or ill defined) · surface (scale, crust, erosion) · palpation (warm, indurated, tender) · blanching · configuration · associated changes in hair, nails and mucosae · and whether it itches.

warnings: A NON-BLANCHING rash in an unwell febrile patient is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise. Give antibiotics; do not wait for a dermatology opinion.
Erythema is unreliable on darker skin. Use texture, palpation, oblique light and comparison with the patient own uninvolved skin.
Individual wheals lasting more than 24 hours or leaving bruising is urticarial VASCULITIS, not urticaria — investigate.
Erosion heals without scarring; ulcer heals with a scar. The words are not interchangeable.
Crust is dried exudate; scale is stratum corneum. Confusing them changes the differential.
A positive Nikolsky sign indicates pemphigus, SSSS or TEN — all serious.
Skin atrophy and telangiectasia suggest topical steroid overuse — look for it, especially on face and flexures.
Shingles does not cross the midline. A "dermatomal" rash that crosses it is something else.
Post-inflammatory pigment change is a major outcome on darker skin. Address it rather than dismissing it.
limitations: Size thresholds (0.5 cm, 1 cm) vary slightly between texts; the principle of flat versus raised versus fluid-filled does not.

flashcards.q: Macule vs papule vs plaque?
flashcards.a: Macule flat; papule raised and small; plaque raised, flat-topped and broad.

flashcards.q: Vesicle vs bulla?
flashcards.a: Both clear fluid — vesicle under about 0.5 cm, bulla larger.

flashcards.q: Erosion vs ulcer?
flashcards.a: Erosion is epidermis only and heals without scar; ulcer reaches dermis and scars.

flashcards.q: What does the glass test distinguish?
flashcards.a: Blanching erythema (vasodilatation) from non-blanching purpura (blood outside vessels).

flashcards.q: Non-blanching rash in a febrile unwell patient?
flashcards.a: Meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise — antibiotics now.

flashcards.q: Wheal lasting more than 24 hours?
flashcards.a: Urticarial vasculitis, not urticaria.

flashcards.q: What is the Koebner phenomenon?
flashcards.a: New lesions along a line of trauma — psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo, warts.

flashcards.q: What is Nikolsky sign?
flashcards.a: Epidermis shears off with lateral pressure — pemphigus, SSSS, TEN.

flashcards.q: What replaces "erythema" on darker skin?
flashcards.a: Texture, induration, warmth, oblique light, and comparison with the patient own skin.

checkboxes: Photograph taken with consent where useful

entries.title: Skin Structure, Its Cells, and Blaschko Lines
entries.summary: Four cell types in the epidermis do four jobs — barrier, pigment, immunity, touch — and each gives rise to its own tumour and its own disease. Blaschko lines are the developmental map that explains why some rashes appear in bizarre streaks.

terms: skin structure, its cells, and blaschko lines

the_layers.epidermis: Stratified squamous epithelium, avascular, nourished by diffusion. From deep to superficial: BASALE (the dividing layer) → SPINOSUM → GRANULOSUM → (LUCIDUM, only in palms and soles) → CORNEUM (the dead, keratinised barrier). Turnover takes about 4 weeks — and in PSORIASIS this accelerates to a few days, which is why the corneum accumulates as thick silvery scale.
the_layers.dermis: PAPILLARY (superficial, fine collagen, capillary loops) and RETICULAR (deep, thick collagen and elastin). Contains vessels, nerves, and the adnexa — hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands. It provides strength (collagen) and recoil (elastin). Loss of elastin and collagen cross-linking is what ageing and photodamage look like.
the_layers.the_basement_membrane_zone: The junction anchoring epidermis to dermis. Its importance is that the LEVEL of separation determines the disease: split ABOVE it (intraepidermal, between keratinocytes) gives PEMPHIGUS with flaccid, fragile blisters that rupture; split AT it (subepidermal) gives BULLOUS PEMPHIGOID with tense, more durable blisters. One anatomical fact explains the entire clinical difference.

the_four_epidermal_cells.keratinocyte: About 90–95%. Makes keratin and the barrier. Gives rise to SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA and (from the basal layer) BASAL CELL CARCINOMA. Genetic defects in its structural proteins cause the ichthyoses and epidermolysis bullosa simplex.

melanocyte.what: In the basal layer. Makes MELANIN in melanosomes and transfers it to surrounding keratinocytes, where it caps the nucleus and shields DNA from ultraviolet damage.
melanocyte.the_crucial_fact: The NUMBER of melanocytes is broadly SIMILAR across all human populations. Skin colour differs because of the AMOUNT, TYPE and PACKAGING of melanin produced and how it is distributed — not because of how many melanocytes there are. This single fact corrects a widespread misconception and explains why vitiligo, albinism and melanoma occur in everyone.
melanocyte.diseases: VITILIGO (autoimmune destruction), ALBINISM (functional enzyme defect with normal cell numbers), MELASMA (overactivity), and MELANOMA (malignancy).

langerhans_cell.what: A DENDRITIC ANTIGEN-PRESENTING cell in the stratum spinosum — the immune sentinel of the skin. It samples antigen, migrates to lymph nodes and presents to T cells.
langerhans_cell.why_it_matters_clinically: It is the cell that makes ALLERGIC CONTACT DERMATITIS possible — a type IV delayed hypersensitivity requiring sensitisation then re-exposure. It is also depleted by ultraviolet light, which is part of why UV is immunosuppressive to the skin and why phototherapy works. Its proliferative disorder is LANGERHANS CELL HISTIOCYTOSIS.

the_four_epidermal_cells.merkel_cell: A mechanoreceptor for light touch, sitting in the basal layer. Its malignancy is MERKEL CELL CARCINOMA — rare, aggressive, associated with Merkel cell polyomavirus and immunosuppression, and often mistaken for a benign cyst until it grows rapidly.

body.the_immune_cells_of_the_skin: Resident memory T cells persist in skin long term and drive recurrent, site-specific disease such as FIXED DRUG ERUPTION — which is why the same patch reappears in the same place each time the drug is taken. Regulatory T cells maintain tolerance; their failure contributes to psoriasis and eczema. Mast cells in the dermis drive urticaria and immediate hypersensitivity.

blaschko_lines.what_they_are: The lines along which EMBRYONIC SKIN CELLS MIGRATED during development. They form V-shapes over the spine, S-shapes on the abdomen, and whorls and streaks on the limbs. They are NOT dermatomes (which follow nerves), NOT Langer lines (which follow collagen tension), and NOT lymphatic drainage.
blaschko_lines.why_a_rash_follows_them: Because they trace CLONES of cells derived from a common ancestor. A rash following Blaschko lines implies MOSAICISM — a population of genetically distinct cells arising from a post-zygotic mutation, or X-inactivation in females (LYONISATION) for an X-linked gene. This is why the pattern is a genuine diagnostic clue and not a curiosity: it tells you the disease is genetic and mosaic.
blaschko_lines.conditions_that_follow_them: Incontinentia pigmenti (X-linked, in females), epidermal naevi, hypomelanosis of Ito, linear lichen planus, linear psoriasis, lichen striatus, and some forms of chimerism.
