blaschko_lines.the_practical_takeaway: If a rash is in bizarre streaks, whorls or a V over the back that respect the midline, think Blaschko and think mosaicism — and, in a female infant with vesicles in streaks, think incontinentia pigmenti and examine the eyes, teeth and CNS.

body.why_all_this_earns_its_place: Each structure predicts a disease. Split above the basement membrane and you get pemphigus; below it, pemphigoid. Destroy melanocytes and you get vitiligo; disable their enzyme and you get albinism. Sensitise Langerhans cells and you get contact dermatitis. Follow the embryonic migration lines and you are looking at a mosaic genetic disease.

warnings: Melanocyte NUMBER is similar across populations — skin colour reflects melanin amount and packaging. This corrects a common misconception.
The level of blister split determines the disease: intraepidermal (pemphigus, flaccid) versus subepidermal (pemphigoid, tense).
Blaschko lines are not dermatomes. A rash following them implies genetic mosaicism and warrants a genetic assessment.
A female infant with vesicles in Blaschko streaks may have incontinentia pigmenti — examine eyes, teeth and CNS.
Merkel cell carcinoma is aggressive and is often mistaken for a benign cyst. Rapid growth in an immunosuppressed or elderly patient warrants urgent biopsy.
Chronic potent topical steroid thins the dermis irreversibly. Recognise atrophy and telangiectasia early.
limitations: A structural and cellular overview; it does not replace histopathological diagnosis.

flashcards.q: Name the four epidermal cell types and their jobs.
flashcards.a: Keratinocyte (barrier), melanocyte (pigment), Langerhans cell (immunity), Merkel cell (touch).

flashcards.q: Why do people differ in skin colour?
flashcards.a: Melanin amount, type and packaging — not melanocyte number, which is broadly similar.

flashcards.q: Pemphigus vs pemphigoid anatomically?
flashcards.a: Pemphigus splits intraepidermally (flaccid blisters); pemphigoid splits subepidermally (tense blisters).

flashcards.q: Which cell causes allergic contact dermatitis?
flashcards.a: The Langerhans cell — antigen presentation driving type IV hypersensitivity.

flashcards.q: What are Blaschko lines?
flashcards.a: The paths of embryonic skin cell migration — V on the back, S on the abdomen, whorls on limbs.

flashcards.q: What does a rash following Blaschko lines imply?
flashcards.a: Genetic mosaicism — post-zygotic mutation or X-inactivation.

flashcards.q: Why is psoriasis scaly?
flashcards.a: Epidermal turnover accelerates from about 4 weeks to a few days, so stratum corneum accumulates.

flashcards.q: Which carcinoma arises from a touch receptor?
flashcards.a: Merkel cell carcinoma — aggressive, polyomavirus-associated.

checkboxes: Blister level considered when a bullous disease is suspected
Blaschko distribution recognised and mosaicism considered
Rapidly growing nodule biopsied rather than observed

entries.title: Pigment Disorders — Vitiligo, Albinism, Melasma and Acanthosis Nigricans
entries.summary: Vitiligo DESTROYS melanocytes; albinism leaves them present but unable to make pigment; melasma makes them overactive. Acanthosis nigricans is not really a pigment disorder at all — it is a visible marker of insulin resistance, and occasionally of an internal cancer.

terms: pigment disorders — vitiligo, albinism, melasma and acanthosis nigricans

the_first_distinction.depigmented: COMPLETE loss of pigment — chalk or milk white, and it glows bright white under a WOOD LAMP. Vitiligo.
the_first_distinction.hypopigmented: REDUCED but not absent pigment — off-white or paler than surrounding skin. Post-inflammatory change, pityriasis alba, pityriasis versicolor, leprosy.
the_first_distinction.why_it_matters: Depigmented versus hypopigmented immediately splits the differential, and a Wood lamp — cheap and quick — makes the distinction reliably, especially on lighter skin where it can be hard to judge by eye.

vitiligo.what: AUTOIMMUNE destruction of melanocytes. Well-demarcated, completely DEPIGMENTED macules and patches, often symmetrical, favouring the face (especially periorificial), hands, elbows, knees, genitals, and areas of trauma (KOEBNER phenomenon). Hair within a patch may turn white (leukotrichia), which predicts poorer repigmentation.
vitiligo.the_associations_to_screen_for: It is an autoimmune disease and it travels with others — AUTOIMMUNE THYROID DISEASE above all (check TSH in everyone), type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, Addison disease and alopecia areata.
vitiligo.the_part_that_is_usually_neglected: The PSYCHOLOGICAL impact is severe and is routinely underestimated by clinicians, particularly in patients with darker skin where the contrast is stark, and in cultures where it carries stigma or is confused with leprosy. Depression, social withdrawal and effects on marriage prospects are real and documented. Ask about it. Treating the skin without acknowledging this misses most of what the disease does.
vitiligo.management: Photoprotection is essential — depigmented skin has NO melanin protection and burns readily and is at risk of UV damage. Topical steroids and calcineurin inhibitors, phototherapy (narrowband UVB), and newer JAK inhibitors. Camouflage cosmetics are genuinely valuable and should be offered, not treated as trivial. Facial and recent lesions respond best; hands and feet respond worst.

albinism.what: An inherited defect in melanin SYNTHESIS. Melanocytes are PRESENT IN NORMAL NUMBERS — they simply cannot make pigment. Most commonly a tyrosinase pathway defect. Oculocutaneous albinism affects skin, hair and eyes; ocular albinism affects mainly the eyes.
albinism.the_eye_involvement_that_is_always_prese: This is NOT a cosmetic condition. Melanin is required for normal development of the retina and the optic pathways, so albinism ALWAYS involves the eyes: NYSTAGMUS, reduced visual acuity, FOVEAL HYPOPLASIA, photophobia, iris transillumination, and MISROUTING of optic nerve fibres at the chiasm. Every person with albinism needs ophthalmological assessment and low-vision support, and children need it early for schooling.
albinism.the_life_threatening_issue: Extremely high risk of SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA and other skin cancers from a young age, because there is no melanin protection at all. In high-UV regions this is a leading cause of premature death in people with albinism. Rigorous, practical, lifelong SUN PROTECTION and regular skin surveillance are the interventions that save lives — and they must be affordable and actually available to be useful.
albinism.the_social_dimension: In parts of sub-Saharan Africa people with albinism face severe stigma, discrimination and, in some regions, targeted violence rooted in harmful superstition. Clinicians should be aware of this, ask about safety, and connect families with advocacy and support organisations. It is part of the care, not outside it.
albinism.syndromic_forms: Hermansky-Pudlak (albinism with a BLEEDING diathesis from platelet storage pool deficiency, and pulmonary fibrosis) and Chediak-Higashi (albinism with severe IMMUNODEFICIENCY). Ask about bleeding and recurrent infection — these change management completely.

melasma.what: Acquired symmetrical HYPERpigmentation, typically on the face — cheeks, forehead, upper lip, chin. Melanocytes are overactive rather than increased in number.
melasma.who_and_why: Predominantly women. Driven by ULTRAVIOLET AND VISIBLE LIGHT exposure, and by hormones — pregnancy ("chloasma", the mask of pregnancy), combined oral contraceptives, and hormone therapy. Commoner and more persistent in people with darker skin.
the_key_management_facts: PHOTOPROTECTION is the foundation, and without it nothing else works. Critically, VISIBLE LIGHT — not just UV — drives melasma in darker skin, so a conventional UV-only sunscreen is insufficient. TINTED sunscreens containing IRON OXIDE block visible light and are meaningfully more effective. This is a specific, practical and frequently omitted piece of advice.
Stop or change the contributing hormonal agent where feasible.
Topical agents (hydroquinone, azelaic acid, tretinoin, combination formulations) and, cautiously, chemical peels or lasers.
It RECURS readily with sun exposure and after pregnancy. Set expectations honestly at the outset — an unrealistic promise of clearance destroys trust.
melasma.the_harm_to_warn_about: Unregulated SKIN-LIGHTENING creams are widely used for melasma and often contain POTENT CORTICOSTEROIDS, MERCURY or high-dose hydroquinone. These cause steroid atrophy, telangiectasia, ochronosis (a paradoxical blue-black staining that is very difficult to reverse), adrenal suppression and mercury toxicity. Ask specifically and non-judgementally what the patient is already using — they frequently will not volunteer it.

acanthosis_nigricans.what: VELVETY, THICKENED, HYPERPIGMENTED skin in FLEXURES — neck, axillae, groin, under the breasts, knuckles. It is a change in skin TEXTURE as much as colour; it is palpable, and on darker skin the texture is the more reliable sign.
acanthosis_nigricans.why_it_happens: INSULIN RESISTANCE. High insulin cross-reacts with IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes and fibroblasts, driving proliferation. It is therefore a VISIBLE MARKER OF A METABOLIC STATE.
acanthosis_nigricans.what_to_do_about_it: It is a prompt to investigate, not a cosmetic problem. Check glucose or HbA1c, lipids, blood pressure and weight. In women also consider POLYCYSTIC OVARY SYNDROME. In children it is a strong marker of insulin resistance and should trigger metabolic assessment. Treating the insulin resistance improves the skin; treating the skin alone does nothing.
acanthosis_nigricans.the_red_flag_variant: MALIGNANT acanthosis nigricans — SUDDEN onset, RAPID progression, EXTENSIVE involvement, involvement of MUCOSAE, palms ("tripe palms") and lips, in an OLDER patient, often with weight LOSS and ITCH. This is a PARANEOPLASTIC sign, most classically of GASTRIC ADENOCARCINOMA. It demands urgent investigation for an internal malignancy. The distinguishing features are the speed, the extent and the mucosal involvement.
acanthosis_nigricans.other_causes: Obesity, PCOS, Cushing syndrome, acromegaly, hypothyroidism, and drugs — nicotinic acid, corticosteroids, and insulin itself at high dose.

post_inflammatory_pigment_change.why_it_deserves_its_own_note: After ANY inflammatory skin condition — acne, eczema, psoriasis, an insect bite, a burn — pigment can increase or decrease at the site. On darker skin this is far more marked, lasts far longer (often many months), and is frequently the aspect the patient cares about MOST, while the clinician regards it as resolved disease.
post_inflammatory_pigment_change.the_practical_consequence: Treat the underlying inflammation EARLY and effectively, because the longer inflammation persists the worse the pigment change. Use photoprotection. Explain the expected timeline honestly — months, not weeks. Do not describe it as "just pigmentation".

warnings: Check TSH and screen for autoimmune disease in everyone with vitiligo.
Depigmented vitiliginous skin has no UV protection and burns easily — photoprotection is medical, not cosmetic.
Albinism ALWAYS involves the eyes. Refer every patient for ophthalmology and low-vision support.
Albinism carries a very high skin cancer risk from a young age. Lifelong sun protection and skin surveillance are life-saving.
Ask about bleeding (Hermansky-Pudlak) and recurrent infection (Chediak-Higashi) in albinism.
In melasma on darker skin, VISIBLE light matters — recommend a tinted, iron-oxide-containing sunscreen, not UV-only.
Ask specifically and non-judgementally about skin-lightening creams. Many contain potent steroids, mercury or high-dose hydroquinone.
Acanthosis nigricans is a marker of insulin resistance — check glucose, lipids and blood pressure, and consider PCOS.
SUDDEN, extensive acanthosis nigricans with mucosal or palmar involvement in an older patient is paraneoplastic — investigate for gastric adenocarcinoma.
Post-inflammatory pigment change is the outcome patients often care about most. Treat inflammation early and set honest timelines.
Address the psychological and social impact of vitiligo and albinism — including stigma and, in some regions, safety.
limitations: Topical agents, phototherapy protocols and depigmenting regimens are service- and country-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Depigmented vs hypopigmented?
flashcards.a: Depigmented is complete loss (vitiligo, glows under Wood lamp); hypopigmented is partial.

flashcards.q: What must be checked in every vitiligo patient?
flashcards.a: Thyroid function — and screen for other autoimmune disease.

flashcards.q: Are melanocytes absent in albinism?
flashcards.a: No — they are present in normal numbers but cannot synthesise melanin.

flashcards.q: Why does albinism always need ophthalmology?
flashcards.a: Melanin is required for retinal and optic pathway development — nystagmus, foveal hypoplasia, chiasmal misrouting.

flashcards.q: Which sunscreen for melasma on darker skin?
flashcards.a: A tinted, iron-oxide-containing one — visible light drives melasma, not just UV.

flashcards.q: What does acanthosis nigricans indicate?
flashcards.a: Insulin resistance — check glucose, lipids, BP, and consider PCOS.

flashcards.q: When is acanthosis nigricans paraneoplastic?
flashcards.a: Sudden, extensive, with mucosal or palmar involvement in an older patient — classically gastric adenocarcinoma.

flashcards.q: What is Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome?
flashcards.a: Albinism with a bleeding diathesis and pulmonary fibrosis.

checkboxes: Wood lamp used to classify pigment loss
TSH and autoimmune screen in vitiligo
Sun protection provided and affordability considered
Malignancy considered if sudden and extensive

entries.title: Skin Cancer — BCC, SCC, Melanoma and the Blistering Diseases
entries.summary: BCC eats locally and almost never spreads; SCC can metastasise; melanoma kills. And on darker skin, melanoma is overwhelmingly ACRAL — soles, palms, nail beds — where nobody looks, which is why it presents late and does worse.

terms: skin cancer — bcc, scc, melanoma and the blistering diseases

basal_cell_carcinoma.appearance: A PEARLY or translucent papule or nodule with ROLLED, raised edges and fine TELANGIECTASIA over the surface. It may ulcerate centrally — the "rodent ulcer". Other forms: superficial (a scaly erythematous patch, often on the trunk, easily mistaken for eczema or psoriasis that will not clear), and morphoeic/infiltrative (a scar-like indurated plaque with ill-defined edges, which is the dangerous one because its true extent is much larger than it appears).
basal_cell_carcinoma.behaviour: LOCALLY invasive and destructive, but metastasis is exceptionally rare. The morbidity is from local destruction — around the eye, nose and ear it can invade cartilage and bone and cause disfigurement.
basal_cell_carcinoma.management: Surgical excision; MOHS micrographic surgery for high-risk sites (central face, periocular, nose, ear), recurrent or morphoeic lesions. Topical or destructive therapies for selected superficial lesions.
basal_cell_carcinoma.the_clue_to_act_on: A lesion on the face that bleeds intermittently, scabs, and then "heals" and recurs over months is a BCC until proven otherwise. Patients describe it as a spot that will not go away.

squamous_cell_carcinoma.appearance: A firm, KERATOTIC, often TENDER nodule or plaque, frequently ulcerated or crusted, on sun-exposed skin. Tenderness is a useful discriminator — BCCs are usually painless.
squamous_cell_carcinoma.the_precursors: ACTINIC KERATOSIS (rough, scaly, "sandpaper" patches — better FELT than seen) and BOWEN DISEASE (SCC in situ — a well-demarcated scaly erythematous patch, commonly on the lower leg, often misdiagnosed as eczema or psoriasis for years).
squamous_cell_carcinoma.behaviour: CAN METASTASISE, usually to regional lymph nodes. Higher risk with: lip and ear sites, size over 2 cm, poor differentiation, perineural invasion, depth, IMMUNOSUPPRESSION, and arising in a chronic wound or scar.
squamous_cell_carcinoma.marjolin_ulcer: SCC arising in a chronic non-healing wound, burn scar, sinus or ulcer — often after many years. Any chronic ulcer that changes, develops rolled or everted edges, becomes exophytic or bleeds must be BIOPSIED. This is genuinely and repeatedly missed, and it is particularly relevant where burn scars and chronic osteomyelitis are common.
squamous_cell_carcinoma.immunosuppression: ORGAN TRANSPLANT recipients have a dramatically increased SCC risk — many-fold — and their SCCs behave more aggressively. They need regular dermatological surveillance and aggressive treatment of precursors. Anyone on long-term immunosuppression deserves the same attention.

melanoma.abcde: ASYMMETRY · BORDER irregular · COLOUR variegated · DIAMETER over 6 mm · EVOLVING. Evolution — change in size, shape, colour, or new symptoms such as bleeding or itch — is the most important single criterion, because a small lesion that is changing beats a large stable one.
melanoma.the_ugly_duckling_sign: Most of a person naevi look broadly alike. The lesion that looks DIFFERENT from the patient own others deserves attention regardless of whether it meets ABCDE. This is often more sensitive than the checklist.

the_critical_point_about_skin_tone.the_pattern: In people with darker skin, melanoma is predominantly ACRAL LENTIGINOUS — on the SOLES, PALMS, and under the NAILS — and in mucosal sites. It is NOT strongly sun-related in these locations, so sun-avoidance messaging does not address it.
the_critical_point_about_skin_tone.why_it_does_worse: Because nobody examines the soles. Presentation is late, at greater depth, and survival is correspondingly worse. This is a difference in DETECTION, not in biology.
the_critical_point_about_skin_tone.what_to_actually_do: EXAMINE THE SOLES, PALMS AND NAILS — of every patient, and specifically in any skin check. Teach patients to look at their own feet. A pigmented lesion on the sole in an adult is melanoma until proven otherwise.
the_critical_point_about_skin_tone.subungual: A pigmented longitudinal nail band that is WIDENING, IRREGULAR, over 3 mm wide, or affecting a SINGLE digit — particularly the thumb or great toe — needs specialist assessment. HUTCHINSON SIGN, pigment spreading onto the surrounding nail fold, is a strong indicator. Do not dismiss it as trauma without a clear, consistent history — and note that a subungual haematoma GROWS OUT with the nail over weeks, whereas melanoma does not.

melanoma.the_other_subtypes: Superficial spreading (commonest overall), NODULAR (rapidly growing, often amelanotic and symmetrical — it breaks the ABCDE rules entirely and is disproportionately lethal for that reason), and lentigo maligna (on chronically sun-damaged facial skin in older people).
melanoma.prognosis: BRESLOW THICKNESS — the depth in millimetres — is the single strongest prognostic factor. Also ulceration and mitotic rate. Sentinel lymph node biopsy for staging in appropriate cases.
melanoma.the_practical_rule: Do NOT do a partial or shave biopsy of a suspected melanoma if avoidable — an excisional biopsy with a narrow margin preserves the ability to measure Breslow thickness accurately, and that measurement determines everything that follows.

the_common_benign_mimic.seborrhoeic_keratosis: Extremely common, benign. Warty, greasy, sharply demarcated, with a characteristic "STUCK ON" appearance as though it could be picked off, and visible keratin plugs. Colour ranges from tan to almost black, which is why it is confused with melanoma. It needs no treatment.
the_common_benign_mimic.the_sign_of_leser_trelat: The SUDDEN eruption of MULTIPLE seborrhoeic keratoses, often with itch, is a rare paraneoplastic sign — classically of gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma. Rare and debated, but worth knowing when the history is genuinely abrupt.

the_two_blistering_diseases_that_must_be.pemphigus_vulgaris: Antibodies against DESMOGLEIN (desmosomes) cause an INTRAEPIDERMAL split. Blisters are FLACCID and rupture easily, so patients often present with painful EROSIONS rather than intact blisters. MUCOSAL involvement — especially painful mouth ulcers — is common and frequently the FIRST sign, preceding skin disease by months. NIKOLSKY POSITIVE. It affects a younger age group and is potentially FATAL without treatment.
the_two_blistering_diseases_that_must_be.bullous_pemphigoid: Antibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins cause a SUBEPIDERMAL split. Blisters are TENSE and durable, on an urticarial base, intensely ITCHY, in ELDERLY patients. Mucosal involvement is uncommon. Nikolsky negative. It often begins with a non-specific itchy urticarial eruption weeks before any blister appears — a prodrome that is regularly misdiagnosed as eczema or scabies.
the_two_blistering_diseases_that_must_be.the_memory_hook: PemphiGUS — Gone (flaccid, ruptures), mucosa involved, younger, more dangerous. PemphiGOID — sOlid/tense, elderly, itchy, mucosa usually spared.
the_two_blistering_diseases_that_must_be.diagnosis: Skin biopsy for histology PLUS a separate PERILESIONAL sample for DIRECT IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE — the immunofluorescence is what makes the diagnosis, and taking it from the wrong site (within the blister rather than adjacent skin) is a common technical error that wastes the test.

the_genodermatoses_worth_recognising.xeroderma_pigmentosum: Autosomal recessive defect in NUCLEOTIDE EXCISION REPAIR — the cell cannot repair UV-induced DNA damage. Extreme photosensitivity, severe freckling in early childhood, and MULTIPLE skin cancers from a very young age, with markedly reduced life expectancy. Requires near-total UV avoidance from infancy and lifelong surveillance. Consider it in a young child with severe sunburn from minimal exposure and early freckling.
the_genodermatoses_worth_recognising.muir_torre_syndrome: SEBACEOUS neoplasms (adenoma, epithelioma, carcinoma) and/or keratoacanthomas together with VISCERAL malignancy — colorectal and genitourinary especially. It is a variant of LYNCH SYNDROME with mismatch repair deficiency. A sebaceous tumour is therefore not a trivial finding: it should prompt a family history, mismatch repair immunohistochemistry, and colorectal screening for the patient and relatives.
the_genodermatoses_worth_recognising.cowden_syndrome: PTEN mutation. Trichilemmomas, oral papillomas and acral keratoses, with macrocephaly, and a high lifetime risk of BREAST, THYROID and ENDOMETRIAL cancer requiring intensive surveillance.
the_genodermatoses_worth_recognising.gorlin_syndrome: PTCH1 mutation — multiple BCCs from a young age, jaw keratocysts, palmar pits and skeletal anomalies.

warnings: EXAMINE THE SOLES, PALMS AND NAILS. In darker skin melanoma is predominantly acral and is missed because nobody looks.
A pigmented lesion on the sole of an adult is melanoma until proven otherwise.
A widening, irregular or single-digit longitudinal nail pigment band needs specialist assessment. A subungual haematoma grows out; melanoma does not.
NODULAR melanoma breaks the ABCDE rules — symmetrical, uniform, sometimes amelanotic, fast-growing. Rapid growth alone warrants urgent referral.
Do not shave-biopsy a suspected melanoma — excisional biopsy preserves accurate Breslow thickness, which determines management.
Any chronic non-healing ulcer or burn scar that changes or develops everted edges must be biopsied — Marjolin ulcer.
Transplant recipients and the long-term immunosuppressed have dramatically higher and more aggressive SCC risk. They need surveillance.
A morphoeic BCC extends far beyond its visible edge — refer for Mohs rather than simple excision.
Painful mouth erosions in a younger adult may be pemphigus vulgaris preceding skin disease by months.
Take direct immunofluorescence from PERILESIONAL skin, not from the blister — wrong-site sampling wastes the test.
An itchy urticarial eruption in an elderly patient may be pre-bullous pemphigoid — do not settle for "eczema".
A sebaceous neoplasm should prompt consideration of Muir-Torre and colorectal screening.
limitations: Excision margins, staging pathways, referral timeframes and adjuvant therapy are guideline-specific and change; follow current local cancer pathways.

flashcards.q: How does BCC classically appear?
flashcards.a: Pearly papule with rolled edges and telangiectasia, sometimes centrally ulcerated.

flashcards.q: Which skin cancer metastasises — BCC or SCC?
flashcards.a: SCC. BCC is locally destructive but almost never metastasises.

flashcards.q: What is a Marjolin ulcer?
flashcards.a: SCC arising in a chronic wound, burn scar or sinus — biopsy any chronic ulcer that changes.

flashcards.q: Where is melanoma found in darker skin?
flashcards.a: Acral sites — soles, palms, nail beds — and mucosae. Examine them.

flashcards.q: What is Hutchinson sign?
flashcards.a: Pigment spreading from a nail band onto the nail fold — suggests subungual melanoma.

flashcards.q: Why is nodular melanoma dangerous?
flashcards.a: It is symmetrical and uniform, so it fails ABCDE, yet grows fast and is disproportionately lethal.

flashcards.q: Strongest melanoma prognostic factor?
flashcards.a: Breslow thickness.

flashcards.q: Pemphigus vs pemphigoid?
flashcards.a: Pemphigus: intraepidermal, flaccid, mucosal, younger, Nikolsky positive, dangerous. Pemphigoid: subepidermal, tense, itchy, elderly.

flashcards.q: Where should immunofluorescence be taken from?
flashcards.a: Perilesional skin, not the blister itself.

flashcards.q: What does a sebaceous neoplasm suggest?
flashcards.a: Muir-Torre syndrome — a Lynch variant. Screen for colorectal and genitourinary cancer.

flashcards.q: What is xeroderma pigmentosum?
flashcards.a: Defective nucleotide excision repair — extreme photosensitivity and skin cancers from early childhood.

checkboxes: Excisional biopsy planned for suspected melanoma
Family history taken where a genodermatosis is suspected

entries.title: Is Adenocarcinoma One Disease? Histological Type Versus Primary Site
entries.summary: Adenocarcinoma is not a disease. It is a DESCRIPTION OF THE CELL — glandular — and it says nothing about behaviour, stage or treatment. "Adenocarcinoma of the pancreas" and "adenocarcinoma of the colon" share a microscope appearance and almost nothing else.

terms: is adenocarcinoma one disease? histological type versus primary site

body.the_question_answered_directly: You asked whether adenocarcinoma is one entity or must always be referred to an organ. The answer: it is NOT one entity. "Adenocarcinoma" names the CELL OF ORIGIN — a glandular, secretory epithelial cell. The primary SITE names the disease. Pathologists report both because each answers a different question, and only the two together are actionable.

the_suffix_tells_you_the_tissue_family.carcinoma: From EPITHELIUM — skin, gut lining, glands, ducts, airways. Around 85–90% of adult cancers. Spreads initially via LYMPHATICS.
the_suffix_tells_you_the_tissue_family.sarcoma: From MESENCHYME — bone, muscle, fat, cartilage, connective tissue. Rare. Spreads initially via BLOOD, which is why sarcomas present with lung metastases and why lymph node sampling matters less.
the_suffix_tells_you_the_tissue_family.blastoma: From embryonic precursor cells — nephroblastoma (Wilms), neuroblastoma, retinoblastoma. Predominantly paediatric.
the_suffix_tells_you_the_tissue_family.the_benign_suffix: -OMA alone usually means benign (adenoma, lipoma, fibroma) — but beware the historical exceptions that are malignant despite the name: MELANOMA, LYMPHOMA, MESOTHELIOMA, SEMINOMA, MYELOMA, GLIOBLASTOMA. This is a real source of confusion for patients and for junior staff.

the_prefix_tells_you_the_cell_type.adeno: GLANDULAR epithelium — it forms glands or makes mucin. Found wherever glands exist: colon, stomach, pancreas, prostate, breast, lung, endometrium, kidney.
the_prefix_tells_you_the_cell_type.squamous: SQUAMOUS epithelium — it makes keratin and has intercellular bridges. Native to skin, oesophagus, cervix, oropharynx, anus — and it arises in the LUNG and BLADDER through METAPLASIA driven by chronic irritation (smoking, schistosomiasis).
the_prefix_tells_you_the_cell_type.small_cell_neuroendocrine: Neuroendocrine cells — lung especially, but also gut and elsewhere.

why_the_same_histology_behaves_different.the_principle: The cell type tells you what it LOOKS like. The organ tells you what it DOES — because behaviour is determined by the surrounding tissue architecture, the blood and lymphatic drainage, the local growth factors and mutations, and how early symptoms appear.

the_worked_comparison.colonic_adenocarcinoma: Arises from an adenoma over years — so screening works, because the precursor is detectable and removable. Drains via portal circulation, so it metastasises to LIVER first. Often symptomatic relatively early (bleeding, obstruction, anaemia). 5-year survival is good when caught early.
the_worked_comparison.pancreatic_adenocarcinoma: No practical screening. Anatomically silent until it is advanced. Invades nerves and vessels early, is desmoplastic and chemoresistant. Most patients are unresectable at diagnosis. Prognosis is dismal.
the_worked_comparison.lung_adenocarcinoma: Driven by targetable mutations (EGFR, ALK, ROS1) in a substantial subset, so MOLECULAR testing changes treatment fundamentally. Metastasises to brain, bone, adrenal and liver.
the_worked_comparison.prostate_adenocarcinoma: Frequently INDOLENT — many men die WITH it rather than OF it, which is why active surveillance is a legitimate strategy. Hormone-sensitive. Metastasises to BONE, characteristically as SCLEROTIC lesions, whereas most other cancers produce lytic lesions.

why_the_same_histology_behaves_different.the_conclusion: Same word under the microscope. Different screening, different staging system, different treatment, and survival ranging from excellent to dismal. "Adenocarcinoma" alone is never a sufficient diagnosis.

how_a_pathologist_finds_the_primary.why_it_matters: Because treatment follows the PRIMARY, not the site of the metastasis. A liver lesion that is metastatic colorectal cancer gets colorectal treatment, not liver cancer treatment.
how_a_pathologist_finds_the_primary.immunohistochemistry: Antibodies against proteins that are retained from the tissue of origin. Common combinations: CK7 and CK20 together (colorectal is classically CK7 negative, CK20 positive; lung and breast are CK7 positive, CK20 negative). TTF-1 for lung and thyroid. CDX2 for gastrointestinal. GATA3 for breast and urothelium. PSA for prostate. Thyroglobulin for thyroid. PAX8 for renal, thyroid and gynaecological.
how_a_pathologist_finds_the_primary.cancer_of_unknown_primary: When no primary is found after appropriate workup. It is treated according to the most likely pattern and increasingly by MOLECULAR profiling. Prognosis is generally poorer, partly because it is often biologically aggressive and partly because targeted treatment depends on knowing the origin.

grade_versus_stage.the_confusion: These are constantly conflated and they mean entirely different things.
grade_versus_stage.grade: How ABNORMAL the cells look — DIFFERENTIATION. Well differentiated resembles the parent tissue and generally behaves better; poorly differentiated or anaplastic looks nothing like it and behaves worse. Grade is about the CELL.
grade_versus_stage.stage: How FAR it has spread — tumour size and local invasion (T), lymph nodes (N), distant metastasis (M). Stage is about the EXTENT.
grade_versus_stage.which_matters_more: STAGE almost always dominates prognosis and determines treatment. A well-differentiated but widely metastatic cancer does far worse than a poorly differentiated but localised one. TNM staging is also organ-specific — a "T2" means something different in breast, colon and lung, so stages cannot be compared across cancers.

carcinoma_in_situ.the_definition: Malignant cells occupying the full thickness of the epithelium but NOT having breached the BASEMENT MEMBRANE.
carcinoma_in_situ.why_that_single_membrane_matters_so_much: Below the basement membrane lie the LYMPHATICS and BLOOD VESSELS. Above it there are none. So a tumour confined above the basement membrane has NO ROUTE TO METASTASISE. In situ disease is, by definition, incapable of spreading — which is why complete local excision is curative and why it is staged as Tis, distinct from any invasive stage.
carcinoma_in_situ.examples: Ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast; cervical intraepithelial neoplasia; Bowen disease (SCC in situ of skin); melanoma in situ (lentigo maligna).
carcinoma_in_situ.the_nuance_worth_stating: Not all in situ disease inevitably progresses, and some would never have harmed the patient — this is the OVERDIAGNOSIS problem, most debated in DCIS and prostate cancer. It is a genuine harm of screening and deserves honest discussion rather than being ignored.
carcinoma_in_situ.the_related_sequence: METAPLASIA (reversible change of one mature cell type to another, an adaptation) → DYSPLASIA (disordered growth, still reversible) → CARCINOMA IN SITU → INVASIVE CARCINOMA. The first three steps are where prevention and cure live; the fourth is where it gets hard.

what_to_ask_when_you_read_a_pathology_re: What is the CELL TYPE (adenocarcinoma, squamous, small cell, sarcoma)?
What is the PRIMARY SITE, and how confident is the pathologist?
What is the STAGE (TNM), and is the resection margin clear?
Are there PREDICTIVE markers — receptor status, molecular mutations, mismatch repair, PD-L1 — that change treatment?
Is there lymphovascular or perineural invasion?

warnings: Adenocarcinoma is a cell description, not a diagnosis. Always establish the primary site — treatment follows the primary, not the metastasis.
Grade and stage are different. Stage usually dominates prognosis.
TNM is organ-specific — stages cannot be compared between cancer types.
Carcinoma in situ cannot metastasise because it has not breached the basement membrane, which is where vessels begin.
Some -oma names are malignant despite the suffix: melanoma, lymphoma, mesothelioma, seminoma, myeloma, glioblastoma.
Sarcomas spread haematogenously, carcinomas lymphatically first — this changes staging investigations.
Lung adenocarcinoma requires molecular testing; a subset is targetable and the treatment differs entirely.
Prostate cancer metastasises to bone as SCLEROTIC lesions, unlike most cancers which are lytic.
Overdiagnosis of in situ disease is a real harm of screening and warrants honest discussion.
limitations: Immunohistochemistry panels, molecular testing availability and staging editions vary by centre and are periodically revised.

flashcards.q: Is adenocarcinoma one disease?
flashcards.a: No — it names the glandular cell of origin. The primary site determines the disease.

flashcards.q: Carcinoma vs sarcoma origin and spread?
flashcards.a: Carcinoma from epithelium, spreads via lymphatics. Sarcoma from mesenchyme, spreads via blood.

flashcards.q: Grade vs stage?
flashcards.a: Grade is how abnormal the cells look; stage is how far it has spread. Stage usually dominates prognosis.

flashcards.q: Why can carcinoma in situ not metastasise?
flashcards.a: It has not breached the basement membrane, and there are no vessels above it.

flashcards.q: Which -oma names are malignant?
flashcards.a: Melanoma, lymphoma, mesothelioma, seminoma, myeloma, glioblastoma.

flashcards.q: CK7−/CK20+ suggests which primary?
flashcards.a: Colorectal.

flashcards.q: Which marker suggests a lung or thyroid primary?
flashcards.a: TTF-1.

flashcards.q: Why do colonic and pancreatic adenocarcinoma differ so much?
flashcards.a: Detectable precursor and early symptoms in colon; silent, desmoplastic and chemoresistant in pancreas.

flashcards.q: Sequence from adaptation to cancer?
flashcards.a: Metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinoma.

checkboxes: Cell type and primary site both established
Predictive molecular markers requested where relevant

entries.title: Breast Cancer — Triple Assessment, Receptors and What Determines Treatment
entries.summary: Every discrete breast lump gets TRIPLE ASSESSMENT — clinical, imaging, biopsy — and each part is scored. The receptors (ER, PR, HER2) then decide the treatment more than the stage does, which is why the biopsy must precede any surgical plan.

terms: breast cancer — triple assessment, receptors and what determines treatment

triple_assessment.the_principle: Every discrete breast lump is assessed three ways, each scored 1 (normal) to 5 (malignant). CONCORDANCE between the three is what gives confidence. DISCORDANCE — for example a benign-looking biopsy from a suspicious-looking mass — means the lesion must be re-sampled or excised, never reassured away.
triple_assessment.clinical: History and examination. Note size, site, consistency, mobility, fixation to skin or chest wall, skin changes, nipple changes and axillary nodes.
triple_assessment.imaging: ULTRASOUND is preferred UNDER about 40 because dense young breast tissue makes mammography insensitive. MAMMOGRAPHY (with ultrasound) is used over 40. MRI for specific indications — lobular cancer, implants, high-risk screening, extent assessment.
triple_assessment.pathology: CORE BIOPSY, not fine needle aspiration, because core gives ARCHITECTURE (invasive versus in situ) and enough tissue for RECEPTOR testing. FNA cannot distinguish invasive from in situ disease, which is the distinction that determines the operation.

what_is_usually_benign.fibroadenoma: The commonest discrete lump in young women. Smooth, firm, highly MOBILE — the "breast mouse". Still needs triple assessment.
what_is_usually_benign.cyst: Smooth, may be tender, fluctuates with the cycle, commonest around the perimenopause. Aspiration is both diagnostic and therapeutic — but BLOODSTAINED aspirate, a RESIDUAL MASS after aspiration, or rapid recurrence all require further assessment.
what_is_usually_benign.fat_necrosis: Follows trauma or surgery. It can be hard, irregular and tethered, and it MIMICS CARCINOMA convincingly on both examination and imaging — a history of trauma is never sufficient to avoid biopsy.
what_is_usually_benign.duct_ectasia: Dilated ducts in older women, causing a green or creamy discharge and sometimes a retroareolar mass and nipple retraction.
what_is_usually_benign.phyllodes_tumour: A fibroepithelial tumour that grows RAPIDLY and can be benign, borderline or malignant. It needs WIDE excision because it recurs locally, and it is often initially mistaken for a fibroadenoma that is simply growing.

the_features_that_demand_urgent_referral: A new discrete, HARD, IRREGULAR, FIXED lump, particularly in an older patient.
Skin TETHERING, dimpling, or PEAU D ORANGE (dermal lymphatic obstruction giving an orange-peel texture).
BLOODSTAINED or single-duct, spontaneous, unilateral nipple discharge.

An eczematous, crusting change of the NIPPLE that does not resolve — PAGET DISEASE OF THE NIPPLE. Unlike eczema it starts on the NIPPLE and spreads to the areola, whereas eczema usually spares the nipple. It indicates underlying malignancy in most cases and is regularly treated as dermatitis for months.

A red, swollen, warm, rapidly progressive breast — INFLAMMATORY BREAST CANCER. It mimics mastitis, but occurs typically in a NON-lactating woman and does NOT resolve with antibiotics. Any "mastitis" not responding within a short course must be re-evaluated, not given a second antibiotic.
A breast lump in a MAN — rarer, but proportionally more likely to be malignant, and frequently presented late.

classification.in_situ: DCIS — malignant cells confined within the ducts, cannot metastasise, often detected as MICROCALCIFICATION on screening. LCIS is better regarded as a RISK MARKER for future cancer in either breast than as a direct precursor.
classification.invasive: Invasive ductal (no special type) is commonest. INVASIVE LOBULAR is important because it grows in single-file strands, so it forms a diffuse thickening rather than a discrete lump, is often occult on mammography, and is more likely to be BILATERAL and multifocal — MRI is frequently needed to assess extent.

the_receptors_that_determine_treatment.er_and_pr: Oestrogen and progesterone receptor. POSITIVE tumours respond to ENDOCRINE therapy — tamoxifen (typically pre-menopausal) or an aromatase inhibitor (post-menopausal, since after menopause oestrogen comes from peripheral aromatisation rather than the ovary, which is precisely why aromatase inhibitors do not work pre-menopausally without ovarian suppression). ER-positive disease can recur LATE, even beyond 10 years, so surveillance and extended endocrine therapy are considerations.
the_receptors_that_determine_treatment.her2: Amplification predicts response to HER2-targeted therapy such as trastuzumab. Historically aggressive, now with much improved outcomes because of targeted treatment. Trastuzumab is CARDIOTOXIC, so cardiac function must be assessed before and monitored during treatment.
the_receptors_that_determine_treatment.triple_negative: ER, PR and HER2 all negative. No endocrine or HER2 target, so chemotherapy is the systemic mainstay. More common in younger women, in BRCA1 carriers, and in women of African ancestry — and it carries a worse prognosis with earlier recurrence. This disparity is partly biological and partly a matter of access and delay, and both need addressing.
the_receptors_that_determine_treatment.the_practical_consequence: Receptor status is obtained from the CORE BIOPSY, before surgery. It determines whether neoadjuvant chemotherapy is offered, and can convert an inoperable tumour into an operable one.

body.genetic_risk: BRCA1 and BRCA2 confer high lifetime risk of breast and OVARIAN cancer; BRCA2 also raises male breast, prostate and pancreatic risk. Refer for genetic assessment with young onset, bilateral disease, male breast cancer, triple-negative disease at a young age, multiple affected relatives, or Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry. It affects surgical choices, risk-reducing options for the patient, screening for relatives, and eligibility for PARP inhibitors.
body.treatment_principles: Surgery (breast-conserving with radiotherapy, or mastectomy — survival is equivalent for suitable tumours, so this can genuinely be the patient choice) plus axillary staging by SENTINEL NODE biopsy where the axilla is clinically negative. Then adjuvant radiotherapy, endocrine therapy, chemotherapy and targeted therapy as indicated by receptor status, stage and genomic assays. Reconstruction should be discussed BEFORE surgery, not after.
body.the_thing_most_often_neglected: Lymphoedema risk counselling, fertility preservation discussion BEFORE chemotherapy in younger women, bone health on aromatase inhibitors, menopausal symptom management, and psychological support. These determine quality of life for years and are frequently deferred until too late to act.

warnings: DISCORDANCE in triple assessment means re-sample or excise. Never reassure on a benign biopsy from a suspicious mass.
Use CORE biopsy, not FNA — only core distinguishes invasive from in situ and provides receptor status.
A red swollen breast in a non-lactating woman that does not settle with antibiotics is inflammatory breast cancer until proven otherwise.
Nipple eczema that starts ON the nipple and does not resolve is Paget disease — eczema usually spares the nipple.
Fat necrosis mimics carcinoma. A history of trauma does not remove the need for biopsy.
Invasive lobular cancer is often occult on mammography and frequently bilateral — consider MRI.
Trastuzumab is cardiotoxic — assess and monitor cardiac function.
Aromatase inhibitors do not work pre-menopausally without ovarian suppression.
ER-positive disease can recur beyond 10 years. Late recurrence is not reassurance failure.
Discuss fertility preservation BEFORE starting chemotherapy in younger women.
A breast lump in a man is proportionally more likely to be malignant and presents late.
Bloodstained cyst aspirate or a residual mass after aspiration requires further assessment.
limitations: Referral criteria, screening intervals, genomic assay use and systemic regimens are guideline- and country-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: What are the three parts of triple assessment?
flashcards.a: Clinical examination, imaging, and core biopsy — each scored, and concordance required.

flashcards.q: Why core biopsy rather than FNA?
flashcards.a: Core shows architecture (invasive vs in situ) and provides receptor status.

flashcards.q: Ultrasound or mammography under 40?
flashcards.a: Ultrasound — dense young breast tissue makes mammography insensitive.

flashcards.q: What is Paget disease of the nipple?
flashcards.a: Eczematous nipple change starting ON the nipple, usually indicating underlying malignancy.

flashcards.q: How does inflammatory breast cancer present?
flashcards.a: Red, swollen, warm breast in a non-lactating woman that does not resolve with antibiotics.

flashcards.q: Why do aromatase inhibitors fail pre-menopausally?
flashcards.a: Ovarian oestrogen production is not blocked — they act on peripheral aromatisation.

flashcards.q: What does triple negative mean and imply?
flashcards.a: ER, PR and HER2 negative — chemotherapy is the systemic mainstay; worse prognosis, commoner in BRCA1 and younger women.

flashcards.q: Which targeted drug is cardiotoxic?
flashcards.a: Trastuzumab — monitor cardiac function.

flashcards.q: Why is invasive lobular cancer easily missed?
flashcards.a: It grows in single file, causing diffuse thickening rather than a lump, and is often mammographically occult.

checkboxes: Core biopsy obtained with receptor testing

entries.title: Gastrointestinal and Lung Cancer — Red Flags and the Paraneoplastic Syndromes
entries.summary: Right-sided colon cancer bleeds silently and presents as ANAEMIA; left-sided obstructs and changes bowel habit. In lung cancer the paraneoplastic syndrome often arrives before the tumour is visible, and knowing which tumour causes which syndrome shortens the diagnosis by months.

terms: gastrointestinal and lung cancer — red flags and the paraneoplastic syndromes

the_side_matters.right_sided: The caecum and ascending colon are WIDE and the stool is LIQUID, so obstruction is late. Blood is mixed in and DIGESTED, so it is not visible. Presentation is therefore OCCULT — IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA, weight loss, fatigue, and sometimes a palpable mass. IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA IN ANY MAN, OR IN ANY POSTMENOPAUSAL WOMAN, IS COLORECTAL CANCER UNTIL EXCLUDED. This is one of the highest-yield rules in general medicine and it is repeatedly treated with iron tablets alone.
the_side_matters.left_sided: Narrower lumen, formed stool — so CHANGE IN BOWEL HABIT, obstruction, tenesmus, and FRESH or dark blood mixed with stool.
the_side_matters.rectal: Fresh bleeding, tenesmus, a sensation of incomplete evacuation. A DIGITAL RECTAL EXAMINATION is essential and is skipped far too often.

colorectal_cancer.risk_and_prevention: Age, family history, adenomatous polyps, inflammatory bowel disease (duration-dependent), LYNCH SYNDROME and FAP, smoking, obesity, processed and red meat, alcohol. Because it arises from an ADENOMA over years, SCREENING WORKS — faecal immunochemical testing and colonoscopy detect and remove the precursor.
colorectal_cancer.lynch_syndrome: Mismatch repair deficiency. Right-sided, younger onset, with endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urothelial and other cancers. Test tumours for mismatch repair or microsatellite instability — it identifies families, and it also PREDICTS RESPONSE TO IMMUNOTHERAPY, so it is both a genetic and a treatment question.

gastric_cancer.presentation: Vague and late — dyspepsia, early satiety, weight loss, anorexia, vomiting, anaemia. Because the symptoms mimic ordinary dyspepsia, it is often treated empirically with acid suppression, which relieves symptoms and delays diagnosis.
gastric_cancer.risk: HELICOBACTER PYLORI (the dominant modifiable factor), smoking, salted and smoked foods, pernicious anaemia, previous gastric surgery, and hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (CDH1 mutation).
gastric_cancer.the_named_signs_of_advanced_disease: VIRCHOW NODE (left supraclavicular — Troisier sign), SISTER MARY JOSEPH nodule (umbilical metastasis), KRUKENBERG tumour (ovarian metastasis, classically signet-ring), and an irregular hard rectal shelf on examination. All indicate advanced disease and all are found only if you examine for them.
gastric_cancer.linitis_plastica: Diffuse infiltration producing a rigid, non-distensible "leather bottle" stomach. It may be missed at endoscopy because the MUCOSA CAN LOOK NORMAL — the abnormality is in the wall. If clinical suspicion is high despite a normal-looking endoscopy, ask for deep biopsies and cross-sectional imaging.

oesophageal_cancer.the_two_types_and_where_they_sit: SQUAMOUS cell carcinoma — UPPER and middle third, driven by SMOKING, ALCOHOL, hot beverages, achalasia and caustic strictures. ADENOCARCINOMA — LOWER third and gastro-oesophageal junction, driven by GORD → BARRETT oesophagus (intestinal metaplasia) → dysplasia → carcinoma. Adenocarcinoma is rising in incidence in high-income countries; squamous predominates in much of Africa and Asia.
oesophageal_cancer.the_cardinal_symptom: PROGRESSIVE DYSPHAGIA — solids first, then liquids. That progression is the discriminator from a benign stricture or motility disorder. Add weight loss, odynophagia, hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal involvement) and anaemia.
oesophageal_cancer.the_rule: ANY new dysphagia in an adult needs URGENT ENDOSCOPY. Do not treat it as reflux and review in six weeks.

the_fundamental_split.small_cell: Central, STRONGLY smoking-related, rapidly growing, usually METASTATIC at presentation. Not usually a surgical disease — chemotherapy and radiotherapy are the mainstay. It is the leading cause of PARANEOPLASTIC syndromes, particularly the endocrine and neurological ones.
the_fundamental_split.non_small_cell: ADENOCARCINOMA (commonest, more peripheral, the type most often seen in never-smokers, and the one with targetable EGFR, ALK and ROS1 mutations), SQUAMOUS (central, cavitates, classically causes PTHrP hypercalcaemia), and LARGE CELL. Surgery is possible in early stage.

lung_cancer.local_complications_worth_naming: PANCOAST TUMOUR at the apex — shoulder and arm pain, HORNER SYNDROME (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) from sympathetic chain involvement, and T1 wasting of the small muscles of the hand. SUPERIOR VENA CAVA OBSTRUCTION — facial and arm swelling, distended non-pulsatile neck veins, headache worse on bending forward — an oncological emergency. RECURRENT LARYNGEAL NERVE palsy causing hoarseness. PHRENIC nerve palsy. Malignant PLEURAL EFFUSION.

paraneoplastic_syndromes.why_they_matter: They are caused by tumour-secreted substances or immune cross-reactivity, NOT by mass effect — so they can appear BEFORE the tumour is detectable, and recognising the syndrome finds the cancer.

endocrine.siadh: HYPONATRAEMIA with concentrated urine in a euvolaemic patient. Classically SMALL CELL lung cancer. Unexplained hyponatraemia in a smoker warrants a chest image.
endocrine.ectopic_acth: Cushing syndrome — but with a distinctive presentation: rapid onset, severe HYPOKALAEMIA and metabolic alkalosis, marked pigmentation, proximal weakness and WEIGHT LOSS rather than the classic body habitus. Small cell lung cancer and carcinoid.
endocrine.hypercalcaemia_of_malignancy: Usually PTHrP secretion — classically SQUAMOUS cell carcinoma of the lung, also renal, head and neck. Distinguished from primary hyperparathyroidism by a SUPPRESSED PTH with a raised calcium. Also caused by bone metastases and by myeloma.

paraneoplastic_syndromes.neurological: LAMBERT-EATON myasthenic syndrome (small cell) — proximal weakness that improves briefly with exertion, absent reflexes, autonomic features. Also cerebellar degeneration, limbic encephalitis, and sensory neuronopathy. These frequently PRECEDE the cancer by months, so a new unexplained syndrome mandates a search and continued surveillance if the first search is negative.
paraneoplastic_syndromes.haematological: Migratory superficial THROMBOPHLEBITIS (TROUSSEAU sign) — classically pancreatic but seen with many adenocarcinomas. Unprovoked or unusual-site venous thrombosis warrants thought about occult malignancy. Also polycythaemia (renal cell, hepatocellular) and anaemia of chronic disease.
paraneoplastic_syndromes.dermatological: ACANTHOSIS NIGRICANS of sudden onset (gastric), DERMATOMYOSITIS (ovarian, lung, gastric, nasopharyngeal), and the sign of Leser-Trélat.
paraneoplastic_syndromes.musculoskeletal: CLUBBING and hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy — periostitis with painful wrists and ankles, associated with non-small cell lung cancer and mesothelioma.

nasopharyngeal_carcinoma.why_it_deserves_naming: It is markedly over-represented in Southern Chinese, South-East Asian and North African populations, and is strongly associated with EPSTEIN-BARR VIRUS, salted fish consumption in childhood, and genetic factors.
nasopharyngeal_carcinoma.presentation: The commonest presenting feature is a PAINLESS NECK LUMP — cervical lymphadenopathy — rather than a nasal symptom. Also UNILATERAL conductive hearing loss or serous otitis media from Eustachian tube obstruction (a unilateral middle ear effusion in an ADULT is nasopharyngeal carcinoma until proven otherwise, and needs nasopharyngoscopy), epistaxis, nasal obstruction, and cranial nerve palsies with skull base invasion.
nasopharyngeal_carcinoma.the_practical_rule: Adult with a persistent unilateral serous otitis media, or an unexplained upper cervical node, needs the nasopharynx visualised. It is treated with radiotherapy and chemoradiotherapy and is curable when caught early.

warnings: Iron deficiency anaemia in any man or postmenopausal woman is colorectal cancer until excluded. Do not simply prescribe iron.
Any new dysphagia in an adult needs urgent endoscopy — progression from solids to liquids is the red flag.
Linitis plastica can look normal at endoscopy — the abnormality is in the wall. Ask for deep biopsies if suspicion is high.
Unilateral serous otitis media in an ADULT is nasopharyngeal carcinoma until proven otherwise — visualise the nasopharynx.
Unexplained hyponatraemia in a smoker warrants a chest image — SIADH from small cell lung cancer.
Hypercalcaemia with a SUPPRESSED PTH suggests malignancy, not hyperparathyroidism.
Superior vena cava obstruction is an oncological emergency.
Paraneoplastic neurological syndromes often precede the tumour — search, and keep searching if the first look is negative.
Unprovoked or unusual-site thrombosis should prompt thought about occult malignancy.
Perform a digital rectal examination — it is skipped far too often in rectal bleeding and altered bowel habit.
Test colorectal tumours for mismatch repair — it identifies Lynch families and predicts immunotherapy response.
Empirical acid suppression relieves gastric cancer symptoms and delays diagnosis. Scope alarm features.
limitations: Referral thresholds, screening programmes, staging and systemic therapy are guideline- and country-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: How does right-sided colon cancer present?
flashcards.a: Occultly — iron deficiency anaemia, weight loss, fatigue. Blood is digested and invisible.

flashcards.q: What must iron deficiency anaemia in a man prompt?
flashcards.a: Investigation for colorectal cancer.

flashcards.q: Name the metastatic signs of gastric cancer.
flashcards.a: Virchow node (Troisier), Sister Mary Joseph nodule, Krukenberg tumour, rectal shelf.

flashcards.q: Which oesophageal cancer arises from Barrett?
flashcards.a: Adenocarcinoma, lower third — from GORD via intestinal metaplasia.

flashcards.q: Which lung cancer causes PTHrP hypercalcaemia?
flashcards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma.

flashcards.q: Which lung cancer causes SIADH and Lambert-Eaton?
flashcards.a: Small cell.

flashcards.q: What is Pancoast syndrome?
flashcards.a: Apical tumour causing shoulder/arm pain, Horner syndrome and small hand muscle wasting.

flashcards.q: How is malignant hypercalcaemia distinguished from hyperparathyroidism?
flashcards.a: PTH is SUPPRESSED in malignancy and raised or inappropriately normal in hyperparathyroidism.

flashcards.q: Commonest presentation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
flashcards.a: A painless neck lump — or unilateral serous otitis media in an adult.

flashcards.q: What is Trousseau sign of malignancy?
flashcards.a: Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis — classically pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

checkboxes: Iron deficiency anaemia investigated, not just treated
Nasopharynx visualised in adult unilateral middle ear effusion
Paraneoplastic syndrome considered as a presenting feature
Smoking status and occupational exposure recorded

entries.title: Delirium Versus Dementia — and the Dementia Subtypes
entries.summary: Delirium is ACUTE, FLUCTUATING and has INATTENTION at its core — and it is a medical emergency with a cause to find. Dementia is chronic and progressive. The commonest error is calling delirium "confusion" in a known dementia patient and stopping looking.

terms: delirium versus dementia — and the dementia subtypes

the_discriminating_table.onset: DELIRIUM: hours to days. DEMENTIA: months to years.
the_discriminating_table.course: DELIRIUM: FLUCTUATES markedly, often worse at night ("sundowning" occurs in both but fluctuation is characteristic of delirium). DEMENTIA: steadily progressive (stepwise in vascular).
the_discriminating_table.attention: DELIRIUM: IMPAIRED — this is the CORE feature and the single best discriminator. DEMENTIA: relatively preserved until late.
the_discriminating_table.consciousness: DELIRIUM: altered, clouded. DEMENTIA: clear until late.
the_discriminating_table.hallucinations: DELIRIUM: common, often VISUAL. DEMENTIA: less common except in Lewy body disease.
the_discriminating_table.reversibility: DELIRIUM: usually reversible if the cause is treated. DEMENTIA: not.
the_discriminating_table.the_practical_test: Test ATTENTION — months of the year backwards, or serial subtraction. Failure of attention in an acutely changed patient is delirium until proven otherwise.

delirium.why_it_is_an_emergency: It is a sign of acute physiological disturbance, associated with increased mortality, prolonged admission, functional decline and an increased risk of subsequent dementia. It is NOT a benign consequence of being old and in hospital.

the_two_types.hyperactive: Agitated, restless, aggressive, hallucinating. Recognised easily because it is disruptive.
the_two_types.hypoactive: WITHDRAWN, drowsy, quiet, slow. It is COMMONER and it is MISSED, because a quiet patient causes no trouble. It carries a WORSE prognosis. Any newly quiet, withdrawn older patient should be screened for delirium, not left alone.

delirium.causes_pinch_me: PAIN · INFECTION · NUTRITION · CONSTIPATION · HYDRATION · MEDICATION · ENVIRONMENT. To which add urinary RETENTION, hypoxia, electrolytes, glucose, alcohol or benzodiazepine WITHDRAWAL, stroke, and post-ictal states. It is frequently MULTIFACTORIAL — finding one cause does not mean you should stop looking.
delirium.the_drugs_to_review_first: ANTICHOLINERGICS above all (oxybutynin, amitriptyline, older antihistamines, some antipsychotics) — cumulative anticholinergic burden is a major and modifiable driver. Also opioids, benzodiazepines, steroids, and levodopa. Deprescribing is a treatment.
delirium.management: FIND AND TREAT THE CAUSE — that is the treatment. Non-pharmacological measures first and always: reorientation, familiar people present, glasses and HEARING AIDS (sensory deprivation is a potent and trivially correctable driver), daylight, sleep hygiene, early mobilisation, hydration, treating pain and constipation. Medication only where there is risk to the patient or others and de-escalation has failed, at the lowest dose and for the shortest time.
delirium.the_specific_prescribing_warnings: AVOID antipsychotics in LEWY BODY dementia and Parkinson disease — severe neuroleptic sensitivity can cause irreversible deterioration. Avoid benzodiazepines EXCEPT in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, where they are the treatment.
delirium.prevention: Multicomponent prevention works — it reduces incidence meaningfully. Orientation, sleep, mobility, vision, hearing and hydration. This is a nursing and system intervention more than a medical one.

the_dementia_subtypes.alzheimer: Commonest. Insidious, gradually progressive. EARLY EPISODIC MEMORY loss (recent events, repeating questions) with later language, visuospatial and executive decline. Amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tau tangles; medial temporal and hippocampal atrophy.
the_dementia_subtypes.vascular: STEPWISE deterioration with vascular risk factors and focal neurological signs. Often mixed with Alzheimer pathology in practice. Management centres on aggressive vascular risk control, which is the only part that can be modified.

lewy_body.the_core_triad: FLUCTUATING cognition with marked variation in attention · recurrent well-formed VISUAL HALLUCINATIONS (often of people or animals) · spontaneous PARKINSONISM. Also REM sleep behaviour disorder, which may precede everything by years, and repeated unexplained falls and syncope from autonomic dysfunction.
lewy_body.the_critical_warning: SEVERE NEUROLEPTIC SENSITIVITY. Antipsychotics can cause profound, sometimes irreversible, deterioration and are potentially fatal. Any patient with fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism must NOT be given a routine antipsychotic for their hallucinations — which is exactly the intuitive response. This is one of the most important prescribing warnings in old-age psychiatry.
lewy_body.the_distinction_from_parkinson_dementia: Arbitrary but conventional — if dementia precedes or arrives within a year of parkinsonism it is Lewy body dementia; if it follows established Parkinson disease by longer, it is Parkinson disease dementia. The pathology overlaps.

the_dementia_subtypes.frontotemporal: YOUNGER onset, often 45–65. PERSONALITY and BEHAVIOUR change — disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behaviours, dietary change with a sweet preference — with memory RELATIVELY PRESERVED early. Or a language variant (primary progressive aphasia). It is frequently misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric illness, a midlife crisis, or a personality disorder for years before the diagnosis is made, and the family suffers enormously in that interval.

body.the_reversible_causes_that_must_be_exclu: B12 and folate deficiency, HYPOTHYROIDISM, neurosyphilis, HIV, chronic subdural haematoma, DEPRESSION ("pseudodementia" — prominent complaints of poor memory with poor effort on testing, and it improves with treatment), medication effects, alcohol, and NORMAL PRESSURE HYDROCEPHALUS — the triad of gait apraxia (a magnetic, shuffling gait), urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment, potentially reversible with shunting. Gait first is the clue.
body.the_diagnostic_approach: A collateral history from someone who knows the person is essential and is the most informative single element. Cognitive testing (MoCA is more sensitive than MMSE for mild impairment and executive dysfunction). Bloods to exclude reversible causes. Imaging. Functional assessment — what has the person stopped being able to do?
body.the_things_that_actually_help: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and memantine give modest symptomatic benefit in selected types. But the interventions that change lives are: advance care planning while capacity remains, carer support and respite, driving assessment, financial and legal safeguarding (lasting power of attorney), falls prevention, treating pain (which is a major and under-recognised cause of agitation in people who cannot report it), and continuity of care.

warnings: Delirium is a medical emergency with a cause to find. Do not accept "confused, known dementia" as an endpoint.
HYPOACTIVE delirium is commoner, more often missed, and has a worse prognosis. Screen the newly quiet patient.
Test ATTENTION — it is the core deficit and the best discriminator.
Avoid antipsychotics in Lewy body dementia and Parkinson disease — severe neuroleptic sensitivity can be irreversible or fatal.
Avoid benzodiazepines in delirium EXCEPT in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
Review anticholinergic burden first — it is a major modifiable driver.
Give the patient their glasses and hearing aids. Sensory deprivation is a potent and trivially correctable cause.
Delirium is usually multifactorial — finding one cause does not mean stopping the search.
Exclude B12, thyroid, syphilis, HIV, subdural haematoma, depression and normal pressure hydrocephalus.
Gait disturbance FIRST with incontinence and cognitive change suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus — potentially reversible.
Frontotemporal dementia is misdiagnosed as psychiatric illness for years. Personality change under 65 with preserved memory should prompt it.
Untreated PAIN is a major cause of agitation in people who cannot report it.
limitations: Cognitive test cut-offs, prescribing and shared-care protocols are service-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Single best discriminator for delirium?
flashcards.a: Impaired ATTENTION, with acute onset and fluctuation.

flashcards.q: Which delirium subtype is missed and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: Hypoactive — quiet patients cause no trouble, and it has a worse prognosis.

flashcards.q: Recite PINCH ME.
flashcards.a: Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment.

flashcards.q: Core features of Lewy body dementia?
flashcards.a: Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism — plus REM sleep behaviour disorder.

flashcards.q: What must never be given routinely in Lewy body dementia?
flashcards.a: Antipsychotics — severe neuroleptic sensitivity, potentially irreversible or fatal.

flashcards.q: How does frontotemporal dementia present?
flashcards.a: Younger onset with personality and behaviour change; memory relatively preserved early.

flashcards.q: Triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus?
flashcards.a: Gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, cognitive impairment — gait first.

flashcards.q: Which drug class should be reviewed first in delirium?
flashcards.a: Anticholinergics — cumulative burden is a major modifiable driver.

checkboxes: Antipsychotics avoided in suspected Lewy body disease
Pain assessed in the non-verbal patient

entries.title: Bipolar Disorder — and Why the Diagnosis Is Usually Late
entries.summary: Patients present in DEPRESSION, not in mania, so bipolar disorder is routinely diagnosed as unipolar depression and treated with an antidepressant alone — which can precipitate mania or rapid cycling. Always ask about elevated mood before prescribing.

terms: bipolar disorder — and why the diagnosis is usually late

the_types.bipolar_1: At least one MANIC episode — severe enough to impair function markedly, or requiring admission, or with psychotic features. Depression usually occurs but is not required for the diagnosis.
the_types.bipolar_2: At least one HYPOMANIC episode plus at least one major DEPRESSIVE episode, and never a full manic episode. Hypomania is milder and does not cause marked impairment or psychosis — which is why it is not reported and often not even remembered as abnormal.
the_types.cyclothymia: Chronic fluctuating subthreshold mood elevation and depression over years.
the_types.mixed_features: Depression and elevation simultaneously — agitated, irritable, sleepless and hopeless together. This state carries a PARTICULARLY HIGH SUICIDE RISK because low mood is combined with the energy and impulsivity to act on it.

why_the_diagnosis_is_missed.the_core_reason: People do not seek help when they feel energetic, confident and productive. They seek help when they are depressed. So the presenting picture is depression, and unless hypomania is actively asked about, it is invisible.
why_the_diagnosis_is_missed.the_average_delay: Diagnosis is commonly delayed by years, during which patients are treated for unipolar depression.
why_the_diagnosis_is_missed.how_to_ask: Ask about periods of DAYS OR MORE of unusually elevated or irritable mood WITH reduced need for sleep and increased activity or energy — and ask a FAMILY MEMBER, who usually recognises it far better than the patient does. Ask specifically about overspending, unusual risk-taking, uncharacteristic sexual behaviour, or starting many projects.
why_the_diagnosis_is_missed.the_pointers_in_a_depressed_patient: Onset before about 25, multiple prior episodes, atypical features (hypersomnia, increased appetite), psychotic depression, POSTPARTUM onset, a FAMILY HISTORY of bipolar disorder, and — importantly — poor or paradoxical response to antidepressants, or a history of "reacting badly" to them.

the_prescribing_hazard.the_rule: ANTIDEPRESSANT MONOTHERAPY in bipolar depression can precipitate a SWITCH to mania, induce a mixed state, or cause RAPID CYCLING. Before prescribing an antidepressant for any depression, screen for a history of elevated mood.
the_prescribing_hazard.what_that_means_practically: Bipolar depression is generally treated with mood stabilisers or specific atypical antipsychotics rather than an antidepressant alone; where antidepressants are used they are usually under mood-stabiliser cover and specialist direction.

body.recognising_mania: Elevated or irritable mood WITH: grandiosity, markedly reduced need for sleep (feeling rested after very little), pressured speech, flight of ideas, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity, and risk-taking with painful consequences — spending, driving, sexual behaviour, business decisions. Psychotic features may occur and are typically mood-congruent (grandiose or persecutory delusions). Insight is characteristically ABSENT, which is why compulsory treatment is sometimes necessary.

the_treatments_and_their_specific_hazard.lithium: The most effective long-term agent and the only one with good evidence for reducing SUICIDE. But it has a NARROW THERAPEUTIC INDEX and needs regular level monitoring plus renal and thyroid function. Toxicity is precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides, and by any acute illness with vomiting or diarrhoea — patients must be told to hold it and seek advice when acutely unwell. Toxicity presents with coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting, confusion and seizures.
the_treatments_and_their_specific_hazard.valproate: Effective, but must NOT be used in women and girls of childbearing potential except under strict conditions — it causes major congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders. This is an absolute practice point and it is still got wrong.
the_treatments_and_their_specific_hazard.lamotrigine: Better for the depressive pole. Must be titrated SLOWLY because of the risk of SEVERE RASH including Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Any rash means stopping and seeking urgent advice.
the_treatments_and_their_specific_hazard.antipsychotics: Several are effective for acute mania and for maintenance; monitor metabolic parameters.
the_treatments_and_their_specific_hazard.non_pharmacological: Psychoeducation, sleep and routine regularity (sleep disruption is both a trigger and an early warning sign), relapse-signature identification, substance avoidance, and family involvement. These are not adjuncts — regular sleep is genuinely protective.

body.the_perinatal_point: Bipolar disorder carries a very high risk of POSTPARTUM PSYCHOSIS, which is a psychiatric emergency with risk to mother and infant. Any woman with bipolar disorder who is pregnant or planning pregnancy needs specialist perinatal mental health input in advance — for medication planning and for a postpartum monitoring plan.
body.risk: Suicide risk is high, particularly in mixed states, in the depressive phase, early in the illness, and with comorbid substance misuse. Assess it explicitly and repeatedly, and involve family in safety planning where the patient consents.

warnings: Screen for elevated mood BEFORE prescribing an antidepressant. Antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate mania or rapid cycling.
Patients present depressed, not manic. Hypomania must be asked about — and ask a family member.
Mixed states carry a particularly high suicide risk — low mood with the energy to act.
Valproate must not be used in women and girls of childbearing potential except under strict conditions.
Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index. Warn about dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides and acute illness.
Lamotrigine must be titrated slowly — any rash means stop and seek urgent advice.
Bipolar disorder carries a high risk of postpartum psychosis. Plan perinatal care in advance.
Sleep disruption is both a trigger and an early warning sign. Regular sleep is genuinely protective.
Insight is characteristically absent in mania.
limitations: Diagnostic criteria, monitoring schedules and prescribing rules are guideline- and jurisdiction-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Bipolar 1 vs 2?
flashcards.a: Type 1 requires a full manic episode; type 2 is hypomania plus major depression, never full mania.

flashcards.q: Why is bipolar disorder diagnosed late?
flashcards.a: Patients present depressed. Hypomania feels good and is never reported unless asked about.

flashcards.q: What is the main prescribing hazard?
flashcards.a: Antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate mania, mixed states or rapid cycling.

flashcards.q: Which mood state carries the highest suicide risk?
flashcards.a: Mixed states — depressed mood with the energy and impulsivity to act.

flashcards.q: Which agent reduces suicide risk?
flashcards.a: Lithium.

flashcards.q: What precipitates lithium toxicity?
flashcards.a: Dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides, and acute illness with vomiting or diarrhoea.

flashcards.q: Why titrate lamotrigine slowly?
flashcards.a: Risk of severe rash including Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

flashcards.q: Which obstetric risk is critical?
flashcards.a: Postpartum psychosis — plan perinatal care in advance.

checkboxes: Elevated mood screened before any antidepressant
Pregnancy status and contraception addressed before valproate
Lithium monitoring arranged and sick-day advice given

entries.title: Substance Misuse — Withdrawal, Overdose and What Actually Reverses What
entries.summary: Only a few substances have a true ANTIDOTE. The rest are supportive care. And the critical asymmetry: OPIOID withdrawal is miserable but rarely kills, while ALCOHOL and BENZODIAZEPINE withdrawal can kill — which is the opposite of what most people assume.

terms: substance misuse — withdrawal, overdose and what actually reverses what

the_governing_asymmetry.withdrawal_that_can_kill: ALCOHOL and BENZODIAZEPINES (and other GABAergic sedatives). Both cause seizures and delirium and both have real mortality. These withdrawals need medically supervised, tapered treatment — never abrupt cessation.
the_governing_asymmetry.withdrawal_that_is_miserable_but_rarely_: OPIOIDS. Severe distress, vomiting, diarrhoea, cramps, dilated pupils, yawning, piloerection — but rarely fatal in an otherwise healthy adult. The exceptions matter: in PREGNANCY, opioid withdrawal risks fetal distress and miscarriage or preterm labour, and severe dehydration can be dangerous in the frail.
the_governing_asymmetry.why_this_matters: The intuitive ranking is backwards. Staff often worry most about the dramatic-looking opioid withdrawal and least about the quiet drinker on a surgical ward who has not had a drink for two days — and it is the second who arrests.

opioids_naloxone.what: A competitive opioid receptor antagonist. Reverses respiratory depression within minutes.
opioids_naloxone.the_critical_point: Naloxone has a SHORTER half-life than most opioids — and far shorter than methadone or modified-release preparations. The patient WILL RE-SEDATE. Never discharge someone who has woken up after naloxone; they need observation, and often an infusion.
opioids_naloxone.the_titration_principle: The aim is ADEQUATE VENTILATION, not full consciousness. Giving a large bolus to a dependent patient precipitates acute withdrawal — vomiting with a compromised airway, agitation, and a patient who then leaves. Titrate to breathing.
opioids_naloxone.harm_reduction: TAKE-HOME naloxone for people who use opioids and for those around them saves lives and should be offered routinely, along with advice never to use alone.

benzodiazepines_flumazenil.why_it_is_rarely_used: It can precipitate SEIZURES that are then REFRACTORY — because the benzodiazepine receptor is blocked, so benzodiazepines cannot treat the seizure. The risk is greatest in chronic benzodiazepine users and in MIXED overdose with a pro-convulsant such as a tricyclic antidepressant. Benzodiazepine overdose alone is rarely fatal, so the risk-benefit usually favours supportive airway management. Flumazenil is reserved for specific situations, chiefly iatrogenic over-sedation in a non-dependent patient.

what_has_a_true_antidote.the_others_worth_knowing: Paracetamol → acetylcysteine. Opioid → naloxone. Beta-blocker → glucagon and high-dose insulin euglycaemia. Calcium channel blocker → calcium, high-dose insulin. Digoxin → digoxin-specific antibody fragments. Iron → desferrioxamine. Methanol and ethylene glycol → fomepizole or ethanol, plus dialysis. Organophosphate → atropine and pralidoxime. Local anaesthetic → lipid emulsion. Warfarin → vitamin K and prothrombin complex. Tricyclic → sodium bicarbonate (for the QRS, not an antidote as such).
what_has_a_true_antidote.what_has_NO_antidote: COCAINE, AMPHETAMINES and other stimulants · CANNABIS · ALCOHOL (acute intoxication) · GHB · KETAMINE · most novel psychoactive substances. Management is entirely SUPPORTIVE — airway, cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation and seizures, fluids, and treating complications.

alcohol.withdrawal_timeline: Tremor, sweating, anxiety and nausea from 6–12 hours. SEIZURES typically 12–48 hours. Alcoholic hallucinosis (hallucinations with an otherwise CLEAR sensorium) 12–24 hours. DELIRIUM TREMENS 48–72 hours or later.
alcohol.delirium_tremens: Confusion and clouded consciousness, vivid hallucinations, marked autonomic instability, fever, and severe tremor. It has significant MORTALITY and is a medical emergency requiring high-dependency care.
alcohol.treatment: Long-acting BENZODIAZEPINES, ideally SYMPTOM-TRIGGERED using a validated scale rather than fixed dosing, which reduces total dose and duration. In significant LIVER disease a shorter-acting agent not requiring hepatic oxidation is preferred.

thiamine_the_non_negotiable_part.why: Chronic alcohol use depletes thiamine. WERNICKE ENCEPHALOPATHY — confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia — is present far more often than the classic triad suggests; most cases do NOT have all three, so waiting for the triad means missing it.
thiamine_the_non_negotiable_part.the_rule: GIVE PARENTERAL THIAMINE BEFORE ANY GLUCOSE LOAD. Glucose consumes the last of the thiamine and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in a susceptible patient. Oral thiamine is inadequate for treatment because absorption is poor and unpredictable.
thiamine_the_non_negotiable_part.the_consequence_of_failure: Untreated Wernicke progresses to KORSAKOFF SYNDROME — irreversible anterograde amnesia with CONFABULATION and relative preservation of other cognition. It is permanent, disabling, and entirely preventable with a cheap vitamin. Few omissions in medicine cost so much for so little.
