alcohol.the_other_things_to_check: Glucose, electrolytes including magnesium and phosphate (REFEEDING risk), liver function and clotting, head injury (a drinker with confusion may have a subdural haematoma, not just withdrawal), infection, and gastrointestinal bleeding.

opioids.overdose: The triad is REDUCED CONSCIOUSNESS, RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION and PINPOINT PUPILS. Treat with airway support and titrated naloxone. Look for a fentanyl or synthetic opioid involvement, which may need larger and repeated doses.
opioids.withdrawal: Treated symptomatically, or better with OPIOID SUBSTITUTION — methadone or buprenorphine. Note that buprenorphine is a PARTIAL agonist with high receptor affinity and can PRECIPITATE withdrawal if given too soon after a full agonist; timing matters and is a specialist decision.
opioids.the_things_that_reduce_deaths: Opioid substitution therapy, take-home naloxone, needle and syringe programmes, testing and treating hepatitis C and HIV, and — critically — recognising the period of HIGHEST OVERDOSE RISK: after a break in use (release from prison, discharge from hospital or detox), when TOLERANCE HAS FALLEN but the usual dose is taken. Every patient leaving such a setting must be warned about this explicitly.

body.stimulants: Cocaine and amphetamines cause agitation, hyperthermia, hypertension, arrhythmia, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, stroke and myocardial infarction. Manage with BENZODIAZEPINES as the primary agent — they treat agitation, hypertension and seizures together — plus active cooling and fluids. Cocaine chest pain: benzodiazepines, nitrates and aspirin; there is a longstanding caution about giving a beta-blocker alone because of the theoretical risk of unopposed alpha stimulation, so follow your local protocol.

nicotine_and_caffeine.nicotine: Withdrawal is irritability, poor concentration, low mood, increased appetite and craving — it is genuinely difficult and it is often trivialised. Effective treatments exist: nicotine replacement (combining a patch with a fast-acting form works better than either alone), varenicline, and bupropion, all more effective when combined with behavioural support. Note that smoking INDUCES CYP1A2 — stopping smoking raises levels of clozapine, olanzapine, theophylline and caffeine, so doses may need review when a patient stops, including on admission to a smoke-free hospital.
nicotine_and_caffeine.caffeine: A genuine dependence with a real withdrawal syndrome — headache, fatigue, poor concentration, low mood — peaking at 1–2 days. Massive overdose causes agitation, vomiting, tachyarrhythmia, seizures and HYPOKALAEMIA, and is potentially fatal; caffeine tablets and energy products make this more accessible than it once was.

the_principles_that_apply_to_all_of_it: Ask about substance use routinely, without judgement, in a way that makes an honest answer possible. Under-reporting is universal and predictable.
Treat withdrawal risk PROACTIVELY on admission — the surgical or medical inpatient who withdraws unexpectedly on day two is a preventable event.
Look for POLY-substance use and for a co-existing mental illness; treating one and ignoring the other fails.
Harm reduction is not a failure of treatment. Keeping someone alive is the precondition for everything else.
Check hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV status and vaccinate for hepatitis B.
Consider the children and dependants of anyone with problematic substance use — safeguarding is part of the assessment.

warnings: ALCOHOL and BENZODIAZEPINE withdrawal can KILL. Opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely fatal. This is the opposite of the common assumption.
GIVE PARENTERAL THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE in any patient at risk. Glucose first can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
Most Wernicke cases do NOT have the full triad. Do not wait for it.
Naloxone is shorter-acting than most opioids — the patient will re-sedate. Never discharge after a single dose.
Titrate naloxone to adequate VENTILATION, not to full consciousness, or you precipitate withdrawal and vomiting.
Flumazenil can precipitate refractory seizures — the receptor it blocks is the one benzodiazepines would act on. Rarely justified.
Buprenorphine can PRECIPITATE withdrawal if given too soon after a full agonist.
Overdose risk is highest after a break in use — prison release, hospital discharge, after detox — because tolerance has fallen. Warn explicitly.
Cocaine, amphetamines, cannabis, GHB and ketamine have NO antidote. Treatment is supportive; benzodiazepines are the workhorse.
A confused drinker may have a subdural haematoma, hypoglycaemia or infection — not just withdrawal.
Stopping smoking raises clozapine, olanzapine and theophylline levels — review doses on admission to a smoke-free hospital.
Consider dependants and safeguarding in every assessment.
limitations: Antidote dosing, withdrawal scales and substitution prescribing are protocol-specific and specialist-directed. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Which withdrawals can kill?
flashcards.a: Alcohol and benzodiazepines. Opioid withdrawal is rarely fatal.

flashcards.q: What must be given before glucose in an alcohol-dependent patient?
flashcards.a: Parenteral thiamine — glucose first can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.

flashcards.q: What does untreated Wernicke become?
flashcards.a: Korsakoff syndrome — irreversible amnesia with confabulation.

flashcards.q: Why must you not discharge after naloxone?
flashcards.a: Naloxone is shorter-acting than most opioids — the patient re-sedates.

flashcards.q: What is the naloxone titration endpoint?
flashcards.a: Adequate ventilation, not full consciousness.

flashcards.q: Why is flumazenil rarely used?
flashcards.a: It can precipitate seizures that benzodiazepines then cannot treat.

flashcards.q: When is opioid overdose risk highest?
flashcards.a: After a break in use — prison release, discharge, detox — when tolerance has fallen.

flashcards.q: Which substances have no antidote?
flashcards.a: Cocaine, amphetamines, cannabis, GHB, ketamine, most novel psychoactive substances.

flashcards.q: Primary drug for stimulant toxicity?
flashcards.a: Benzodiazepines — they treat agitation, hypertension and seizures together.

flashcards.q: What happens to clozapine levels when a patient stops smoking?
flashcards.a: They RISE — smoking induces CYP1A2.

checkboxes: Blood-borne virus testing and hepatitis B vaccination offered

entries.title: Safeguarding Children — Recognising Abuse and Neglect
entries.summary: The single most important rule is that a bruise in a baby who is NOT INDEPENDENTLY MOBILE is abnormal until explained. Beyond specific injuries, the strongest signals are a history that does not fit, a history that changes, and delay in seeking help.

terms: safeguarding children — recognising abuse and neglect

the_governing_principles: The CHILD’S WELFARE is paramount. It outranks the therapeutic relationship with the parent and it outranks your discomfort.
Safeguarding is EVERYONE’S responsibility, not the specialist’s alone. You do not need to be certain, and it is not your job to investigate or to establish what happened.
You need only a REASONABLE CONCERN to refer. The threshold for referral is far lower than the threshold for proof.
CONSENT is not required to share information where a child may be at risk of significant harm. Confidentiality does not override child protection.
DOCUMENT contemporaneously, factually and precisely — what you saw, what was said and by whom, in their own words. Your notes may be read in court years later.
If you do not refer because you assumed someone else would, that is the failure mode that recurs in every serious case review.

the_history_matters_more_than_the_injury.why: Most abusive injuries are not individually diagnostic. What raises concern is the FIT between the injury and the account.
the_features_that_should_concern_you: A history that is INCONSISTENT with the injury, or with the child’s DEVELOPMENTAL STAGE — an account of a child rolling off a bed before they can roll at all.
A history that CHANGES between tellings or between carers.
DELAY in seeking help without adequate explanation.
NO history offered at all for an obvious injury.
The injury blamed on a SIBLING or on the child themselves.
REPEATED attendances, or attendances at different hospitals.
Interaction that is concerning — a frozen, watchful child; a child who does not seek comfort from the carer; or hostility, indifference or intoxication in the carer.
Known domestic abuse, parental substance misuse or parental mental illness — the "toxic trio", which substantially raises risk.

physical_abuse_the_specific_patterns.the_cardinal_rule: BRUISING IN A CHILD WHO IS NOT INDEPENDENTLY MOBILE IS ABNORMAL until proven otherwise. "Those who don’t cruise rarely bruise." A bruise in a non-mobile infant requires explanation and, in most systems, a referral.
physical_abuse_the_specific_patterns.sites_that_concern: Bruising to the EARS, NECK, cheeks, trunk, buttocks, genitalia, and the inner arms or thighs. Accidental bruises occur over BONY PROMINENCES on the front of a mobile child — shins, knees, forehead, elbows.
physical_abuse_the_specific_patterns.patterned_injury: Bruises carrying the shape of an implement, a hand, or a ligature; grip marks; bite marks. Any patterned mark deserves careful description, measurement and photography with consent.
physical_abuse_the_specific_patterns.burns: Concerning features include a sharply demarcated "GLOVE AND STOCKING" distribution or immersion line, symmetrical burns to buttocks or perineum, sparing of flexures (from the child flexing away), and multiple small circular burns of uniform size.
physical_abuse_the_specific_patterns.fractures: Any fracture in a NON-MOBILE infant. POSTERIOR RIB fractures, METAPHYSEAL corner or "bucket-handle" fractures, and multiple fractures of DIFFERENT AGES are of particular concern. A SKELETAL SURVEY is indicated in infants where physical abuse is suspected — follow local protocol.
physical_abuse_the_specific_patterns.oral: A TORN FRENULUM in a non-mobile infant is a classic concerning finding.
physical_abuse_the_specific_patterns.abusive_head_trauma: The combination of subdural haemorrhages, RETINAL HAEMORRHAGES and encephalopathy in an infant. Presentation can be non-specific — vomiting, irritability, poor feeding, apnoea, seizures — so it is missed. Any infant with unexplained encephalopathy or seizures needs neuroimaging and a formal RETINAL examination by an ophthalmologist.
physical_abuse_the_specific_patterns.the_mimics_you_must_consider_fairly: Coagulopathy and bleeding disorders, osteogenesis imperfecta, birth trauma, Mongolian blue spots (congenital dermal melanocytosis — commonly and harmfully mistaken for bruising in infants with darker skin; they are blue-grey, over the sacrum and buttocks, present from birth, and do NOT change colour like a bruise), cultural practices such as cupping or coining, and metabolic bone disease of prematurity. Considering these fairly is part of good safeguarding, not an alternative to it.

neglect.why_it_is_the_most_common_and_most_misse: Neglect causes the greatest cumulative harm and features in the largest share of serious case reviews, but it has no single dramatic moment. It is a PATTERN over time, so it is visible only if someone looks across contacts rather than at one.
neglect.what_it_looks_like: Faltering growth without a medical cause · persistent poor hygiene, dental decay, untreated infestation · inadequate clothing for the weather · repeatedly missed appointments and immunisations ("WAS NOT BROUGHT" is the correct phrase — a child does not choose to miss an appointment) · developmental delay from lack of stimulation · a child who is frequently unsupervised or given inappropriate caring responsibility · unmet medical needs including uncollected prescriptions.

body.emotional_abuse: Persistent criticism, humiliation, rejection, scapegoating, withholding affection, exposure to domestic abuse, or imposing developmentally inappropriate expectations. It underlies most other forms and is the hardest to evidence — but it is not lesser.

sexual_abuse.what_a_clinician_needs_to_know: Most children who have been sexually abused have NORMAL physical examinations. A normal examination NEVER excludes abuse. The disclosure is the evidence.
sexual_abuse.concerning_presentations: Sexually transmitted infection or pregnancy in a child · anogenital injury or bleeding without adequate explanation · sexualised behaviour inappropriate to developmental stage · recurrent unexplained abdominal pain, enuresis or encopresis · self-harm, eating disorder, running away, substance use, or abrupt behavioural change.
sexual_abuse.the_examination_rule: Do NOT perform an intimate examination to "check". Forensic examination must be done ONCE, by a specifically trained practitioner, in the correct setting. A well-meaning look causes distress and can destroy evidence.
sexual_abuse.if_a_child_discloses: LISTEN. Do not ask leading or probing questions and do not interview — that is for trained interviewers, and poor questioning can render evidence unusable. Do not promise confidentiality; explain honestly that you must tell someone whose job is to keep them safe. Record their EXACT words. Reassure them that they are believed and that it is not their fault. Then refer immediately.

body.fabricated_or_induced_illness: Where a carer exaggerates, fabricates or induces illness. Suspect it with symptoms witnessed only by one carer, inconsistency between reported severity and observed state, results that do not fit, extensive investigations without a diagnosis, and a carer who resists reassurance or seeks further intervention. This is a high-stakes and complex area — it must be escalated to senior paediatric and safeguarding colleagues, never managed alone or confronted directly.
what_to_actually_do: Ensure the child is SAFE right now, and medically assessed and treated.
Document contemporaneously — verbatim quotes, body maps, measurements, times. Sign and date.
Discuss with your SAFEGUARDING LEAD or senior paediatrician the same day. Do not sit on it.
REFER to children’s social care per your local pathway; follow a verbal referral with a written one.
Consider SIBLINGS and any other children in the household — they are at risk too, and this is routinely forgotten.
Do NOT confront the carer with an accusation, and do not attempt to investigate. Explain honestly and neutrally that you are required to share concerns.
Follow up. Confirm the referral was received and acted on; escalate if not.

warnings: Bruising in a child who is not independently mobile is abnormal until proven otherwise.
You do not need certainty to refer. Reasonable concern is the threshold, and investigating is not your job.
Consent is not required to share information where a child may be at risk of significant harm.
A normal examination NEVER excludes sexual abuse. Most examinations are normal.
Do not perform an intimate examination to "check" — forensic examination is done once, by a trained practitioner.
If a child discloses, listen and record verbatim. Do not ask leading questions or interview them.
Never promise a child confidentiality you cannot keep.
Always consider siblings and other children in the household.
Mongolian blue spots are commonly mistaken for bruising in infants with darker skin — they are present from birth and do not change colour.
Consider coagulopathy and osteogenesis imperfecta fairly — but never as a reason to avoid referral.
Any infant with unexplained encephalopathy or seizures needs neuroimaging and formal retinal examination.
Use "was not brought" rather than "did not attend" — a child cannot bring themselves.
Assuming someone else will refer is the failure that recurs in every serious case review.
limitations: Referral pathways, thresholds, statutory duties and documentation standards are JURISDICTION-SPECIFIC. This entry describes principles; you must follow your national and local safeguarding procedures.
This is a recognition and referral reference. It does not replace safeguarding training, which is mandatory and recurrent.

flashcards.q: What is the cardinal rule about bruising in infants?
flashcards.a: A bruise in a child who is not independently mobile is abnormal until explained.

flashcards.q: What raises concern more than the injury itself?
flashcards.a: A history that does not fit, changes between tellings, or is delayed.

flashcards.q: Does consent limit information sharing in child protection?
flashcards.a: No. Consent is not required where a child may be at risk of significant harm.

flashcards.q: Does a normal genital examination exclude sexual abuse?
flashcards.a: No — most examinations are normal. The disclosure is the evidence.

flashcards.q: What should you do if a child discloses?
flashcards.a: Listen, do not ask leading questions, record verbatim, do not promise confidentiality, refer immediately.

flashcards.q: Which fractures are of particular concern in infants?
flashcards.a: Posterior rib, metaphyseal corner/bucket-handle, and multiple fractures of different ages.

flashcards.q: What is abusive head trauma?
flashcards.a: Subdural haemorrhage, retinal haemorrhage and encephalopathy in an infant — presentation is often non-specific.

flashcards.q: Which benign finding is mistaken for bruising on darker skin?
flashcards.a: Mongolian blue spot — present from birth, sacral, does not change colour.

flashcards.q: Why is neglect the most missed form?
flashcards.a: It is a pattern over time with no single dramatic moment — visible only across contacts.

checkboxes: Child is safe and medically assessed
History and injuries documented verbatim with body map
Developmental stage compared against the account
Follow-up arranged and escalation if no response

entries.title: Exploitation, Trafficking and Female Genital Mutilation
entries.summary: Trafficked and exploited people are usually seen in healthcare at some point and are almost never identified, because they do not present as victims. The clinician’s job is to create a moment ALONE with an interpreter who is not the accompanying person — that single act is what makes disclosure possible.

terms: exploitation, trafficking and female genital mutilation

trafficking_and_exploitation.why_clinicians_matter: A large proportion of trafficked people access healthcare while being exploited — for injuries, infections, pregnancy or mental health crises. They are rarely recognised. Healthcare is often the ONLY setting where they are briefly away from the person controlling them, which makes the clinical encounter genuinely consequential.
what_should_raise_concern: A person ACCOMPANIED by someone who ANSWERS FOR THEM, will not leave them alone, holds their documents, or insists on interpreting.
Inconsistent or rehearsed-sounding history; vagueness about their address, their work, or how they came to the country.
No identity documents, or documents held by someone else.
Signs of physical abuse, malnutrition, untreated chronic conditions, or occupational injury.
Multiple sexually transmitted infections, repeated terminations, or evidence of sexual violence.
Fearfulness, hypervigilance, avoidance of eye contact, deference to the accompanying person.
Working excessive hours, unpaid or with debt owed to an employer, or living at the workplace.

In children and young people: unexplained gifts, money or phones; older "boyfriends" or associates; going missing; carrying drugs or large sums of cash (COUNTY LINES exploitation); and being found far from home.

the_single_most_important_action.what: SEE THE PERSON ALONE, and use a PROFESSIONAL INTERPRETER — never a family member, never the accompanying person, and never a child.
the_single_most_important_action.how_to_do_it_safely: Normalise it: "It is our routine policy to see everyone on their own for part of the consultation." Do not signal suspicion in front of the accompanying person — that can escalate danger for the patient after they leave.
the_single_most_important_action.why_it_matters_so_much: Disclosure is impossible in the presence of the controlling person, and using them as an interpreter guarantees a false history. This one procedural habit is the difference between identification and not.

trafficking_and_exploitation.how_to_ask: Non-judgemental, open, and framed around safety rather than immigration or criminality: "Are you free to leave where you are living?" · "Does anyone take your wages or your documents?" · "Do you feel safe where you are staying?" · "Is anyone making you do something you do not want to do?"
trafficking_and_exploitation.what_to_do: Treat the medical problem. Assess immediate safety. Refer per your national mechanism for trafficking and modern slavery. In CHILDREN, exploitation is a child protection matter and must be referred to children’s social care regardless of whether the young person perceives themselves as a victim — they frequently do not, because grooming works by producing apparent consent. Document carefully. Give information about support services in a form that is SAFE to carry, or memorable rather than physical if carrying it would be dangerous.
trafficking_and_exploitation.the_thing_to_avoid: Do NOT confront or alert the suspected controlling person, and do not tell the patient you are calling the authorities in front of them. Escalating visibly can put the patient at serious risk once they leave your department.

female_genital_mutilation.what_it_is: Partial or total removal of the external female genitalia, or other injury to the female genital organs, for non-medical reasons. It has NO health benefits and causes lifelong harm. It is a violation of human rights and is illegal in many jurisdictions, including where performed abroad.

the_who_classification.type_1: Clitoridectomy — partial or total removal of the clitoral glans and/or prepuce.
the_who_classification.type_2: Excision — partial or total removal of the clitoral glans and the labia minora, with or without the labia majora.
the_who_classification.type_3: INFIBULATION — narrowing of the vaginal opening by creating a covering seal, formed by repositioning the labia, with or without removal of the clitoral glans. This is the type causing the most severe obstetric and urological consequences.
the_who_classification.type_4: All other harmful procedures — pricking, piercing, incising, scraping, cauterising.

female_genital_mutilation.immediate_complications: Severe pain, haemorrhage, shock, sepsis, tetanus, urinary retention, injury to adjacent tissue, transmission of blood-borne viruses, and death.
female_genital_mutilation.long_term_complications: Chronic pain, recurrent urinary and genital infections, dysmenorrhoea and haematocolpos, urinary difficulty and retention, keloid and inclusion cysts, sexual dysfunction and dyspareunia, infertility, and significant psychological consequences including post-traumatic stress, anxiety and depression.
female_genital_mutilation.obstetric_consequences: Prolonged and obstructed labour, perineal tears, postpartum haemorrhage, emergency caesarean, obstetric fistula, and increased perinatal mortality. Type 3 requires planned DEINFIBULATION, ideally ANTENATALLY rather than in labour, by a trained practitioner.
female_genital_mutilation.the_absolute_prohibition: RE-INFIBULATION after childbirth is unlawful in many jurisdictions and is never clinically justified. It must not be performed, and a request for it should be handled sensitively but firmly, with an explanation.
female_genital_mutilation.clinical_care: Ask sensitively and without judgement, using neutral language and the term the woman herself uses. Use a professional female interpreter where needed. Explain what you are doing before examining. Offer deinfibulation where appropriate, psychological support, and sexual health care. Document the type. Recognise that the woman is not responsible for what was done to her and may have complex feelings about her family and community — hostility from a clinician ends the conversation and the care.

the_safeguarding_duty.the_core_point: FGM in a girl under 18 is CHILD ABUSE. It must be referred to children’s social care and, in many jurisdictions, reported to police — in some, including the UK, there is a MANDATORY REPORTING duty for regulated professionals who identify FGM in a girl under 18.
the_safeguarding_duty.risk_to_others: A woman with FGM means her DAUGHTERS and other girls in the family may be at risk. This requires a family risk assessment, not just care for the individual. Risk is higher around school holidays and travel to countries where prevalence is high.
the_safeguarding_duty.related: Consider FORCED MARRIAGE and so-called "honour"-based abuse in the same assessment — they frequently co-occur. Never use family members as interpreters or mediators in any of these situations.

body.the_common_thread: In all of these, the person in front of you may not identify as a victim, may not want intervention, and may be at greater risk if you act clumsily. The safe actions are the same: see them alone, use a professional interpreter, ask openly, document carefully, refer through the proper mechanism, and never confront the person exercising control.

warnings: SEE THE PATIENT ALONE and use a PROFESSIONAL interpreter — never the accompanying person, a family member, or a child.
Do not confront or alert a suspected controlling person. Visible escalation can put the patient in serious danger after they leave.
A child or young person who is being exploited usually does not see themselves as a victim — grooming produces apparent consent. Refer regardless.
FGM in a girl under 18 is child abuse. Many jurisdictions impose a MANDATORY reporting duty on regulated professionals.
A woman with FGM means daughters and other girls in the family may be at risk — assess the family, not only the patient.
RE-INFIBULATION is never justified and is unlawful in many jurisdictions.
Deinfibulation for type 3 should be planned ANTENATALLY, not performed in labour.
Use the woman’s own terminology and avoid judgemental language — hostility ends the consultation and the care.
Consider forced marriage and honour-based abuse alongside FGM; never involve family as mediators.
Give support information in a form that is safe for the person to carry — or not at all if carrying it is dangerous.
limitations: Mandatory reporting duties, referral mechanisms and legal definitions are JURISDICTION-SPECIFIC and vary substantially. You must follow your national law and local policy.
This entry supports recognition and referral. It does not replace mandatory safeguarding training or specialist FGM services.

flashcards.q: What is the single most important action in suspected trafficking?
flashcards.a: See the person alone, with a professional interpreter — not the accompanying person.

flashcards.q: How do you create that opportunity safely?
flashcards.a: Normalise it as routine policy; do not signal suspicion in front of the accompanying person.

flashcards.q: Why refer an exploited young person who denies being a victim?
flashcards.a: Grooming produces apparent consent. It remains child protection.

flashcards.q: What is FGM type 3?
flashcards.a: Infibulation — narrowing of the vaginal opening with a covering seal. Most severe obstetric consequences.

flashcards.q: When should deinfibulation be done?
flashcards.a: Planned antenatally by a trained practitioner, not in labour.

flashcards.q: Is re-infibulation ever acceptable?
flashcards.a: No — never clinically justified and unlawful in many jurisdictions.

flashcards.q: What does FGM in a woman imply for her family?
flashcards.a: Daughters and other girls may be at risk — a family risk assessment is needed.

flashcards.q: What are county lines indicators in a young person?
flashcards.a: Unexplained money, phones or gifts, going missing, found far from home, carrying drugs or cash.

checkboxes: Referral made through the correct national mechanism
Mandatory reporting duty checked and discharged
Support information given only if safe to carry

entries.title: Safeguarding Adults — Elder Abuse, Capacity and Coercion
entries.summary: Adult safeguarding turns on CAPACITY. An adult with capacity may make what looks like an unwise decision — but capacity is decision-specific, and it is undermined by coercion, so "she chose to go home" is not the end of the assessment.

terms: safeguarding adults — elder abuse, capacity and coercion

the_categories.physical: Assault, inappropriate restraint, or misuse of medication — including SEDATION used for the convenience of carers, which is a widely under-recognised form of abuse.
the_categories.neglect_and_acts_of_omission: Ignoring medical or care needs, failing to provide food, fluid, warmth or medication, withholding aids such as glasses, hearing aids or walking frames. This is the commonest form in institutional settings.
the_categories.psychological: Threats, humiliation, intimidation, isolation from family and friends, controlling contact.
the_categories.financial: The commonest form reported in older people — theft, fraud, misuse of a power of attorney, pressure over wills or property, unexplained withdrawals, sudden changes in living arrangements or in a will.
the_categories.sexual: Any sexual act without valid consent, including where capacity to consent is absent.
the_categories.discriminatory: Abuse based on age, disability, race, religion, gender or sexuality.
the_categories.organisational: Poor institutional care — rigid routines, lack of dignity, inadequate staffing. It is often systemic rather than the act of one person.
the_categories.self_neglect: Now widely recognised as a safeguarding concern in its own right, and one of the hardest, because it collides directly with autonomy.

what_should_raise_concern: INJURIES inconsistent with the explanation, or with the person’s mobility.
Multiple injuries of DIFFERENT AGES; injuries in unusual sites; grip marks.
PRESSURE ULCERS, dehydration, malnutrition, poor hygiene, untreated conditions.
Repeated missed appointments or repeated attendances.
A CARER who answers for the person, will not leave them alone, or is hostile, dismissive or intoxicated.
Fearfulness or a change in behaviour in the presence of a particular person.
Unexplained financial changes, or a person who has no access to their own money.
Medication that is not being given as prescribed, or excessive sedation.

capacity_the_central_concept.the_presumption: Every adult is PRESUMED to have capacity unless established otherwise. Capacity is DECISION-SPECIFIC and TIME-SPECIFIC — a person may lack capacity for a complex financial decision but retain it for where they live, and capacity can fluctuate.
capacity_the_central_concept.the_functional_test: Can the person UNDERSTAND the relevant information, RETAIN it long enough to decide, USE OR WEIGH it, and COMMUNICATE their decision? Failure of any one, caused by an impairment of mind or brain, means they lack capacity for that decision.
capacity_the_central_concept.the_practical_duty: You must take all practicable steps to SUPPORT capacity before concluding it is absent — hearing aids, glasses, interpreter, simpler language, written or visual aids, choosing the right time of day, treating delirium or infection first. Assessing capacity in an untreated delirium and recording "lacks capacity" is a common and serious error.
capacity_the_central_concept.unwise_decisions: A person with capacity is ENTITLED to make a decision others consider unwise. That is not evidence of incapacity — but it is also not the end of the enquiry, because of coercion.
capacity_the_central_concept.the_coercion_caveat: Capacity assumes the decision is the person’s OWN. Where someone is subject to COERCION or UNDUE INFLUENCE, an apparently capacitous decision may not be freely made. This is why seeing the person ALONE is essential before accepting a decision to return to a situation you are worried about.
capacity_the_central_concept.best_interests: Where capacity is absent, decisions are made in the person’s BEST INTERESTS — considering their past and present wishes, beliefs and values, and consulting those close to them. It is not simply the clinically optimal choice. Check for a valid advance decision or a registered attorney with the relevant authority.

domestic_abuse_and_coercive_control.the_point_often_missed: Domestic abuse is not limited to physical violence and is not limited to younger people or to women. COERCIVE CONTROL — a pattern of intimidation, isolation, monitoring, financial restriction and degradation — is itself abuse and is a criminal offence in some jurisdictions.
domestic_abuse_and_coercive_control.clinical_indicators: Repeated attendance with vague or minor complaints, injuries inconsistent with the account, delay in presenting, chronic pain, depression, anxiety, substance misuse, and a partner who will not leave the room.
domestic_abuse_and_coercive_control.pregnancy: Domestic abuse frequently BEGINS or ESCALATES in pregnancy and the postpartum period. Routine enquiry in antenatal care exists for that reason.
domestic_abuse_and_coercive_control.the_highest_risk_moment: Risk of serious harm is greatest around SEPARATION. Any safety plan must account for that rather than simply advising the person to leave.

body.the_carer_dimension: Some abuse arises from carer stress, exhaustion and lack of support rather than malice — this does not make it acceptable or excuse it, but it changes the intervention: respite, support and services may resolve it where a punitive approach would not. Assess the carer’s needs as part of the response.
what_to_do: Ensure IMMEDIATE SAFETY, and treat the medical problem.
SEE THE PERSON ALONE. This is as important here as in child safeguarding and is skipped far more often.
Assess CAPACITY for the specific decision, supporting it properly first.
DOCUMENT factually — verbatim quotes, body map, measurements.
Where the person has capacity, seek their CONSENT to refer — but refer WITHOUT consent if others are at risk, if a crime has been committed, if there is coercion, or if your local policy requires it.
Refer to adult safeguarding per your local pathway; involve the police where a crime is suspected.
Consider OTHER people at risk — other residents in a care home, other dependants, children in the household.
Escalate organisational concerns about an institution, not just the individual case.

warnings: SEE THE PERSON ALONE before accepting any decision about discharge or living arrangements.
Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific. Assess for THIS decision, at THIS time.
Do not assess capacity during untreated delirium or infection and record it as settled.
Take all practicable steps to support capacity first — hearing aids, glasses, interpreter, timing.
An unwise decision is not incapacity — but coercion can make an apparently capacitous decision not truly the person’s own.
Financial abuse is the commonest reported form in older people. Ask who manages the money.
Sedation for carer convenience is abuse.
Domestic abuse often begins or escalates in pregnancy.
Risk of serious harm peaks around separation — a safety plan must account for that.
Withholding glasses, hearing aids or walking aids is neglect, not a minor omission.
Consider other people at risk — other care home residents, dependants, children in the household.
Escalate organisational concerns, not only the individual case.
limitations: Capacity legislation, safeguarding duties and referral routes are JURISDICTION-SPECIFIC. Follow your national law and local policy.
This entry supports recognition and referral; it does not replace mandatory safeguarding or capacity training.

flashcards.q: What are the four elements of the functional capacity test?
flashcards.a: Understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate the decision.

flashcards.q: Is capacity global?
flashcards.a: No — it is decision-specific and time-specific, and it can fluctuate.

flashcards.q: Does an unwise decision indicate incapacity?
flashcards.a: No. But check for coercion, which can make a decision not truly the person’s own.

flashcards.q: Commonest reported form of elder abuse?
flashcards.a: Financial abuse.

flashcards.q: Which everyday omission counts as neglect?
flashcards.a: Withholding glasses, hearing aids or walking aids.

flashcards.q: When does domestic abuse commonly begin or escalate?
flashcards.a: In pregnancy and the postpartum period.

flashcards.q: When is the risk of serious harm highest?
flashcards.a: Around separation — safety planning must account for it.

flashcards.q: What must you do before accepting a discharge decision you are worried about?
flashcards.a: See the person alone.

checkboxes: Capacity assessed for the specific decision after supporting it
Delirium and infection treated before formal capacity assessment
Consent sought where capacity present, and overridden only on stated grounds

entries.title: Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding — Structured History
entries.summary: Two questions decide the pace: how much, and how fast. Then establish whether this is VARICEAL or not, because that changes the drugs, the urgency and the prognosis before endoscopy has happened.

the_presenting_complaint.appearance_of_the_vomitus: FRESH RED blood means active brisk bleeding. COFFEE GROUND means blood altered by gastric acid — slower or stopped. Ask them to describe it or show a photograph; "vomiting blood" covers both and they are different problems.
the_presenting_complaint.volume_and_frequency: How many episodes, and how much each time — use household measures (a teaspoon, a cupful, a bowlful) because millilitres mean nothing to most people.
the_presenting_complaint.onset_and_duration: When did it start, and is it continuing?
the_presenting_complaint.melaena: BLACK, TARRY, offensive, sticky stool. It indicates blood that has been DIGESTED, so it implies an upper GI source and at least a moderate volume. Distinguish it from the harmless black stool of IRON tablets or bismuth, which is not tarry and not offensive. Ask directly about the smell — patients remember it.
the_presenting_complaint.haematochezia: FRESH blood per rectum usually means a LOWER GI source — but a MASSIVE upper GI bleed can transit fast enough to present as fresh red blood with SHOCK. Fresh rectal bleeding in a shocked patient should not be assumed to be lower GI.
the_presenting_complaint.the_two_mimics: HAEMOPTYSIS (coughed, frothy, bright, alkaline) and swallowed blood from EPISTAXIS or a dental source. Ask specifically — patients often cannot tell you whether they coughed or vomited it.

the_associated_symptoms_and_what_each_ru.dizziness_syncope_breathlessness: Indicates significant volume loss. This, not the appearance of the vomit, is the best bedside marker of severity.
the_associated_symptoms_and_what_each_ru.abdominal_pain: Epigastric pain relieved or worsened by food suggests PEPTIC ULCER. Sudden severe pain with peritonism suggests PERFORATION rather than simple bleeding.
the_associated_symptoms_and_what_each_ru.retching_before_the_blood: Vomiting or retching FIRST, then blood, is the classic MALLORY-WEISS story — a mucosal tear from the retching itself.

establishing_whether_this_is_variceal.why_it_matters_before_endoscopy: Variceal bleeding has much higher mortality and needs different immediate treatment — vasoactive therapy and antibiotics — started on suspicion rather than after diagnosis.
establishing_whether_this_is_variceal.what_to_ask_and_look_for: Known chronic liver disease or cirrhosis · ALCOHOL history, asked properly in units and honestly · viral hepatitis risk factors · previous variceal bleed or banding · known ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy · and on examination the STIGMATA of chronic liver disease — spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, caput medusae, splenomegaly, ascites, asterixis.

body.drugs_and_risk_factors: NSAIDs (including over-the-counter and traditional remedies — ask specifically, people do not consider them "medication") · ASPIRIN and other antiplatelets · ANTICOAGULANTS including DOACs, and when the last dose was · CORTICOSTEROIDS · SSRIs · previous ulcer or Helicobacter pylori · previous GI bleeding · smoking · alcohol.
body.past_history_and_comorbidity: Cardiac and respiratory disease determine how poorly they will tolerate anaemia and how cautious transfusion must be. Renal impairment affects drug handling. Previous aortic graft raises the rare but lethal AORTO-ENTERIC FISTULA — always ask about previous aortic surgery in a massive upper GI bleed.
body.examination_priorities: Airway and conscious level · pulse, blood pressure, POSTURAL drop, capillary refill · signs of chronic liver disease · abdominal tenderness and peritonism · DIGITAL RECTAL EXAMINATION to confirm melaena — this is essential and is often omitted.
body.investigations: Full blood count (a NORMAL haemoglobin early does not exclude major bleeding — it takes hours to fall), urea and electrolytes (a DISPROPORTIONATELY RAISED UREA relative to creatinine supports an upper GI source, from absorbed protein), liver function, clotting, group and SAVE or CROSSMATCH, venous gas for lactate and rapid haemoglobin.
body.scoring_and_disposal: The GLASGOW-BLATCHFORD score identifies very low-risk patients who may avoid admission; the ROCKALL score estimates mortality and rebleeding, pre- and post-endoscopy. Use whichever your service uses, and do not let a low score override a patient who looks unwell.
body.the_immediate_actions_in_parallel_with_t: Two large-bore cannulae · resuscitate with fluid and blood as needed · correct coagulopathy · in suspected VARICEAL bleeding start a vasoactive agent and PROPHYLACTIC ANTIBIOTICS (which independently reduce mortality — a frequently forgotten but evidence-based step) · discuss urgent ENDOSCOPY timing · involve seniors early.

warnings: A normal haemoglobin early does NOT exclude major bleeding — it takes hours to fall.
Fresh rectal bleeding in a SHOCKED patient may be a massive upper GI bleed, not a lower GI source.
Give prophylactic ANTIBIOTICS in suspected variceal bleeding — they independently reduce mortality and are routinely forgotten.
Ask about NSAIDs specifically, including over-the-counter and traditional remedies — people do not report them as medication.
Ask about previous aortic surgery — aorto-enteric fistula is rare and lethal.
Perform a digital rectal examination to confirm melaena.
Black stool from iron or bismuth is not tarry or offensive — do not mistake it for melaena, or melaena for it.
A disproportionately raised urea supports an upper GI source.
Do not let a low risk score override a patient who looks unwell.
limitations: Transfusion thresholds, endoscopy timing, scoring cut-offs and drug choices are protocol-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Fresh red vs coffee ground vomitus?
flashcards.a: Fresh means active brisk bleeding; coffee ground means altered by acid — slower or stopped.

flashcards.q: What distinguishes melaena from iron-related black stool?
flashcards.a: Melaena is tarry, sticky and offensive. Iron stool is not.

flashcards.q: What does retching before the blood suggest?
flashcards.a: Mallory-Weiss tear.

flashcards.q: Which forgotten intervention reduces mortality in variceal bleeding?
flashcards.a: Prophylactic antibiotics.

flashcards.q: Why can the haemoglobin be normal?
flashcards.a: It is a concentration — it takes hours to fall after acute blood loss.

flashcards.q: Which past surgical history is critical to ask about?
flashcards.a: Aortic graft surgery — aorto-enteric fistula.

flashcards.q: Why does urea rise disproportionately?
flashcards.a: Absorbed blood protein is a nitrogen load — it supports an upper GI source.

checkboxes: Full drug history including OTC and traditional remedies
Group and save or crossmatch sent
Risk score calculated and seniors involved

entries.title: Oliguria, Frothy Urine and Body Swelling — Structured History
entries.summary: Three questions in order: is there OBSTRUCTION (reversible today), is this PRE-RENAL (reversible today), or is it INTRINSIC? Frothy urine plus swelling points to nephrotic-range protein loss and needs a different workup from oliguria alone.

terms: oliguria, frothy urine and body swelling — structured history

the_presenting_complaint.quantify_the_urine: Oliguria is conventionally under 0.5 mL/kg/hour, or under about 400 mL/day. ANURIA — essentially no urine — is a different and narrower problem: think complete OBSTRUCTION, a vascular catastrophe, or a blocked catheter. Always ask whether a catheter is in and whether it has been flushed, because a blocked catheter is the commonest cause of sudden "anuria" on a ward.
the_presenting_complaint.timing: When was it first noticed, and was it sudden or gradual? Sudden complete cessation points to obstruction.
the_presenting_complaint.colour: COCA-COLA or smoky urine suggests glomerular haematuria (nephritic). Frank red blood suggests a urological source. Concentrated dark urine suggests dehydration.
the_presenting_complaint.frothy_urine: Persistent froth that does not clear indicates significant PROTEINURIA. It is a genuinely useful lay symptom and is rarely asked about. Ask how long it has been there.

body_swelling_where_it_starts_matters.periorbital_and_facial_first_worse_in_th: Suggests a RENAL cause — low oncotic pressure distributes with gravity overnight, so it collects in the loose periorbital tissue while lying flat. This is the classic nephrotic pattern and is prominent in children.
body_swelling_where_it_starts_matters.ankles_and_legs_first_worse_in_the_eveni: Suggests a CARDIAC or venous cause, or hypoalbuminaemia in an ambulant patient.
body_swelling_where_it_starts_matters.abdominal_distension: Ascites — consider liver disease, or severe nephrotic syndrome.
body_swelling_where_it_starts_matters.generalised: Anasarca — severe hypoalbuminaemia from any cause.

the_three_questions_in_order.one_is_it_obstructed: Ask about poor stream, hesitancy, terminal dribbling, incomplete emptying, nocturia (prostatic disease); known pelvic malignancy; renal stones; a single functioning kidney. SCAN THE BLADDER. Obstruction is the fully reversible cause and it is missed by not looking for it.
the_three_questions_in_order.two_is_it_pre_renal: Ask about vomiting, diarrhoea, reduced intake, bleeding, burns, fever and sepsis; diuretics; and the drugs that impair autoregulation — ACE inhibitors and ARBs, NSAIDs, and diuretics, the so-called TRIPLE WHAMMY, which together are a well-described cause of avoidable AKI.
the_three_questions_in_order.three_is_it_intrinsic: Then think glomerular, tubular, interstitial or vascular — and the history below points the way.

the_aetiological_questions_and_what_each.recent_sore_throat_or_skin_infection: POST-STREPTOCOCCAL glomerulonephritis — classically 1 to 3 weeks after a THROAT infection or 3 to 6 weeks after a SKIN infection. IgA nephropathy by contrast produces haematuria within 1 to 2 DAYS of an upper respiratory infection — the interval is the discriminator and it is worth asking precisely.
the_aetiological_questions_and_what_each.analgesic_use: NSAID use, including traditional and over-the-counter preparations, causing interstitial nephritis or pre-renal injury. Ask about quantity and duration, not just whether they take them.
the_aetiological_questions_and_what_each.sharing_of_sharps_tattoos_transfusions_u: Screens for HIV, hepatitis B and C — all cause specific glomerular disease (HIVAN, membranous, membranoproliferative). Ask sensitively and in private.
the_aetiological_questions_and_what_each.rash_joint_pains_oral_ulcers_photosensit: LUPUS nephritis and other connective tissue disease.
the_aetiological_questions_and_what_each.haemoptysis_with_haematuria: PULMONARY-RENAL syndrome — anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture) or ANCA-associated vasculitis. This combination is a medical emergency and must not be treated as two separate problems.
the_aetiological_questions_and_what_each.recent_contrast_or_new_drugs: Contrast nephropathy; aminoglycosides; vancomycin; proton pump inhibitors and antibiotics causing interstitial nephritis (look for rash, fever and eosinophilia).
the_aetiological_questions_and_what_each.muscle_pain_or_a_long_lie_or_seizures: RHABDOMYOLYSIS — check CK and potassium urgently.
the_aetiological_questions_and_what_each.weight_loss_bone_pain_back_pain: MYELOMA — check calcium, protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains. Myeloma is a classic missed cause of unexplained renal failure, especially with anaemia and a raised calcium.
the_aetiological_questions_and_what_each.diabetes_and_hypertension_duration: The commonest causes of chronic kidney disease worldwide. Ask about duration, control, and whether retinopathy is present — diabetic nephropathy almost always accompanies retinopathy, so its absence should make you question the diagnosis.
the_aetiological_questions_and_what_each.family_history: ADPKD, Alport syndrome, sickle cell disease.

body.examination_priorities: Volume status — postural blood pressure, JVP, mucous membranes, skin turgor, capillary refill · oedema distribution and whether it pits · blood pressure · PALPABLE BLADDER · abdominal masses or bruits · rash, joint swelling, uveitis · chest for crackles and effusions · rectal examination for prostate.
body.investigations: URINE DIPSTICK first and immediately — blood and protein together suggest a glomerular cause and change everything. Then urine microscopy for RED CELL CASTS (glomerulonephritis) and a protein:creatinine or albumin:creatinine ratio. Bloods: renal profile, calcium, bone profile, albumin, CK, full blood count, clotting, inflammatory markers, and where indicated ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, complement, immunoglobulins and electrophoresis, hepatitis and HIV serology. ULTRASOUND to exclude obstruction and assess size — small kidneys mean chronic disease.
body.the_immediate_priorities: POTASSIUM and an ECG first — hyperkalaemia kills before the creatinine matters. Then fluid status, stop nephrotoxics, relieve obstruction, treat sepsis, and identify indications for dialysis (AEIOU).

warnings: Check POTASSIUM and get an ECG immediately — hyperkalaemia kills before anything else does.
Scan the bladder. Obstruction is the fully reversible cause and is missed by not looking.
Sudden anuria on a ward is a blocked catheter until proven otherwise.
Blood AND protein on dipstick together suggests a glomerular cause — escalate, do not observe.
Haemoptysis with haematuria is a pulmonary-renal syndrome and a medical emergency.
Post-streptococcal nephritis follows infection by weeks; IgA nephropathy follows by days. The interval discriminates.
Diabetic nephropathy almost always accompanies retinopathy — its absence should make you question the diagnosis.
Consider myeloma in unexplained renal failure, especially with anaemia, raised calcium or bone pain.
Ask about NSAIDs and traditional remedies specifically — patients do not report them as medication.
Small kidneys on ultrasound mean chronic disease, which changes the entire plan.
limitations: Investigation panels and referral thresholds are service-specific.

flashcards.q: What defines oliguria?
flashcards.a: Under 0.5 mL/kg/hour, or about 400 mL/day. Anuria is a different, narrower problem.

flashcards.q: What does periorbital swelling worse in the morning suggest?
flashcards.a: A renal cause — the classic nephrotic pattern.

flashcards.q: What does frothy urine indicate?
flashcards.a: Significant proteinuria.

flashcards.q: Post-streptococcal vs IgA nephropathy timing?
flashcards.a: Post-strep: 1 to 3 weeks after throat, 3 to 6 after skin. IgA: 1 to 2 days after an URTI.

flashcards.q: Haemoptysis plus haematuria?
flashcards.a: Pulmonary-renal syndrome — anti-GBM or ANCA vasculitis. Emergency.

flashcards.q: What is the triple whammy?
flashcards.a: ACE inhibitor or ARB, plus diuretic, plus NSAID — a well-described cause of avoidable AKI.

flashcards.q: First two investigations in oliguria?
flashcards.a: Potassium with an ECG, and a urine dipstick.

flashcards.q: What does absent retinopathy imply in presumed diabetic nephropathy?
flashcards.a: Question the diagnosis — they usually coexist.

entries.title: Seizure, Cough, Chest Pain and Generalised Weakness — Structured Histories
entries.summary: Four presentations, four structures. In seizure the value is almost entirely in the EYEWITNESS account. In cough it is the duration. In chest pain it is what you rule out before you rule anything in. In weakness it is whether it is truly neurological at all.

terms: seizure, cough, chest pain and generalised weakness — structured histories

seizure.the_governing_principle: The patient cannot tell you what happened during the event. THE EYEWITNESS ACCOUNT IS THE INVESTIGATION — obtain it directly, by telephone if necessary. A clerking without it is largely guesswork, and this is the single most consequential omission in seizure assessment.
seizure.before_pre_ictal: What were they doing? Standing (favours syncope), lying (favours seizure)? Any warning — an AURA such as a rising epigastric sensation, an unusual smell, or a focal sensory or motor symptom, which suggests a FOCAL onset and localises it. Prodromal pallor, sweating, nausea and tunnel vision favour SYNCOPE. Triggers: sleep deprivation, alcohol or its withdrawal, flashing lights, missed medication, fever in a child, recreational drugs.
seizure.during_ictal: DURATION — ask them to estimate, and note that observers overestimate substantially; ask what they did in that time to calibrate it. Was there a CRY at onset? Were the movements generalised and rhythmic, or focal, or asynchronous and thrashing? Were the EYES OPEN (usual in seizure) or closed and resisting opening (which favours a non-epileptic attack)? Colour — pale (syncope) or cyanosed (seizure)? TONGUE BITING, especially LATERAL, is quite specific for a generalised seizure; tip biting is less so. Incontinence occurs in both and is far less discriminating than commonly taught.
seizure.after_post_ictal: CONFUSION and drowsiness lasting minutes to hours strongly favours a seizure; rapid, complete recovery within seconds favours SYNCOPE. Headache, myalgia, TODD PARESIS (a transient focal weakness after a focal seizure, which mimics stroke and is misdiagnosed as one). Any injury sustained.
seizure.the_wider_history: Number and pattern of previous episodes · birth history, developmental delay, febrile convulsions, head injury, meningitis, CNS infection, stroke, tumour · FAMILY history · alcohol and drug history · adherence to antiepileptics and any recent dose change or new interacting drug · pregnancy status and contraception (enzyme-inducing drugs and teratogenicity) · DRIVING, occupation, and activities such as swimming or bathing alone.
seizure.the_things_that_must_be_excluded: HYPOGLYCAEMIA — check the glucose in every seizure, always. Also electrolytes (sodium, calcium, magnesium), eclampsia in any pregnant or recently pregnant woman, meningitis or encephalitis, intracranial haemorrhage or mass, and drug or alcohol withdrawal.
seizure.the_practical_duties: Advise about DRIVING and about safety (showers rather than baths, not swimming alone, care with heights and machinery). These conversations are legally and practically important and are regularly forgotten in the acute setting.

cough.duration_first: ACUTE under 3 weeks — usually infective. SUBACUTE 3 to 8 weeks — often post-infectious. CHRONIC over 8 weeks — a different differential entirely. Duration is the first branch point and it determines everything after it.
cough.character_and_timing: DRY or PRODUCTIVE. Worse at NIGHT (asthma, reflux, heart failure) or in the MORNING (COPD, bronchiectasis). Seasonal or exposure-related. Barking (croup), whooping with post-tussive vomiting (pertussis, which occurs in adults and is under-diagnosed).
cough.sputum: Volume, colour, consistency. Copious purulent sputum daily for years suggests BRONCHIECTASIS. Frothy PINK sputum suggests pulmonary oedema. HAEMOPTYSIS must be quantified and taken seriously.
cough.associated_symptoms: Fever, night sweats, weight loss (TB, malignancy, lymphoma) · breathlessness and exercise tolerance in real terms (how many steps, how far on the flat) · chest pain, pleuritic or otherwise · wheeze · hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal involvement, or reflux) · heartburn and regurgitation · postnasal drip and sinus symptoms.
cough.the_chronic_cough_triad: Most chronic cough with a normal chest film in a non-smoker is one of three things: UPPER AIRWAY COUGH SYNDROME (postnasal drip), ASTHMA including cough-variant asthma, or GASTRO-OESOPHAGEAL REFLUX. And always ask about ACE INHIBITORS — a dry cough may start months or even a year after starting one, so patients and clinicians do not connect them.
cough.the_exposure_history_that_is_routinely_s: SMOKING in pack-years, and second-hand smoke · BIOMASS FUEL exposure — cooking on wood, charcoal, dung or crop residue indoors is a major global cause of COPD, particularly in women who have never smoked, and it is almost never asked about · OCCUPATION — dust, asbestos, silica, farming, birds · TB CONTACT and previous TB treatment · travel · HIV status · pets and birds.
cough.red_flags: Haemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats, hoarseness, dysphagia, a smoker over 40 with a new or changed cough, clubbing, a cough that does not resolve, or focal chest signs — all warrant a chest image and further thought.

chest_pain_socrates.the_structure: SITE · ONSET · CHARACTER · RADIATION · ASSOCIATED symptoms · TIMING · EXACERBATING and relieving factors · SEVERITY.

what_each_element_actually_discriminates.onset: MAXIMAL AT ONSET suggests AORTIC DISSECTION or pulmonary embolism. Crescendo over minutes suggests ischaemia.
what_each_element_actually_discriminates.character: Crushing, heavy or tight suggests ischaemia. TEARING suggests dissection. SHARP and PLEURITIC suggests pleura, pericardium or PE. Burning suggests reflux — but reflux and ischaemia are frequently indistinguishable by character alone, and "it felt like indigestion" has killed people.
what_each_element_actually_discriminates.radiation: To jaw, neck or left arm suggests ischaemia. THROUGH TO THE BACK suggests dissection. To the shoulder tip suggests diaphragmatic irritation.
what_each_element_actually_discriminates.exacerbating_and_relieving: Worse on INSPIRATION or coughing means pleuritic. Worse LYING FLAT and better sitting forward suggests PERICARDITIS. Reproducible on palpation suggests musculoskeletal — but tenderness does NOT exclude a serious cause and has been documented in myocardial infarction. Related to exertion and relieved by rest suggests angina.
what_each_element_actually_discriminates.associated: Sweating, nausea and vomiting raise the probability of a serious cardiac cause substantially. Breathlessness, syncope, palpitations, fever, haemoptysis, and calf pain or swelling.

chest_pain_socrates.the_five_that_must_be_actively_excluded: Acute coronary syndrome · AORTIC DISSECTION · PULMONARY EMBOLISM · TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX · OESOPHAGEAL RUPTURE (Boerhaave — severe pain after forceful vomiting, with subcutaneous emphysema). Also consider pericarditis with tamponade.
chest_pain_socrates.the_atypical_warning: WOMEN, OLDER people, people with DIABETES and those with chronic kidney disease present atypically — breathlessness alone, epigastric discomfort, fatigue, nausea, syncope or confusion. A low threshold for an ECG in these groups saves lives.
chest_pain_socrates.the_risk_factors: Smoking, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, family history of premature cardiovascular disease, previous events, cocaine use, and — for PE — immobility, surgery, malignancy, pregnancy, oestrogen therapy and previous VTE.

generalised_body_weakness.the_first_question: Does the patient mean WEAKNESS (reduced power) or FATIGUE (reduced energy with normal power)? They are used interchangeably by patients and mean completely different things. Ask about a specific TASK: can you rise from a chair without using your arms? Can you lift a saucepan onto a high shelf? Can you climb stairs?

if_it_is_true_weakness.distribution: PROXIMAL (rising from a chair, combing hair) suggests MYOPATHY, inflammatory myositis, steroid or statin myopathy, thyroid disease, osteomalacia. DISTAL (buttons, keys, foot drop, tripping) suggests NEUROPATHY. Focal or one-sided suggests a central lesion. Ascending and symmetrical suggests GUILLAIN-BARRE. FATIGABLE, worse through the day, with ptosis or diplopia, suggests MYASTHENIA.
if_it_is_true_weakness.time_course: Sudden — stroke, cord compression, hypokalaemia. Days to weeks — Guillain-Barre, myositis, cord compression. Months to years — muscular dystrophy, motor neurone disease, chronic neuropathy.
if_it_is_true_weakness.the_red_flags: Any SENSORY LEVEL, bladder or bowel disturbance, or back pain with weakness means CORD COMPRESSION — an emergency needing urgent MRI. Respiratory or bulbar involvement means monitor the FVC.

generalised_body_weakness.the_causes_that_are_not_neurological_and: ANAEMIA · hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia, hypophosphataemia · hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism · Addison disease · diabetes · chronic infection including HIV and TB · MALIGNANCY · heart failure · chronic kidney or liver disease · DEPRESSION · malnutrition and vitamin D deficiency · sleep apnoea · and DRUGS — statins, steroids, diuretics causing hypokalaemia.
generalised_body_weakness.the_aetiological_questions_worth_asking_: Recent SORE THROAT or diarrhoeal illness (Guillain-Barre, post-streptococcal disease) · ANALGESIC and traditional remedy use · SHARING OF SHARPS, tattoos, transfusions and sexual history (HIV) · alcohol · weight change · fever and night sweats · family history of muscle disease · exposure to organophosphates or heavy metals.
generalised_body_weakness.the_essential_early_tests: Glucose, full blood count, electrolytes INCLUDING potassium, calcium, magnesium and phosphate, renal and liver function, TSH, CK, inflammatory markers, and HIV where relevant. Hypokalaemia and hypercalcaemia in particular are trivially reversible causes of profound weakness and must be excluded before anything elaborate.

warnings: In seizure, obtain the EYEWITNESS account — by telephone if necessary. Without it the assessment is guesswork.
Check the GLUCOSE in every seizure.
Eyes CLOSED and resisting opening favours a non-epileptic attack; eyes are usually open in a seizure.
Todd paresis mimics stroke after a focal seizure.
Discuss DRIVING and safety after any seizure — it is regularly forgotten acutely.
Ask about biomass fuel exposure in chronic cough — it is a major global cause of COPD in never-smokers and is almost never asked.
An ACE inhibitor cough can begin up to a year after starting the drug, so the link is missed.
Chest pain MAXIMAL AT ONSET suggests dissection or PE, not ischaemia.
Chest wall tenderness does NOT exclude myocardial infarction.
Women, older people and people with diabetes present atypically — have a low threshold for an ECG.
Separate weakness from fatigue by asking about a specific task.
A sensory level, or back pain with weakness, means cord compression — urgent MRI.
Exclude hypokalaemia and hypercalcaemia early in any weakness — both are trivially reversible.
limitations: Templates support a structured history; they do not replace examination, investigation or clinical judgement.

flashcards.q: What is the single most important element of a seizure history?
flashcards.a: The eyewitness account — obtain it directly, by telephone if needed.

flashcards.q: What post-event feature best separates seizure from syncope?
flashcards.a: Prolonged post-ictal confusion versus rapid complete recovery.

flashcards.q: What does lateral tongue biting suggest?
flashcards.a: A generalised seizure — it is reasonably specific. Incontinence is not.

flashcards.q: First branch point in a cough history?
flashcards.a: Duration — acute under 3 weeks, subacute 3 to 8, chronic over 8.

flashcards.q: Three commonest causes of chronic cough with a normal film?
flashcards.a: Upper airway cough syndrome, asthma, and reflux — plus ACE inhibitors.

flashcards.q: What does pain maximal at onset suggest?
flashcards.a: Aortic dissection or pulmonary embolism.

flashcards.q: Does chest wall tenderness exclude MI?
flashcards.a: No — it has been documented in myocardial infarction.

flashcards.q: How do you separate weakness from fatigue?
flashcards.a: Ask about a specific task — rising from a chair without using the arms.

flashcards.q: Proximal vs distal weakness?
flashcards.a: Proximal suggests myopathy; distal suggests neuropathy.

flashcards.q: Which weakness finding is an emergency?
flashcards.a: A sensory level or back pain with weakness — cord compression, urgent MRI.

checkboxes: Eyewitness account obtained for any seizure
Five lethal causes of chest pain actively considered
Potassium and calcium checked in weakness

entries.title: Local Anaesthetics and LA Systemic Toxicity
entries.summary: The maximum dose is by WEIGHT and it is routinely exceeded. Toxicity starts with tingling lips and a metallic taste, progresses to seizures, and ends in cardiac arrest — and the treatment is LIPID EMULSION, which every place that injects local anaesthetic must have immediately available.

terms: local anaesthetics and la systemic toxicity

body.how_they_work: They block voltage-gated SODIUM channels from inside the axon, preventing depolarisation. They work best on SMALL, MYELINATED fibres — so pain and temperature go first, then touch, then motor. That order explains why a patient can feel pressure and movement while feeling no pain, and telling them so in advance prevents a great deal of distress.
body.why_they_fail_in_infected_tissue: Local anaesthetics are weak BASES. They must be UN-IONISED to cross the axonal membrane. Infected tissue is ACIDIC, which pushes the drug into its ionised form so it cannot enter the axon. This is why anaesthetising an abscess is difficult, and why a field or regional block placed away from the infected area works better than injecting into it.

the_dose_is_by_weight.the_principle: Maximum doses are expressed in mg per kg. The commonest serious error is thinking in millilitres and volumes rather than in milligrams for that patient — especially in CHILDREN and small adults, where a volume that seems modest can be a large dose.
the_dose_is_by_weight.the_percentage_conversion: A 1% solution contains 10 mg per mL. So 1% = 10 mg/mL, 0.5% = 5 mg/mL, 2% = 20 mg/mL. Every calculation starts here, and getting this conversion wrong is a documented cause of overdose.
the_dose_is_by_weight.adrenaline: Adding adrenaline causes vasoconstriction, which SLOWS systemic absorption. It therefore allows a HIGHER maximum dose, prolongs the block, and reduces bleeding. Avoid in patients where vasoconstriction is undesirable, and follow current guidance about digits and appendages — the traditional absolute prohibition has been substantially revised, but local policy governs.
the_dose_is_by_weight.confirm_locally: Actual maximum doses differ between agents, between formulations with and without adrenaline, and between national formularies. Look them up every time. Scout deliberately does not state doses.

last_local_anaesthetic_systemic_toxicity.how_it_happens: Excessive total dose, INADVERTENT INTRAVASCULAR INJECTION, or rapid absorption from a vascular site (intercostal blocks absorb fastest). It can also occur with a delayed onset, so monitoring must continue after the injection is finished.

the_progression.early_cns_excitation: PERIORAL TINGLING and numbness of the tongue · METALLIC TASTE · TINNITUS · light-headedness, visual disturbance · agitation, confusion, slurred speech. These are the WARNING signs and they are the point at which to stop injecting immediately.
the_progression.then_cns_depression: Muscle twitching, then SEIZURES, then coma and respiratory arrest.
the_progression.then_cardiovascular: Hypertension and tachycardia initially, then bradycardia, conduction block, ventricular arrhythmias, profound myocardial depression and CARDIAC ARREST.
the_progression.the_important_caveat: This orderly progression is NOT reliable. Cardiovascular collapse can be the FIRST manifestation, particularly with BUPIVACAINE, which is the most cardiotoxic of the common agents and binds cardiac sodium channels avidly and dissociates slowly.

the_management: Call for help. Airway, 100% oxygen, and ventilate — hypoxia and acidosis markedly worsen toxicity.
Give LIPID EMULSION per your local protocol — it acts as a "lipid sink", drawing the lipophilic drug out of cardiac tissue.
If cardiac arrest occurs, start CPR and continue for a PROLONGED period — recovery after very long resuscitation is well documented, because the drug redistributes. Do not stop early.
AVOID lidocaine as an antiarrhythmic here (it is another sodium channel blocker). Avoid vasopressin. Use reduced doses of adrenaline per protocol.
Continue monitoring for at least several hours afterwards — recurrence happens.
last_local_anaesthetic_systemic_toxicity.prevention: ASPIRATE before injecting and repeat during injection. Inject SLOWLY and in INCREMENTS. Talk to the patient throughout — an awake patient reporting a metallic taste is the earliest and best monitor you have. Use the lowest effective dose and concentration. Consider ultrasound guidance. And know where the lipid emulsion is kept BEFORE you need it.

agent_specific_points.lidocaine: Fast onset, short to medium duration. The workhorse.
agent_specific_points.bupivacaine_and_levobupivacaine: Slower onset, LONG duration. Most CARDIOTOXIC. Levobupivacaine and ropivacaine are less cardiotoxic alternatives and are preferred for large-volume blocks.
agent_specific_points.prilocaine: Used in intravenous regional anaesthesia. Causes METHAEMOGLOBINAEMIA at higher doses — suspect it with cyanosis that does NOT improve with oxygen, chocolate-brown blood, and a saturation reading stuck around 85% that does not fit the clinical picture. Treated with methylene blue.
agent_specific_points.topical_preparations: EMLA and tetracaine gels are systemically absorbed, particularly through broken or inflamed skin and mucosa, and over large areas in small children. Overdose from topical agents is documented and is easy to forget.

warnings: Calculate the maximum dose in mg/kg for THAT patient. Thinking in millilitres is the commonest route to overdose.
A 1% solution is 10 mg/mL. Getting this conversion wrong causes overdose.
Cardiovascular collapse can be the FIRST sign of toxicity, especially with bupivacaine. Do not rely on the warning symptoms appearing first.
Know where the LIPID EMULSION is before you inject. Every site injecting local anaesthetic must have it immediately available.
In LAST cardiac arrest, continue CPR for a prolonged period — recovery after long resuscitation is well documented.
Do NOT use lidocaine as an antiarrhythmic in LAST — it is another sodium channel blocker.
Aspirate before and during injection, inject slowly in increments, and keep talking to the patient.
Local anaesthetics work poorly in infected, acidic tissue — block away from the infection instead.
Prilocaine causes methaemoglobinaemia — cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen with a saturation stuck near 85%.
Topical anaesthetics are absorbed systemically, especially through broken skin and in small children.
Warn the patient they will feel pressure and movement but not pain — motor and pressure fibres are blocked last.
limitations: Maximum doses, lipid emulsion regimens and guidance on adrenaline in digits are formulary- and protocol-specific. Scout deliberately states no doses.

flashcards.q: How much drug is in a 1% solution?
flashcards.a: 10 mg per mL.

flashcards.q: Why do local anaesthetics fail in infected tissue?
flashcards.a: Acidity ionises the drug so it cannot cross the axonal membrane. Block away from the infection.

flashcards.q: Earliest symptoms of LAST?
flashcards.a: Perioral tingling, metallic taste, tinnitus, light-headedness.

flashcards.q: Which agent is most cardiotoxic?
flashcards.a: Bupivacaine — and collapse may be the first sign, without warning symptoms.

flashcards.q: Treatment of LAST?
flashcards.a: Stop injecting, airway and oxygen, benzodiazepine for seizures, lipid emulsion, prolonged CPR if arrested.

flashcards.q: Which antiarrhythmic must be avoided in LAST?
flashcards.a: Lidocaine — it is another sodium channel blocker.

flashcards.q: Which agent causes methaemoglobinaemia?
flashcards.a: Prilocaine — cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, saturation stuck near 85%.

flashcards.q: Why does adrenaline allow a higher maximum dose?
flashcards.a: Vasoconstriction slows systemic absorption.

checkboxes: Lipid emulsion location confirmed before injecting

entries.title: Induction Agents, Muscle Relaxants and Neuraxial Anaesthesia
entries.summary: Each induction agent is chosen for its HAEMODYNAMICS: propofol drops the pressure, ketamine maintains it, etomidate is cardiostable but suppresses the adrenals. Suxamethonium is fast but releases potassium — and in the wrong patient that causes cardiac arrest.

terms: induction agents, muscle relaxants and neuraxial anaesthesia

induction_agents.the_choosing_principle: In a haemodynamically unstable patient, the agent matters more than almost anything else you do. All induction agents cause some cardiovascular depression, and the sicker the patient the smaller the dose required.
induction_agents.propofol: Rapid, smooth, with antiemetic properties and quick clear-headed recovery. But it causes significant VASODILATATION and myocardial depression — HYPOTENSION is its defining problem, dangerous in the shocked, hypovolaemic or elderly patient. It also causes pain on injection. PROPOFOL INFUSION SYNDROME is a rare but often fatal complication of prolonged high-dose infusion, especially in children and in critical care — metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, arrhythmia and cardiac failure.
induction_agents.ketamine: A dissociative agent that MAINTAINS or increases blood pressure and heart rate through sympathetic stimulation, and PRESERVES airway reflexes and respiratory drive better than the others. It is BRONCHODILATING and provides ANALGESIA. This combination makes it the agent of choice in the shocked or asthmatic patient and in prehospital and austere settings. Drawbacks: EMERGENCE PHENOMENA (vivid dreams, hallucinations, agitation — reduced by a benzodiazepine and a quiet recovery), increased secretions, and caution where a rise in blood pressure is undesirable. Note that in a patient with EXHAUSTED catecholamine reserves ketamine can still cause hypotension, because its indirect sympathomimetic effect has nothing left to release — this is a subtlety that catches people out in profound shock.
induction_agents.etomidate: The most CARDIOSTABLE induction agent, which is why it is attractive in cardiac disease. But it causes ADRENAL SUPPRESSION after even a SINGLE DOSE, by inhibiting 11-beta-hydroxylase. This is controversial in terms of outcome but is a real pharmacological effect, and it has substantially reduced its use in sepsis. Also causes myoclonus and pain on injection.
induction_agents.thiopental: A barbiturate — rapid onset, anticonvulsant, reduces cerebral metabolic rate. Historically used for rapid sequence induction and in status epilepticus. Causes hypotension and is contraindicated in PORPHYRIA.

depolarising_suxamethonium.what: Binds and PERSISTENTLY activates the acetylcholine receptor, causing initial FASCICULATIONS then flaccid paralysis. Fastest onset and shortest duration of any relaxant, which is why it has been the traditional agent for rapid sequence induction.
depolarising_suxamethonium.the_potassium_problem: It causes a small potassium rise in everyone. But in patients with UP-REGULATED extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors, that rise is MASSIVE and can cause cardiac arrest. The at-risk groups are: BURNS (from about 24–48 hours until healing is complete, often months) · SPINAL CORD INJURY and other DENERVATION · prolonged IMMOBILITY or critical illness myopathy · MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY and other myopathies · severe intra-abdominal sepsis. Also avoid in pre-existing hyperkalaemia and in renal failure with a high potassium.
depolarising_suxamethonium.the_other_hazards: MALIGNANT HYPERTHERMIA trigger · raised intraocular, intracranial and intragastric pressure · bradycardia especially in children and with repeat doses · SUXAMETHONIUM APNOEA from pseudocholinesterase deficiency, where paralysis is prolonged for hours and the patient must remain sedated and ventilated until it wears off (the error is allowing them to wake paralysed) · myalgia.

neuromuscular_blockers.non_depolarising: ROCURONIUM (fast onset at higher dose, making it a suxamethonium alternative for rapid sequence induction), vecuronium, atracurium (Hofmann elimination — degrades independently of liver and kidney, so it is the choice in organ failure) and cisatracurium. They are COMPETITIVE antagonists.
neuromuscular_blockers.reversal: NEOSTIGMINE with an antimuscarinic (glycopyrronium or atropine — required to prevent bradycardia and secretions). SUGAMMADEX encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium and reverses even PROFOUND block rapidly, which has changed rescue in a "cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate" situation. Monitor depth of block objectively with a TRAIN-OF-FOUR — clinical assessment alone misses residual paralysis, which causes postoperative airway obstruction and aspiration.
neuromuscular_blockers.the_absolute_rule: NEVER PARALYSE A PATIENT WHO IS NOT ADEQUATELY ANAESTHETISED. Paralysis without anaesthesia produces AWARENESS — being conscious, in pain, and unable to move or signal. It is one of the most traumatic experiences in medicine and causes lasting psychological harm.

neuraxial_anaesthesia.spinal: A single injection of a small volume into the SUBARACHNOID space, BELOW the termination of the spinal cord (about L1–L2 in adults, so injection is at L3–L4 or below). Rapid, dense, reliable block of limited duration.
neuraxial_anaesthesia.epidural: A catheter into the EPIDURAL space, allowing a larger volume and CONTINUOUS or repeated dosing. Slower onset, segmental, titratable, and can be continued for postoperative analgesia or labour.

the_complications_that_matter.hypotension: From SYMPATHETIC blockade causing vasodilatation — expected, and more marked with a higher block and in the hypovolaemic. Pre-load, vasopressors, and in pregnancy LEFT LATERAL TILT to relieve aortocaval compression.
the_complications_that_matter.post_dural_puncture_headache: From CSF leak. POSTURAL — markedly worse sitting or standing, relieved by lying flat. That postural character is the diagnostic feature. Commoner with larger and cutting needles, and in young women. Managed conservatively at first; an EPIDURAL BLOOD PATCH is definitive for severe or persistent cases. A headache after neuraxial anaesthesia that is NOT postural should prompt thought about other causes including subdural haematoma and cerebral venous thrombosis.
the_complications_that_matter.total_spinal: Inadvertent intrathecal injection of an epidural dose. Rapidly ascending block causing profound hypotension, bradycardia, respiratory failure and loss of consciousness. Managed with airway support, ventilation, fluids and vasopressors — it is survivable if recognised immediately.
the_complications_that_matter.vertebral_canal_haematoma_and_abscess: RARE but CATASTROPHIC. Suspect with severe back pain, a block that is DENSER or LONGER than expected, a block that RECURS after wearing off, new weakness, or bladder dysfunction.
