It needs IMMEDIATE MRI and urgent neurosurgical decompression — the window to preserve function is measured in hours. Regular neurological observation after neuraxial blockade exists precisely to catch this.
the_complications_that_matter.the_anticoagulation_rule: Timing of neuraxial procedures around anticoagulants and antiplatelets is governed by strict published intervals, for insertion AND for catheter removal. Removing a catheter at the wrong time is as dangerous as inserting it at the wrong time — and it is the step more often forgotten.

neuraxial_anaesthesia.contraindications: Patient refusal, local infection at the site, uncorrected coagulopathy or therapeutic anticoagulation, raised intracranial pressure, severe uncorrected hypovolaemia, and severe fixed cardiac output states such as critical aortic stenosis.

warnings: NEVER paralyse a patient who is not adequately anaesthetised — awareness under paralysis causes lasting psychological harm.
Suxamethonium causes dangerous hyperkalaemia in burns (after 24–48 hours), denervation, spinal cord injury, prolonged immobility and myopathy. Avoid it in those groups.
Suxamethonium is a malignant hyperthermia trigger.
In suxamethonium apnoea the patient must stay sedated and ventilated — never allow them to wake paralysed.
Propofol causes hypotension — dangerous in shock, hypovolaemia and the elderly. Reduce the dose in the sick.
Ketamine can still cause hypotension in profound shock, once catecholamine reserves are exhausted.
Etomidate suppresses the adrenals after a single dose.
Use objective train-of-four monitoring — clinical assessment misses residual paralysis.
A post-neuraxial headache that is NOT postural is not a typical dural puncture headache — consider subdural haematoma or venous thrombosis.
Severe back pain, a denser or longer block than expected, or a block that recurs, suggests vertebral canal haematoma — immediate MRI, the window is hours.
Anticoagulation timing rules apply to catheter REMOVAL as well as insertion, and removal is the step more often forgotten.
In pregnancy use left lateral tilt to relieve aortocaval compression after neuraxial block.
limitations: All doses, anticoagulation intervals, monitoring standards and block techniques are protocol-specific and require appropriate training. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Which induction agent best maintains blood pressure?
flashcards.a: Ketamine — sympathetic stimulation. But it can still drop pressure in exhausted catecholamine reserves.

flashcards.q: What is the defining problem with propofol?
flashcards.a: Hypotension from vasodilatation and myocardial depression.

flashcards.q: What is etomidate’s specific drawback?
flashcards.a: Adrenal suppression after even a single dose.

flashcards.q: Which groups must not receive suxamethonium?
flashcards.a: Burns after 24–48 hours, denervation, spinal cord injury, prolonged immobility, myopathy, hyperkalaemia.

flashcards.q: What is suxamethonium apnoea?
flashcards.a: Prolonged paralysis from pseudocholinesterase deficiency — keep sedated and ventilated.

flashcards.q: Which relaxant is safest in liver and renal failure?
flashcards.a: Atracurium — Hofmann elimination is organ-independent.

flashcards.q: What reverses profound rocuronium block?
flashcards.a: Sugammadex.

flashcards.q: What characterises post-dural puncture headache?
flashcards.a: It is POSTURAL — worse upright, relieved lying flat.

flashcards.q: Which signs suggest vertebral canal haematoma?
flashcards.a: Severe back pain, block denser or longer than expected, block recurring, new weakness or bladder dysfunction.

checkboxes: Agent chosen for haemodynamic state and dose reduced if sick
Anticoagulation intervals checked for insertion AND removal
Lipid emulsion and difficult airway equipment available

entries.title: Gastroschisis, Omphalocele and the Pharyngeal Pouch
entries.summary: Both are bowel outside the abdomen at birth, and the difference is one thing: is there a COVERING SAC? Omphalocele has one and comes with other anomalies; gastroschisis has none, so the bowel is exposed — which makes it the more urgent problem in the first hours.

terms: gastroschisis, omphalocele and the pharyngeal pouch

body.the_single_distinguishing_question: IS THERE A SAC? That answers almost everything else.

omphalocele_exomphalos.the_defect: A MIDLINE defect at the umbilicus. The umbilical cord inserts INTO the sac. The herniated contents are COVERED by a membrane (peritoneum and amnion).
omphalocele_exomphalos.the_contents: May include LIVER as well as bowel — a large defect containing liver is more complex to close.
omphalocele_exomphalos.the_critical_association: Omphalocele is strongly associated with OTHER ANOMALIES in a large proportion of cases — CHROMOSOMAL (trisomy 13, 18, 21), CARDIAC defects (the most important to find, and present in a substantial minority), BECKWITH-WIEDEMANN syndrome (macrosomia, macroglossia, hypoglycaemia from hyperinsulinism, and a risk of Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma requiring tumour surveillance), and genitourinary anomalies. So a baby with an omphalocele needs a FULL anomaly assessment — echocardiography, karyotype, and a glucose check — not just a surgical plan.
omphalocele_exomphalos.management: The sac protects the bowel, so it is less immediately urgent than gastroschisis unless it ruptures. Closure may be primary or staged; very large defects may be managed non-operatively at first with topical agents to epithelialise the sac.

gastroschisis.the_defect: A defect in the abdominal wall, almost always to the RIGHT of a NORMALLY INSERTED umbilical cord. There is NO SAC — the bowel is directly exposed to amniotic fluid in utero and to air after birth.
gastroschisis.the_consequences_of_having_no_sac: Exposure causes a thickened, inflamed, matted "peel" on the bowel, with dysmotility that persists after closure. After birth the exposed bowel loses HEAT and FLUID at a very high rate, and is at risk of infection and of VOLVULUS or ischaemia if the mesenteric base twists at the narrow defect.
gastroschisis.associations: Usually ISOLATED — associated anomalies are uncommon apart from intestinal atresia. It is associated with YOUNGER maternal age and with smoking and recreational drug use, and its incidence has been rising.
the_immediate_management_priorities: Do NOT let the bowel dry or cool. Cover the exposed bowel and the lower body with CLINGFILM or a bowel bag immediately — not wet gauze, which accelerates heat loss by evaporation. This is the single most important first action.
Nurse in a way that avoids KINKING the mesentery — often right lateral position — and inspect the bowel colour repeatedly for signs of ischaemia.
Generous intravenous FLUID — losses are far higher than they appear.
Nasogastric tube on free drainage to decompress.
Thermoregulation, intravenous antibiotics, and urgent transfer to a paediatric surgical centre.
gastroschisis.closure: Primary closure if the abdomen will accommodate it, otherwise a staged SILO with gradual reduction. Watch for ABDOMINAL COMPARTMENT SYNDROME after closure — a forced primary closure can compromise ventilation, venous return and renal perfusion. Prolonged ileus is expected and parenteral nutrition is usually needed.

body.explaining_it_to_a_family_in_plain_langu: Both mean the baby was born with some of the bowel outside the tummy, because the abdominal wall did not finish closing early in pregnancy. In one type (omphalocele) the bowel is inside a thin bag at the belly button, which protects it — but we must check the heart and other organs carefully, because this type often comes with other differences. In the other type (gastroschisis) there is no bag, so the bowel is bare and we must cover it and keep it warm and moist straight away, and it usually happens on its own without other problems. Both are repaired with surgery, and in both the bowel often takes weeks to start working properly afterwards, so the baby will be fed through a drip for a while. This is nothing the parents did or failed to do.

pharyngeal_pouch_zenker_diverticulum.what: A pulsion diverticulum through KILLIAN DEHISCENCE — a weak area in the posterior pharyngeal wall between the two parts of the inferior constrictor. It results from failure of the cricopharyngeus to relax, so pressure forces mucosa outward. It is therefore a FALSE diverticulum (mucosa and submucosa only).
pharyngeal_pouch_zenker_diverticulum.features: DYSPHAGIA · REGURGITATION of UNDIGESTED food, often hours later and typically on lying down at night · HALITOSIS · a gurgling sound in the neck · a neck lump that may be compressible · cough and recurrent ASPIRATION PNEUMONIA · weight loss. The combination of regurgitating recognisable undigested food with halitosis is close to diagnostic and is often the detail that unlocks it.
pharyngeal_pouch_zenker_diverticulum.the_important_practical_warning: BLIND NASOGASTRIC TUBE insertion or endoscopy risks PERFORATING the pouch, because the tube preferentially enters the pouch rather than the oesophagus. If a pharyngeal pouch is known or suspected, do not pass a tube blindly — the diagnosis must be communicated to anyone about to instrument the upper airway or oesophagus.
pharyngeal_pouch_zenker_diverticulum.diagnosis: BARIUM SWALLOW is the investigation of choice and demonstrates it clearly. Endoscopy carries perforation risk and is used with care.
pharyngeal_pouch_zenker_diverticulum.management: Endoscopic stapling or diverticulotomy, or open surgery with cricopharyngeal myotomy. Myotomy addresses the underlying cause; simply removing the pouch without it risks recurrence. There is a small long-term risk of carcinoma developing within a long-standing pouch.

warnings: Cover exposed bowel in gastroschisis with clingfilm or a bowel bag IMMEDIATELY — wet gauze accelerates heat loss by evaporation.
Fluid losses in gastroschisis are far higher than they appear. Resuscitate generously.
Avoid kinking the mesentery and inspect bowel colour repeatedly — volvulus and ischaemia at the defect are real risks.
Every omphalocele needs echocardiography, karyotype and a glucose check — associated anomalies are common and cardiac disease is the one that matters most.
Beckwith-Wiedemann causes neonatal hypoglycaemia and needs tumour surveillance.
Watch for abdominal compartment syndrome after closure of an abdominal wall defect.
Do NOT pass a nasogastric tube blindly in a known or suspected pharyngeal pouch — perforation risk.
Regurgitation of undigested food with halitosis in an elderly patient suggests a pharyngeal pouch — barium swallow, not blind endoscopy.
A pharyngeal pouch causes recurrent aspiration pneumonia that is treated repeatedly without the cause being found.
Cricopharyngeal myotomy addresses the cause; removing the pouch alone risks recurrence.
limitations: Surgical technique, transfer arrangements and neonatal fluid regimens are unit-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Single question separating gastroschisis from omphalocele?
flashcards.a: Is there a covering sac? Omphalocele has one; gastroschisis does not.

flashcards.q: Where is the defect in gastroschisis?
flashcards.a: To the RIGHT of a normally inserted umbilical cord.

flashcards.q: Which has more associated anomalies?
flashcards.a: Omphalocele — chromosomal, cardiac, Beckwith-Wiedemann, genitourinary.

flashcards.q: First action in gastroschisis?
flashcards.a: Cover the bowel and lower body with clingfilm or a bowel bag — not wet gauze.

flashcards.q: What must be checked in every omphalocele?
flashcards.a: Echocardiogram, karyotype and glucose.

flashcards.q: Where does a pharyngeal pouch herniate?
flashcards.a: Through Killian dehiscence, from failure of cricopharyngeus to relax.

flashcards.q: Classic pharyngeal pouch symptoms?
flashcards.a: Dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, gurgling neck, aspiration.

flashcards.q: What must not be done in a pharyngeal pouch?
flashcards.a: Blind NG tube insertion — it perforates the pouch.

checkboxes: Bowel covered and warmed immediately in gastroschisis
Mesenteric kinking avoided and perfusion monitored
Echocardiogram, karyotype and glucose in omphalocele
Pouch communicated to anyone instrumenting the oesophagus

entries.title: Diarrhoea, Constipation and Fever — Mechanism-Based Management
entries.summary: In diarrhoea, REHYDRATION saves lives and antibiotics rarely do. The one rule that must never be broken: do NOT give antimotility drugs in bloody diarrhoea or suspected dysentery — it prolongs the illness and risks toxic megacolon and haemolytic uraemic syndrome.

terms: diarrhoea, constipation and fever — mechanism-based management

diarrhoea_by_mechanism.why_mechanism_beats_a_list_of_organisms: It tells you what to do before any result returns.
diarrhoea_by_mechanism.secretory: Active ion and water secretion. Large volume, WATERY, and it CONTINUES DURING FASTING. Classic example CHOLERA — profuse "rice water" stool with rapid, life-threatening dehydration. Also enterotoxigenic E. coli, and hormone-secreting tumours (VIPoma, carcinoid).
diarrhoea_by_mechanism.osmotic: Unabsorbed solute draws water in. It STOPS WHEN THE PATIENT FASTS — the discriminating feature. Lactose intolerance, magnesium-containing laxatives and antacids, sorbitol.
diarrhoea_by_mechanism.inflammatory_dysentery: Mucosal invasion and inflammation. SMALLER volume, with BLOOD and MUCUS, FEVER, tenesmus and abdominal pain. Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella, invasive E. coli, Entamoeba histolytica, and inflammatory bowel disease.
diarrhoea_by_mechanism.motility: Irritable bowel syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, autonomic neuropathy, post-vagotomy.
diarrhoea_by_mechanism.malabsorptive: Steatorrhoea — pale, bulky, offensive, floating, difficult to flush. Coeliac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, bacterial overgrowth, giardiasis.

what_actually_saves_lives_in_acute_diarr.rehydration: The overwhelming majority of deaths from diarrhoea are from DEHYDRATION, not from the organism. ORAL REHYDRATION SOLUTION works because glucose-coupled sodium transport in the small bowel remains INTACT even in cholera — glucose drags sodium and water across with it. That single physiological fact is one of the highest-impact discoveries in modern medicine. Use ORS wherever the patient can drink; intravenous fluid where there is shock, severe dehydration, or persistent vomiting.
what_actually_saves_lives_in_acute_diarr.zinc: In CHILDREN in settings where deficiency is common, zinc supplementation reduces the duration and severity of the episode and reduces recurrence over the following months. It is cheap, effective and under-used, and it is recommended alongside ORS.
what_actually_saves_lives_in_acute_diarr.continued_feeding: Do NOT starve a child with diarrhoea. Continue breastfeeding and age-appropriate food — withholding feeds worsens malnutrition and delays mucosal recovery.

when_antibiotics_help_and_when_they_harm.usually_not: Most acute gastroenteritis is viral or self-limiting bacterial. Antibiotics do not shorten it meaningfully, cause harm, and drive resistance.
when_antibiotics_help_and_when_they_harm.consider_them: Severe illness with systemic features, cholera, invasive Shigella or typhoid, giardiasis and amoebiasis, Clostridioides difficile, travellers with severe symptoms, and the immunocompromised, very young or very frail. Follow local guidance, which must reflect local resistance patterns.
when_antibiotics_help_and_when_they_harm.the_specific_hazard: In SHIGA TOXIN-PRODUCING E. COLI (including O157), antibiotics may INCREASE the risk of HAEMOLYTIC URAEMIC SYNDROME. Bloody diarrhoea in a child with a rising creatinine, falling platelets and anaemia is HUS until proven otherwise — and it is a reason for caution with antibiotics, not a reason to give them.

the_antimotility_rule.the_rule: Do NOT give LOPERAMIDE or other antimotility agents in BLOODY diarrhoea, suspected dysentery, suspected C. difficile, or in young children.
the_antimotility_rule.why: Slowing transit retains toxin and organism, prolonging illness and increasing the risk of TOXIC MEGACOLON and, in Shiga toxin disease, of haemolytic uraemic syndrome. In young children antimotility agents also cause dangerous sedation and ileus.
the_antimotility_rule.where_it_is_reasonable: Mild, non-bloody, afebrile diarrhoea in an adult where symptom control matters — for example travel — with clear advice to stop if fever or blood appears.

body.assessing_dehydration_practically: In children: alertness, thirst, sunken eyes, tears, mucous membranes, skin pinch (turgor), capillary refill, urine output, and WEIGHT — weight change is the most objective measure available and is rarely used. Classify as no, some, or severe dehydration and treat by plan. In adults: postural blood pressure, pulse, mucous membranes, urine output, and mental state.

constipation.the_first_step: Ask what the patient means — infrequency, hard stool, straining, or a sense of incomplete evacuation. They are different problems.
constipation.red_flags_requiring_investigation: NEW change in bowel habit over 50 · rectal bleeding · unexplained weight loss · iron deficiency anaemia · a family history of colorectal cancer · abdominal or rectal mass · tenesmus.
constipation.the_causes_to_exclude: HYPOTHYROIDISM, HYPERCALCAEMIA, hypokalaemia, diabetes, Parkinson disease, spinal cord lesions, and DRUGS — OPIOIDS above all, plus anticholinergics, iron, calcium channel blockers, antipsychotics, some antidepressants and diuretics. Obstruction must be excluded before treating.
constipation.the_laxative_classes: BULK-FORMING (ispaghula) — need adequate fluid intake, and are unsuitable in opioid-induced constipation or where there is impaction. OSMOTIC (macrogol, lactulose) — draw water in. STIMULANT (senna, bisacodyl) — increase motility. SOFTENERS (docusate). SUPPOSITORIES and ENEMAS for rectal loading. Peripheral opioid antagonists for opioid-induced constipation.
constipation.the_two_practical_points: FIRST, examine the rectum — treating "constipation" without knowing whether the rectum is loaded or empty is guesswork, and a loaded rectum needs rectal treatment rather than more oral laxative. SECOND, OVERFLOW DIARRHOEA from faecal impaction is regularly misdiagnosed as simple diarrhoea and treated with antidiarrhoeals, which makes it considerably worse. Loose stool in a frail or immobile patient should prompt a rectal examination, not loperamide.
constipation.prescribing_alongside_opioids: Anyone started on a regular opioid should be prescribed a laxative at the same time, PROPHYLACTICALLY. Tolerance to constipation does not develop, unlike tolerance to the other effects.

fever.the_patterns_and_their_limits: CONTINUOUS (little variation) · REMITTENT (fluctuates but never reaches normal) · INTERMITTENT (returns to normal — classically malaria, and the tertian and quartan periodicities relate to the species) · RELAPSING (febrile periods separated by afebrile days — borreliosis) · PEL-EBSTEIN (cyclical fever over days to weeks, classically Hodgkin lymphoma, though rarely seen). These patterns are of modest diagnostic value in isolation and are often obscured by antipyretics — do not lean on them heavily.
fever.the_first_priority_anywhere_malaria_is_e: FEVER IN A MALARIA-ENDEMIC AREA, OR AFTER TRAVEL TO ONE, IS MALARIA UNTIL EXCLUDED. Test — do not treat empirically without testing where testing is available, because presumptive treatment drives resistance and misses other diagnoses. A single negative smear does not exclude it; repeat.
fever.severe_malaria_features: Impaired consciousness or convulsions, prostration, respiratory distress or acidosis, hypoglycaemia (which is easy to miss and rapidly fatal), severe anaemia, jaundice, renal impairment, shock, bleeding, and high parasitaemia. Any one of these makes it SEVERE malaria requiring parenteral treatment and admission — the distinction from uncomplicated malaria drives everything.
fever.fever_of_unknown_origin: The classic four groups are INFECTION (tuberculosis, endocarditis, abscess, HIV), MALIGNANCY (lymphoma, renal cell, hepatocellular), NON-INFECTIOUS INFLAMMATORY disease (adult-onset Still, giant cell arteritis, vasculitis, lupus), and MISCELLANEOUS (DRUG FEVER — commonly overlooked, so review every drug including recent ones; thromboembolism; factitious fever; hyperthyroidism). A careful, repeated history and examination outperforms a scattergun of investigations.
fever.the_things_not_to_miss: NEUTROPENIC SEPSIS in anyone on chemotherapy — antibiotics within the hour · MENINGITIS · malaria · endocarditis in anyone with a murmur, prosthetic valve or injecting drug use · and remember that the ELDERLY, the very young and the immunosuppressed may be seriously infected with LITTLE OR NO FEVER, and hypothermia in sepsis carries a worse prognosis than fever.

warnings: Do NOT give loperamide in bloody diarrhoea, suspected dysentery or C. difficile — risk of toxic megacolon and haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
Antibiotics in Shiga toxin-producing E. coli may increase the risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
Rehydration, not antibiotics, is what saves lives in acute diarrhoea. ORS works because glucose-coupled sodium transport stays intact.
Do not starve a child with diarrhoea — continue breastfeeding and feeding.
Give zinc to children with diarrhoea where deficiency is prevalent.
Examine the rectum before treating constipation — a loaded rectum needs rectal treatment.
OVERFLOW diarrhoea from impaction is misdiagnosed as diarrhoea and made worse by antidiarrhoeals. Loose stool in a frail patient means a rectal examination.
Prescribe a laxative prophylactically with any regular opioid — tolerance to constipation does not develop.
Fever in or after travel to a malaria-endemic area is malaria until excluded. One negative smear does not exclude it.
Check GLUCOSE in severe malaria — hypoglycaemia is easy to miss and rapidly fatal.
The elderly, neonates and the immunosuppressed may be septic with no fever. Hypothermia in sepsis is worse, not better.
Review every drug in fever of unknown origin — drug fever is commonly overlooked.
Exclude obstruction before treating constipation, and investigate a new change in bowel habit over 50.
limitations: Antibiotic choice, malaria treatment regimens and rehydration plans are governed by national and local guidelines and resistance patterns. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Secretory vs osmotic diarrhoea?
flashcards.a: Secretory continues during fasting; osmotic stops when the patient fasts.

flashcards.q: Why does ORS work even in cholera?
flashcards.a: Glucose-coupled sodium transport in the small bowel remains intact and drags water across.

flashcards.q: When must loperamide be avoided?
flashcards.a: Bloody diarrhoea, dysentery, C. difficile, and young children.

flashcards.q: Which infection makes antibiotics risky in bloody diarrhoea?
flashcards.a: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli — antibiotics may increase HUS risk.

flashcards.q: What is overflow diarrhoea?
flashcards.a: Loose stool passing around faecal impaction — worsened by antidiarrhoeals. Examine the rectum.

flashcards.q: What should be co-prescribed with every regular opioid?
flashcards.a: A laxative, prophylactically.

flashcards.q: What is fever in a returning traveller until proven otherwise?
flashcards.a: Malaria — test, and repeat if negative.

flashcards.q: Name features that define SEVERE malaria.
flashcards.a: Impaired consciousness, convulsions, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, severe anaemia, jaundice, renal failure, shock, high parasitaemia.

flashcards.q: Four categories of fever of unknown origin?
flashcards.a: Infection, malignancy, non-infectious inflammatory disease, miscellaneous (including drug fever).

checkboxes: ORS started where the patient can drink
Zinc given to children where indicated
Antimotility agents withheld if blood or fever
Malaria test sent in any relevant fever
Drug chart reviewed in prolonged fever

entries.title: Cardiomyopathies and Wolff-Parkinson-White
entries.summary: HOCM is the one that kills young athletes, and its murmur behaves BACKWARDS — louder on standing and Valsalva, quieter on squatting. In WPW with atrial fibrillation, AV-nodal blockers can cause ventricular fibrillation, so the intuitive drug is the fatal one.

dilated_cardiomyopathy.what: A dilated, poorly contracting ventricle with systolic failure. The commonest cardiomyopathy.
dilated_cardiomyopathy.causes: Idiopathic and genetic (a substantial proportion — so take a family history) · ALCOHOL · viral myocarditis · PERIPARTUM · thyroid disease · haemochromatosis · chemotherapy, notably ANTHRACYCLINES and trastuzumab · tachycardia-induced (which is reversible if the arrhythmia is controlled — worth remembering, because it is a curable cardiomyopathy) · nutritional (thiamine deficiency, wet beriberi) · HIV · Chagas disease where endemic.
dilated_cardiomyopathy.peripartum: Develops in the last month of pregnancy or the first five months postpartum. It is under-recognised because breathlessness and oedema are attributed to normal pregnancy. It carries a real risk of recurrence in subsequent pregnancies, which must be discussed before another conception.
dilated_cardiomyopathy.management: Standard heart failure therapy, treat the cause, consider device therapy and anticoagulation where indicated.

hypertrophic_cardiomyopathy.what: Genetic (usually autosomal dominant sarcomeric protein mutation) causing inappropriate LEFT VENTRICULAR HYPERTROPHY, often asymmetric septal hypertrophy, with a small stiff cavity and DIASTOLIC dysfunction. Where there is dynamic outflow tract obstruction it is called HOCM.
hypertrophic_cardiomyopathy.why_it_matters: It is the leading cause of SUDDEN CARDIAC DEATH IN YOUNG PEOPLE AND ATHLETES, and the first presentation is frequently death. Family screening therefore saves lives — every first-degree relative of an affected person needs assessment.

the_murmur_that_behaves_backwards.the_rule: The murmur is an EJECTION SYSTOLIC murmur that gets LOUDER when preload or afterload FALLS, because a smaller cavity worsens the dynamic obstruction. So it is LOUDER on STANDING and on VALSALVA, and QUIETER on SQUATTING or with handgrip.
the_murmur_that_behaves_backwards.why_this_is_diagnostically_powerful: Aortic stenosis does the OPPOSITE — it gets QUIETER on standing and Valsalva, because less blood is crossing the valve. Standing the patient up is a free bedside test that separates the two, and it is rarely performed.

hypertrophic_cardiomyopathy.other_features: Exertional syncope or pre-syncope (an ominous symptom that demands urgent assessment), angina with normal coronaries, palpitations, breathlessness, a JERKY carotid pulse, a double apical impulse, and a fourth heart sound. ECG shows LVH with deep T-wave inversion, and echocardiography shows the hypertrophy and SYSTOLIC ANTERIOR MOTION of the mitral valve.
hypertrophic_cardiomyopathy.the_prescribing_hazard: AVOID anything that reduces preload or afterload or increases contractility, because all of them WORSEN the dynamic obstruction: NITRATES, ACE inhibitors, diuretics in excess, digoxin, and inotropes. Beta-blockers and rate-limiting calcium channel blockers are the mainstay because they slow the heart and allow filling. Giving GTN to a patient with chest pain who turns out to have HOCM can precipitate collapse.
hypertrophic_cardiomyopathy.risk_and_management: Risk stratify for sudden death (family history of sudden death, unexplained syncope, massive hypertrophy, non-sustained VT, abnormal blood pressure response to exercise) and consider an implantable defibrillator. Advise on exercise restriction per specialist guidance. Screen the family.

restrictive_cardiomyopathy.what: A stiff, non-compliant ventricle with impaired FILLING but often preserved systolic function. It causes predominantly RIGHT-sided failure with a raised JVP, ascites and oedema out of proportion to the pulmonary findings.
restrictive_cardiomyopathy.causes: AMYLOIDOSIS (the commonest and most important — suspect it with heart failure plus a thick ventricle on echo but LOW voltages on ECG, which is a discordance that should always prompt the thought), sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis, endomyocardial fibrosis (important in tropical regions), radiation, and hypereosinophilic syndrome.
restrictive_cardiomyopathy.the_key_differential: CONSTRICTIVE PERICARDITIS produces a very similar picture but is SURGICALLY CURABLE, so distinguishing them matters enormously. Imaging, haemodynamics and pericardial calcification help.

body.arvc: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy — fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricle causing ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death, again typically in young people and often provoked by exercise. Look for epsilon waves and T-wave inversion in V1 to V3. Another cause for family screening.
body.takotsubo: Stress-induced apical ballooning, classically in postmenopausal women after intense emotional or physical stress. It MIMICS acute myocardial infarction with ST elevation and raised troponin, but the coronaries are unobstructed and the ventricle recovers over weeks. It cannot be distinguished from MI without angiography, so it is not a diagnosis to make in the emergency department.

wolff_parkinson_white.what: An ACCESSORY PATHWAY (bundle of Kent) connecting atrium to ventricle directly, bypassing the AV node.
wolff_parkinson_white.the_resting_ecg: SHORT PR interval, a DELTA WAVE (slurred upstroke of the QRS from early ventricular activation through the pathway), and a widened QRS. Repolarisation abnormalities may mimic ischaemia or a prior infarct.

the_tachycardias.orthodromic: Commonest. Conducts DOWN the AV node and BACK UP the accessory pathway, giving a NARROW complex regular tachycardia. It looks like ordinary SVT and is treated as such.
the_tachycardias.antidromic: Conducts DOWN the accessory pathway and back up the AV node, giving a BROAD complex tachycardia easily mistaken for ventricular tachycardia.

the_lethal_scenario.what_happens: If ATRIAL FIBRILLATION develops in a patient with WPW, the accessory pathway can conduct the chaotic atrial impulses to the ventricle WITHOUT the rate-limiting protection of the AV node. This produces a very fast, IRREGULAR, BROAD complex tachycardia with varying QRS morphology, and it can degenerate into VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION.
the_lethal_scenario.the_fatal_error: Giving an AV-NODAL BLOCKING drug — ADENOSINE, VERAPAMIL, DILTIAZEM, BETA-BLOCKERS or DIGOXIN — blocks the normal route and pushes ALL conduction down the accessory pathway, accelerating the ventricular rate and precipitating ventricular fibrillation. These are exactly the drugs a clinician reaches for in a fast irregular rhythm, which is why this must be known before it is met.
the_lethal_scenario.what_to_do_instead: For an IRREGULAR broad complex tachycardia, treat as pre-excited AF: if unstable, SYNCHRONISED DC CARDIOVERSION. If stable, use an agent that acts on the accessory pathway per your local protocol, and involve cardiology urgently.
the_lethal_scenario.the_recognition_rule: FAST, IRREGULAR, BROAD and with VARYING QRS shapes = pre-excited AF until proven otherwise. Do not give adenosine.

wolff_parkinson_white.definitive_treatment: Catheter ABLATION of the accessory pathway is curative and is offered to symptomatic patients and to those with high-risk features.

warnings: In WPW with atrial fibrillation, AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin) can precipitate ventricular fibrillation. A fast, irregular, broad complex tachycardia with varying QRS shapes is pre-excited AF until proven otherwise.
The HOCM murmur is LOUDER on standing and Valsalva and QUIETER on squatting — the opposite of aortic stenosis. Stand the patient up.
Avoid nitrates, excess diuretics, ACE inhibitors, digoxin and inotropes in HOCM — they worsen dynamic obstruction.
Exertional syncope in a young person is an ominous symptom — assess urgently before attributing it to anything benign.
Screen first-degree relatives in HOCM and ARVC. The first presentation can be sudden death.
Heart failure with a thick ventricle on echo but LOW ECG voltages suggests cardiac amyloidosis.
Constrictive pericarditis mimics restrictive cardiomyopathy and is surgically curable — distinguish them.
Peripartum cardiomyopathy is missed because breathlessness and oedema are attributed to pregnancy. It recurs in later pregnancies.
Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is reversible if the rhythm is controlled.
Takotsubo cannot be distinguished from MI without angiography — do not diagnose it in the emergency department.
limitations: Risk stratification, device indications, ablation selection and drug choices are specialist- and protocol-directed. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: How does the HOCM murmur respond to standing?
flashcards.a: It gets LOUDER — reduced preload worsens the dynamic obstruction. Aortic stenosis gets quieter.

flashcards.q: Which drugs must be avoided in HOCM?
flashcards.a: Nitrates, excess diuretics, ACE inhibitors, digoxin and inotropes.

flashcards.q: What is the ECG triad of WPW?
flashcards.a: Short PR, delta wave, widened QRS.

flashcards.q: Why are AV-nodal blockers dangerous in WPW with AF?
flashcards.a: They divert all conduction down the accessory pathway, accelerating the ventricle into VF.

flashcards.q: How do you recognise pre-excited AF?
flashcards.a: Fast, irregular, broad complex with varying QRS morphology.

flashcards.q: Orthodromic vs antidromic AVRT?
flashcards.a: Orthodromic goes down the AV node (narrow); antidromic goes down the pathway (broad, mimics VT).

flashcards.q: Which echo–ECG discordance suggests amyloid?
flashcards.a: Thick ventricle on echo with LOW voltages on ECG.

flashcards.q: Which cardiomyopathy is curable by rate control?
flashcards.a: Tachycardia-induced.

checkboxes: Family history of sudden death taken
Murmur assessed with standing and squatting
ECG examined for delta wave and voltages
Adenosine withheld in irregular broad complex tachycardia

entries.title: Hypertension — End-Organ Stigmata, ECG Potassium Changes and the J-Curve
entries.summary: Long-standing hypertension writes itself on the arteries, the heart, the eyes and the kidneys — and each sign has a mechanism. Separately: in potassium disturbance the ECG matters more than the number, and it is the change you treat.

terms: hypertension — end-organ stigmata, ecg potassium changes and the j-curve

the_arterial_wall.what_you_feel: A THICKENED, hard, sometimes tortuous and palpable radial or brachial artery. In advanced cases the vessel is palpable even when compressed (the historical "pipe-stem" artery).
the_arterial_wall.the_mechanism: Sustained high pressure causes HYPERTROPHY of vascular smooth muscle and increased collagen deposition in the media, plus fragmentation of elastin. The vessel becomes thicker and STIFFER. Stiffness matters clinically: it raises SYSTOLIC pressure and WIDENS THE PULSE PRESSURE, so isolated systolic hypertension in older people is a disease of arterial stiffness rather than of increased resistance alone.
the_arterial_wall.the_related_finding: A wide pulse pressure with a collapsing character has other causes (aortic regurgitation, thyrotoxicosis, anaemia, arteriovenous fistula) which should be considered rather than assumed to be age.

the_displaced_apex_beat.what_you_feel: Two distinct abnormalities that are frequently conflated. A HEAVING or SUSTAINED, forceful apex in a NORMAL position indicates PRESSURE overload — concentric left ventricular hypertrophy from hypertension or aortic stenosis. A DISPLACED apex (lateral to the midclavicular line and below the fifth intercostal space), diffuse and thrusting, indicates VOLUME overload with DILATATION — aortic or mitral regurgitation, or dilated cardiomyopathy.
the_displaced_apex_beat.the_mechanism: Pressure overload produces sarcomeres added in PARALLEL, thickening the wall without enlarging the cavity — so the apex is forceful but not displaced. Volume overload adds sarcomeres in SERIES, lengthening fibres and enlarging the cavity — so the apex moves. Recognising which one you are feeling tells you the mechanism before any imaging.
the_displaced_apex_beat.the_accompanying_sign: A FOURTH HEART SOUND is common in hypertensive heart disease — it is atrial contraction against a stiff, non-compliant ventricle, and it disappears in atrial fibrillation because there is no coordinated atrial contraction.

the_eye.why_it_is_the_only_place_you_see_arterie: Fundoscopy is the only direct view of small arteries in the living body, which is why hypertensive retinopathy is such a useful proxy for what is happening in the brain and kidney.
the_eye.the_progression: Generalised ARTERIOLAR NARROWING and increased light reflex ("SILVER" or "COPPER WIRING") from wall thickening · ARTERIOVENOUS NIPPING where a thickened arteriole compresses a vein at a crossing point · FLAME haemorrhages and COTTON WOOL SPOTS (retinal nerve fibre layer infarcts) and hard exudates · then PAPILLOEDEMA.
the_eye.the_emergency: PAPILLOEDEMA with severe hypertension indicates a HYPERTENSIVE EMERGENCY requiring same-day treatment and admission. Bilateral disc swelling in a hypertensive patient must never be treated as an outpatient problem.

the_peripheral_stigmata_and_why_each_occ.the_kidney: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis — a slow rise in creatinine with modest proteinuria and small, smooth kidneys. Hypertension is both a cause and a consequence of renal disease, and untangling which came first matters for management.

the_ecg_of_potassium.the_governing_principle: The ECG matters more than the number, in both directions. Treat the ECG and the patient, not the laboratory value alone — and remember that the RATE OF CHANGE matters as much as the absolute level, because a slow rise is tolerated far better than a rapid one.
the_ecg_of_potassium.hyperkalaemia_progression: TALL, PEAKED, narrow-based TENTED T waves (earliest) → FLATTENING and then LOSS of the P wave with a prolonged PR → WIDENING of the QRS → the QRS merging with the T wave into a SINE WAVE pattern → ventricular fibrillation or asystole. The sine wave is a peri-arrest finding and demands immediate treatment.
the_ecg_of_potassium.hypokalaemia_progression: ST DEPRESSION and T-wave FLATTENING → prominent U WAVES (a positive deflection after the T wave, best seen in the mid-precordial leads) → the T and U waves merging, which can be mistaken for a long QT → and increased risk of ventricular arrhythmia, particularly TORSADES DE POINTES.
the_two_practical_points: ALWAYS check MAGNESIUM alongside potassium. Hypokalaemia is often refractory to replacement until magnesium is corrected, because magnesium is required for cellular potassium retention. Replacing potassium repeatedly without checking magnesium is a common and futile exercise.
DIGOXIN toxicity is precipitated by hypokalaemia, and the two frequently coexist because diuretics cause both the low potassium and the setting in which digoxin is used.

the_j_shaped_curve.the_blood_pressure_j_curve: The observation that cardiovascular events rise at very LOW achieved diastolic pressures as well as at high ones. The likely explanation is partly that CORONARY PERFUSION occurs during DIASTOLE, so an excessively low diastolic pressure may compromise it in patients with existing coronary disease — and partly REVERSE CAUSATION, in that sick, frail patients have low blood pressure because they are sick. The practical consequence is caution about aggressive lowering in frail, elderly patients with established coronary disease, without abandoning treatment of genuine hypertension.

the_alcohol_j_curve.the_claim: Older observational studies suggested that light to moderate drinkers had LOWER cardiovascular and stroke risk than abstainers, producing a J- or U-shaped curve, with harm at higher intake.
the_alcohol_j_curve.why_it_is_now_strongly_contested: The apparent protection at low intake is substantially explained by CONFOUNDING and by SICK-QUITTER BIAS — the "abstainer" group in many studies included former drinkers who had stopped because of ill health, making abstainers look unhealthy. Studies that separate lifelong abstainers, and MENDELIAN RANDOMISATION studies using genetic variants in alcohol metabolism, largely fail to reproduce a protective effect. Current major guidance is that there is NO safe level established as beneficial, and that any cardiovascular benefit is at best small and outweighed by cancer risk, which rises from low levels of intake.
the_alcohol_j_curve.the_stroke_specific_point: The relationship differs by stroke type — the evidence for any protective association is weaker for HAEMORRHAGIC stroke, and heavy drinking clearly increases both haemorrhagic stroke and atrial fibrillation ("holiday heart"), which itself causes ischaemic stroke.
the_alcohol_j_curve.what_to_tell_a_patient: Do not advise anyone to start drinking, or continue drinking, for cardiovascular benefit. That advice has been given and is not supportable.

warnings: Papilloedema with severe hypertension is a hypertensive emergency needing same-day treatment — never an outpatient problem.
Distinguish a HEAVING apex in normal position (pressure overload) from a DISPLACED apex (volume overload and dilatation). They mean different things.
In potassium disturbance, treat the ECG and the patient, not the number. Rate of change matters as much as the level.
A sine-wave ECG in hyperkalaemia is a peri-arrest finding — treat immediately.
Always check MAGNESIUM in hypokalaemia — potassium replacement fails until magnesium is corrected.
Hypokalaemia precipitates digoxin toxicity, and the two commonly coexist through diuretic use.
Do not advise anyone to drink alcohol for cardiovascular benefit — the J-curve is substantially explained by sick-quitter bias and confounding.
Be cautious about aggressive blood pressure lowering in frail elderly patients with established coronary disease.
A wide pulse pressure has causes other than arterial stiffness — consider aortic regurgitation, thyrotoxicosis and anaemia.
A fourth heart sound disappears in atrial fibrillation because coordinated atrial contraction is lost.
limitations: Blood pressure targets, potassium treatment thresholds and alcohol guidance are guideline- and country-specific and are periodically revised. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Heaving vs displaced apex beat?
flashcards.a: Heaving in normal position = pressure overload (hypertrophy). Displaced = volume overload (dilatation).

flashcards.q: Why does pressure overload not displace the apex?
flashcards.a: Sarcomeres are added in parallel, thickening the wall without enlarging the cavity.

flashcards.q: Why does arterial stiffness widen the pulse pressure?
flashcards.a: A stiff aorta cannot buffer systole, so systolic pressure rises while diastolic falls.

flashcards.q: Order of ECG changes in hyperkalaemia?
flashcards.a: Tented T waves, loss of P, widening QRS, sine wave, then VF or asystole.

flashcards.q: ECG of hypokalaemia?
flashcards.a: ST depression, flat T waves, prominent U waves, T-U fusion, risk of torsades.

flashcards.q: Why does potassium replacement fail sometimes?
flashcards.a: Uncorrected hypomagnesaemia — magnesium is needed for cellular potassium retention.

flashcards.q: What is the alcohol J-curve, and why is it doubted?
flashcards.a: Apparent protection at low intake — largely explained by sick-quitter bias and confounding; not reproduced by Mendelian randomisation.

flashcards.q: What does papilloedema with hypertension mean?
flashcards.a: A hypertensive emergency — same-day treatment and admission.

checkboxes: Apex beat character and position both described
ECG obtained in any potassium disturbance
Alcohol advice given without implying cardiovascular benefit

entries.title: Inotropes, Vasopressors and Cardiorenal Syndrome
entries.summary: Ask one question first: is the problem PUMP or PIPES? A vasopressor squeezes the vessels; an inotrope makes the heart squeeze harder. Giving the wrong one wastes time in a patient who has none — and neither works in an empty tank.

the_first_question.pump_or_pipes: Blood pressure is cardiac output multiplied by systemic vascular resistance. If the vessels are dilated (SEPSIS, anaphylaxis, neurogenic shock) the problem is the PIPES and the answer is a VASOPRESSOR. If the heart is failing to eject (cardiogenic shock, severe myocardial dysfunction) the problem is the PUMP and the answer is an INOTROPE. Many critically ill patients need both.
the_first_question.the_precondition: NEITHER WORKS IN AN EMPTY TANK. Assess and correct volume status first — starting a vasopressor in a profoundly hypovolaemic patient raises the pressure by squeezing an underfilled circulation, at the cost of tissue perfusion. And exclude the obstructive causes (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, massive PE), where drugs are not the treatment at all.

the_receptors.alpha_1: Vascular smooth muscle. Stimulation causes VASOCONSTRICTION, raising systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure.
the_receptors.beta_1: Cardiac. Stimulation increases CONTRACTILITY (inotropy) and RATE (chronotropy).
the_receptors.beta_2: Vascular and bronchial smooth muscle. Stimulation causes vasoDILATATION and bronchodilatation.
the_receptors.dopaminergic: Renal and splanchnic vasodilatation at low dose.

the_agents.noradrenaline: Predominantly ALPHA with modest beta-1. The first-line VASOPRESSOR in septic and most vasodilatory shock — it raises pressure with relatively little tachycardia. Requires central access ideally, because EXTRAVASATION causes tissue necrosis.
the_agents.adrenaline: Alpha AND beta. Vasoconstrictor, inotrope and chronotrope. First line in ANAPHYLAXIS and cardiac arrest. In shock it causes more tachyarrhythmia and raises LACTATE through beta-2 mediated glycolysis — so a rising lactate on adrenaline is not necessarily worsening perfusion, which is a genuine interpretive trap.
the_agents.dobutamine: Predominantly BETA-1 with some beta-2. A pure INOTROPE that increases contractility and cardiac output but can DROP the blood pressure through beta-2 vasodilatation. Useful in cardiogenic shock with adequate pressure, often combined with noradrenaline.
the_agents.dopamine: Dose-dependent effects. Now largely superseded — it causes more arrhythmia than noradrenaline in shock, and the concept of a "renal dose" protecting the kidney has been disproven and should be abandoned.
the_agents.vasopressin: Acts on V1 receptors independently of adrenergic pathways, which makes it useful as an adjunct when catecholamine requirements are escalating, and in vasoplegia.
the_agents.milrinone_and_levosimendan: Inodilators — they increase contractility while reducing afterload, without acting through beta receptors, so they retain effect in patients on chronic BETA-BLOCKERS. Both cause hypotension. Milrinone accumulates in renal impairment.
the_agents.phenylephrine: Pure alpha-1. Raises pressure with reflex bradycardia; useful in specific situations such as tachyarrhythmia with hypotension.

the_principles_that_matter_more_than_the: Treat the CAUSE. Vasopressors buy time; they do not fix sepsis, tamponade or infarction.
Use the LOWEST dose for the SHORTEST time to an agreed target — usually a mean arterial pressure, individualised to the patient (a chronically hypertensive patient may need a higher target).
Monitor PERFUSION, not just pressure — lactate clearance, urine output, capillary refill, mental state. A normal blood pressure achieved by intense vasoconstriction can coexist with dying tissue.
Vasoconstrictors cause DIGITAL, MESENTERIC and RENAL ischaemia at high doses. Look at the fingers and toes.
Extravasation of a vasoconstrictor causes necrosis — use central access where possible and know the local treatment for extravasation.
Correct calcium, acidosis and hypoxia — catecholamines work poorly in severe acidosis.

cardiorenal_syndrome.the_concept: Dysfunction of the heart and kidney where each drives the other. It is classified into five types by which organ fails first and whether the process is acute or chronic.

the_five_types.type_1: ACUTE cardiac dysfunction causing ACUTE kidney injury — for example acute decompensated heart failure or cardiogenic shock precipitating AKI.
the_five_types.type_2: CHRONIC cardiac dysfunction causing CHRONIC kidney disease.
the_five_types.type_3: ACUTE kidney injury causing ACUTE cardiac dysfunction — through fluid overload, hyperkalaemic arrhythmia, uraemic pericarditis or acidosis.
the_five_types.type_4: CHRONIC kidney disease causing chronic cardiac disease — accelerated atherosclerosis, left ventricular hypertrophy, and the very high cardiovascular mortality of chronic kidney disease.
the_five_types.type_5: SECONDARY — a systemic condition damaging both, such as sepsis, amyloidosis, diabetes or lupus.

cardiorenal_syndrome.the_mechanism_that_changed_practice: The traditional model attributed renal impairment in heart failure to LOW CARDIAC OUTPUT and poor forward perfusion. The evidence now shows that VENOUS CONGESTION — raised central venous pressure transmitted back to the renal veins — is a more important driver. Raised renal venous pressure reduces the transrenal perfusion gradient and raises interstitial pressure, impairing filtration.
cardiorenal_syndrome.the_practical_consequence: This inverts the instinct. In a congested patient whose creatinine is rising, the answer is often MORE decongestion rather than less — stopping diuretics and giving fluid to "protect the kidney" can make both organs worse. A modest rise in creatinine during effective decongestion is common and does not by itself mean the diuretic should be stopped. This is a genuinely counterintuitive point and it must be applied with careful assessment of volume status, not as a blanket rule.
cardiorenal_syndrome.diuretic_resistance: Common. Causes include poor absorption from gut oedema, hypoalbuminaemia, low renal perfusion, high sodium intake, NSAIDs, and compensatory distal tubular hypertrophy. Strategies include adequate dosing, intravenous rather than oral administration, and SEQUENTIAL NEPHRON BLOCKADE by adding a thiazide-like agent to a loop diuretic — which is effective and requires close electrolyte monitoring.
cardiorenal_syndrome.what_to_actually_do: Assess volume status carefully and repeatedly. Optimise heart failure therapy. Avoid nephrotoxics. Monitor potassium closely, especially when combining renin-angiotensin blockade with mineralocorticoid antagonists. Recognise that both organs must be managed together, and involve cardiology and nephrology jointly rather than sequentially.

warnings: Neither inotropes nor vasopressors work in an empty tank. Correct volume status and exclude obstructive causes first.
A rising lactate on ADRENALINE may be beta-2 mediated glycolysis, not worsening perfusion.
"Renal dose" dopamine does not protect the kidney. The concept is disproven and should be abandoned.
Monitor perfusion — lactate, urine output, capillary refill, mental state — not blood pressure alone.
Extravasation of a vasoconstrictor causes tissue necrosis. Use central access and know the local treatment.
Check the fingers and toes on high-dose vasoconstrictors — digital ischaemia is a real complication.
In cardiorenal syndrome, VENOUS CONGESTION is often the driver. Stopping diuretics and giving fluid to protect the kidney can worsen both organs.
A modest creatinine rise during effective decongestion does not automatically mean stopping the diuretic.
Milrinone and levosimendan retain effect in patients on beta-blockers, but both cause hypotension.
Catecholamines work poorly in severe acidosis — correct it.
limitations: All agents, doses, targets and monitoring are protocol-specific and require critical care expertise. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Vasopressor or inotrope — how do you choose?
flashcards.a: Pipes (vasodilated, e.g. sepsis) need a vasopressor; pump failure needs an inotrope. Often both.

flashcards.q: First-line vasopressor in septic shock?
flashcards.a: Noradrenaline.

flashcards.q: Why can dobutamine drop the blood pressure?
flashcards.a: Beta-2 mediated vasodilatation alongside its inotropic effect.

flashcards.q: Why might lactate rise on adrenaline?
flashcards.a: Beta-2 stimulated glycolysis — not necessarily worsening perfusion.

flashcards.q: Is there a renal-protective dose of dopamine?
flashcards.a: No. The concept is disproven.

flashcards.q: Which inotropes work despite beta-blockade?
flashcards.a: Milrinone and levosimendan — they bypass beta receptors.

flashcards.q: Name the five cardiorenal types.
flashcards.a: Acute cardio-renal, chronic cardio-renal, acute reno-cardiac, chronic reno-cardiac, and secondary.

flashcards.q: What drives renal impairment in heart failure more than low output?
flashcards.a: Venous congestion raising renal venous and interstitial pressure.

flashcards.q: What is sequential nephron blockade?
flashcards.a: Adding a thiazide-like diuretic to a loop diuretic to overcome resistance — needs close electrolyte monitoring.

checkboxes: Volume status assessed before starting any agent
Perfusion markers monitored, not pressure alone
Congestion assessed before reducing diuretics in cardiorenal syndrome

entries.title: Peripheral Neuropathy — Pattern, Fibre Type and Cause
entries.summary: Classify by PATTERN before hunting causes: symmetrical length-dependent, mononeuropathy, or mononeuritis multiplex. Mononeuritis multiplex is the one that matters most urgently, because it usually means VASCULITIS and needs treatment within days.

terms: peripheral neuropathy — pattern, fibre type and cause

step_one_the_pattern.symmetrical_length_dependent_polyneuropa: The commonest. It begins in the LONGEST nerves, so it starts at the TOES and ascends, and reaches the fingers only once the legs are affected to about knee level — producing the classic GLOVE AND STOCKING distribution. The order matters: feet first, hands later. Hands first should make you doubt this pattern.
step_one_the_pattern.mononeuropathy: A single nerve — usually COMPRESSION or entrapment. Median at the wrist (carpal tunnel), ulnar at the elbow, common peroneal at the fibular head (causing FOOT DROP), radial in the spiral groove ("Saturday night palsy"), lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh (meralgia paraesthetica).

mononeuritis_multiplex.what: Several INDIVIDUAL, NAMED nerves affected sequentially and asymmetrically — a foot drop on one side, then a wrist drop on the other. As more nerves are involved it can become confluent and MIMIC a symmetrical polyneuropathy, which is how it gets missed.
mononeuritis_multiplex.why_it_is_urgent: The commonest cause is VASCULITIS — infarction of the vasa nervorum. That means a systemic vasculitis (ANCA-associated, polyarteritis nodosa, rheumatoid, lupus, cryoglobulinaemia) which may simultaneously be destroying kidneys and lungs. It needs urgent investigation and immunosuppression, often within days.
mononeuritis_multiplex.other_causes: Diabetes, LEPROSY (the commonest infectious cause worldwide and a critical consideration in endemic regions), HIV, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, Lyme disease, and hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies.
mononeuritis_multiplex.the_rule: Asymmetric, stepwise, multi-nerve neuropathy is vasculitis until proven otherwise. Check urine dipstick, inflammatory markers, ANCA and renal function the same day.

step_one_the_pattern.radiculopathy_and_plexopathy: A dermatomal or myotomal pattern points to a root or plexus lesion rather than a peripheral nerve — check for neck or back pain, and remember that cord compression can present with limb symptoms.

step_two_the_fibre_type.large_fibre: Numbness, tingling, loss of VIBRATION and PROPRIOCEPTION, ABSENT REFLEXES, sensory ataxia with a positive Romberg, and weakness. Detected by nerve conduction studies.
step_two_the_fibre_type.small_fibre: BURNING pain, allodynia, altered pain and temperature sensation, and AUTONOMIC features. Reflexes and nerve conduction studies are NORMAL — which is why patients are frequently told "the tests are normal, there is nothing wrong". Small fibre neuropathy is real, is diagnosed by skin biopsy or quantitative sensory testing, and is commonly caused by diabetes and impaired glucose tolerance.
step_two_the_fibre_type.autonomic: Postural hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, bladder dysfunction, abnormal sweating, and — importantly in diabetes — a SILENT myocardial infarction and impaired hypoglycaemia awareness.
step_two_the_fibre_type.motor_predominant: Suggests Guillain-Barré, CIDP, lead poisoning, porphyria, or hereditary motor neuropathy.

step_three_axonal_or_demyelinating.axonal: Far commoner. Length-dependent, gradual, with reduced amplitudes on nerve conduction. Causes are the metabolic and toxic list below.
step_three_axonal_or_demyelinating.demyelinating: Slowed conduction velocities. Fewer causes, and they are more often TREATABLE — Guillain-Barré, CIDP, paraprotein-associated neuropathy, and hereditary (Charcot-Marie-Tooth). CIDP in particular responds to immunotherapy and is worth actively excluding, because it is a treatable cause of progressive disability.

the_causes_worth_working_through.the_common_metabolic: DIABETES (by far the commonest in most settings — and impaired glucose tolerance alone causes small fibre neuropathy) · chronic KIDNEY disease · HYPOTHYROIDISM · liver disease.
the_causes_worth_working_through.nutritional_and_toxic: ALCOHOL (both directly toxic and through thiamine deficiency) · VITAMIN B12 deficiency · thiamine, B6 (deficiency AND excess both cause neuropathy — pyridoxine in high dose is neurotoxic) · vitamin E · copper deficiency, which is a recognised complication of bariatric surgery and of zinc excess.
the_causes_worth_working_through.drugs: ISONIAZID (prevented by pyridoxine — this is why pyridoxine is co-prescribed, a high-yield and frequently forgotten point) · METRONIDAZOLE with prolonged use · VINCRISTINE and platinum agents · amiodarone · nitrofurantoin · phenytoin · linezolid · some antiretrovirals · thalidomide.
the_causes_worth_working_through.infective: HIV (and some of its treatments) · LEPROSY — think of it in any endemic region, particularly with thickened palpable nerves and anaesthetic skin patches, because it is treatable and disability is preventable · Lyme disease · hepatitis C with cryoglobulinaemia · diphtheria.
the_causes_worth_working_through.immune_and_paraproteinaemic: Guillain-Barré, CIDP, vasculitis, Sjögren, coeliac disease, and paraproteinaemia — always send protein electrophoresis and free light chains in an unexplained neuropathy, because myeloma and MGUS-associated neuropathy are treatable and are missed.
the_causes_worth_working_through.hereditary: Charcot-Marie-Tooth — pes cavus, hammer toes, inverted champagne bottle legs, a slowly progressive course from childhood, and often an unrecognised family history. Ask to look at relatives feet.
the_causes_worth_working_through.other: Amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, malignancy and paraneoplastic syndromes, critical illness polyneuropathy.

body.the_practical_workup: Glucose or HbA1c and an oral glucose tolerance test if normal but suspicion is high · B12 and folate · TSH · renal and liver function · full blood count and ESR · protein electrophoresis and free light chains · HIV where relevant · ANA and ANCA if asymmetric or systemic features · nerve conduction studies. Reserve broader testing for atypical or progressive cases.
body.management_principles: Treat the CAUSE — this is the only thing that alters the course. FOOT CARE and protection is critical in any sensory neuropathy, because insensate feet ulcerate, and that is preventable. Neuropathic pain agents help symptoms but not the nerve. Physiotherapy, orthotics for foot drop, and falls prevention. Address driving where proprioception is impaired.

warnings: Asymmetric, stepwise, multi-nerve neuropathy is VASCULITIS until proven otherwise — investigate the same day with urine dipstick, ANCA and renal function.
Small fibre neuropathy has NORMAL reflexes and NORMAL nerve conduction. Do not tell the patient nothing is wrong.
Consider LEPROSY in endemic regions — thickened nerves with anaesthetic skin patches. It is treatable and disability is preventable.
Co-prescribe pyridoxine with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy.
Vitamin B6 causes neuropathy in DEFICIENCY and in EXCESS — ask about supplements.
Send protein electrophoresis and free light chains in unexplained neuropathy — paraproteinaemic causes are treatable and missed.
CIDP is treatable — actively exclude it in a progressive demyelinating neuropathy.
Insensate feet ulcerate. Foot care and protection prevent amputation and is the highest-value intervention.
Autonomic neuropathy causes silent myocardial infarction and impaired hypoglycaemia awareness in diabetes.
Hands affected before feet argues against a length-dependent polyneuropathy — reconsider the pattern.
limitations: Investigation panels and neuropathic pain regimens are protocol-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Why is the pattern glove and stocking?
flashcards.a: It is length-dependent — the longest axons fail first, so feet precede hands.

flashcards.q: What does mononeuritis multiplex usually mean?
flashcards.a: Vasculitis — infarction of the vasa nervorum. Urgent.

flashcards.q: Why are small fibre neuropathy patients told nothing is wrong?
flashcards.a: Reflexes and nerve conduction studies are normal — it needs skin biopsy or QST.

flashcards.q: Which nerve palsy causes foot drop?
flashcards.a: Common peroneal at the fibular head.

flashcards.q: Why is pyridoxine given with isoniazid?
flashcards.a: To prevent isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy.

flashcards.q: Which vitamin harms in both deficiency and excess?
flashcards.a: B6 (pyridoxine).

flashcards.q: Which demyelinating neuropathy is treatable and often missed?
flashcards.a: CIDP.

flashcards.q: Which infectious neuropathy is critical in endemic regions?
flashcards.a: Leprosy — thickened nerves, anaesthetic patches, preventable disability.

checkboxes: Glucose, B12, TSH, renal and electrophoresis sent
Nerve conduction requested where it will change management

entries.title: Optic Neuritis, Trigeminal Neuralgia and Cerebellar Ataxia
entries.summary: Optic neuritis gives pain on eye movement with a RELATIVE AFFERENT PUPILLARY DEFECT — and colour vision is lost out of proportion to acuity. Trigeminal neuralgia in a young patient, or with sensory loss, is not idiopathic and needs imaging.

terms: optic neuritis, trigeminal neuralgia and cerebellar ataxia

optic_neuritis.the_classic_presentation: SUBACUTE monocular visual loss over hours to days, with PAIN ON EYE MOVEMENT (present in the large majority and a very useful discriminator from other causes of visual loss), and a RELATIVE AFFERENT PUPILLARY DEFECT.
optic_neuritis.the_disproportionate_colour_loss: COLOUR VISION — particularly red — is lost OUT OF PROPORTION to the loss of acuity. Ask the patient to compare the redness of an object with each eye; they will describe it as washed out or grey on the affected side. This is a simple bedside test that requires no equipment and is highly suggestive.

the_rapd.how_to_elicit: The SWINGING LIGHT TEST. Move the light between the eyes. In a relative afferent pupillary defect, when the light swings TO the affected eye BOTH pupils paradoxically DILATE, because the afferent signal from that eye is weaker than the consensual signal it was receiving from the healthy eye.
the_rapd.why_it_matters: It is an OBJECTIVE sign of optic nerve or extensive retinal dysfunction. It cannot be feigned, and it is not caused by cataract or refractive error — so it separates true optic nerve disease from media opacity and from functional visual loss.

optic_neuritis.the_fundus: In RETROBULBAR neuritis the disc looks NORMAL — "the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing", which is the majority in adults. In papillitis the disc is swollen. A normal fundus therefore does not exclude the diagnosis.
optic_neuritis.uhthoff_phenomenon: Transient worsening of vision (or other neurological symptoms) with a RISE IN BODY TEMPERATURE — a hot bath, exercise, fever. It reflects conduction failure in demyelinated axons at higher temperature, and it is not a relapse. Recognising it prevents unnecessary treatment and unnecessary alarm.

the_association_and_the_atypical_feature.typical: Unilateral, painful, with partial recovery over weeks. It is strongly associated with MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS and is frequently the first presentation — so it mandates MRI of brain and orbits, which also gives prognostic information about MS risk.
the_association_and_the_atypical_feature.atypical_features_that_change_the_diagno: BILATERAL simultaneous involvement · SEVERE loss with POOR recovery · marked disc swelling or haemorrhage · absence of pain · progression beyond two weeks · involvement in a child. These point to NMOSD (aquaporin-4) or MOGAD rather than MS, and they need specific antibody testing and different treatment — including the fact that several MS disease-modifying therapies WORSEN NMOSD.

optic_neuritis.the_differential_that_must_not_be_missed: GIANT CELL ARTERITIS in anyone over 50 — painless sudden visual loss, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, raised inflammatory markers. It is treated on suspicion with steroids because the other eye is at imminent risk. Also non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, compressive lesions, toxic and nutritional optic neuropathy (including B12 deficiency, methanol and ethambutol), and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy.

trigeminal_neuralgia.the_character: BRIEF, PAROXYSMAL, ELECTRIC-SHOCK-LIKE or stabbing pain in the distribution of one or more trigeminal divisions — usually V2 and V3, rarely V1 alone. Each paroxysm lasts seconds, though attacks cluster. It is strictly UNILATERAL in the great majority.
trigeminal_neuralgia.the_triggers: Light touch to a TRIGGER ZONE — washing the face, shaving, brushing teeth, a breeze, chewing, talking. The fact that a light touch triggers agonising pain while firm pressure may not is characteristic. Patients may stop eating and washing, and lose weight, and the condition carries a genuine risk of depression and suicidality.
trigeminal_neuralgia.the_cause: Most commonly NEUROVASCULAR CONFLICT — a vessel, usually the superior cerebellar artery, compressing the trigeminal root entry zone and causing focal demyelination.
the_red_flags_that_mean_it_is_secondary: Any SENSORY LOSS or other neurological deficit on examination — idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia has a NORMAL examination.
Deafness or other cranial nerve involvement.
Poor or absent response to carbamazepine.
These point to MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS (trigeminal neuralgia can be its presenting feature, especially in a young patient) or to a cerebellopontine angle tumour. Every patient warrants MRI.
trigeminal_neuralgia.management: CARBAMAZEPINE is first line and the response is often dramatic — a poor response should make you question the diagnosis. It requires monitoring for hyponatraemia, blood dyscrasias and rash, and it is a potent enzyme inducer with many interactions (including reducing the efficacy of hormonal contraception). Oxcarbazepine and other agents are alternatives. Surgical options include microvascular decompression, which is definitive in suitable patients, and ablative procedures. Ordinary analgesics including opioids are largely ineffective, and prescribing them is a common early error.

cerebellar_ataxia.the_signs_mnemonic_danish: DYSDIADOCHOKINESIA · ATAXIA (gait and truncal) · NYSTAGMUS · INTENTION TREMOR · SLURRED, staccato or scanning SPEECH · HYPOTONIA and pendular reflexes. Add DYSMETRIA (past-pointing) and REBOUND phenomenon.

localisation.midline_vermis: TRUNCAL ataxia and gait ataxia with relatively preserved limb coordination — the patient is unsteady sitting and walking but finger-nose may be near normal. Classic in alcohol-related degeneration and in midline tumours (medulloblastoma in children).
localisation.hemispheric: IPSILATERAL limb ataxia — cerebellar signs are on the SAME side as the lesion, unlike the cerebral cortex. This is a frequently forgotten and clinically useful rule.
localisation.nystagmus: Fast phase TOWARDS the side of the lesion.

cerebellar_ataxia.the_essential_distinction_from_sensory_a: ROMBERG TEST. In SENSORY ataxia (loss of proprioception — B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis, sensory neuropathy) the patient is reasonably steady with eyes open but falls when they CLOSE, because vision was compensating. In CEREBELLAR ataxia the patient is unsteady with eyes OPEN and closing them makes little additional difference — so Romberg is NEGATIVE. Romberg tests proprioception, not cerebellar function, and this is very commonly misunderstood.

the_causes.acute: STROKE (a cerebellar stroke can present with isolated vertigo and ataxia and is repeatedly misdiagnosed as peripheral vertigo — the presence of gait ataxia severe enough to prevent walking, or any other neurological sign, should prompt imaging) · alcohol intoxication · drug toxicity, notably PHENYTOIN, carbamazepine and lithium · Wernicke encephalopathy · post-infectious cerebellitis in children.
the_causes.subacute_or_chronic: Alcohol-related degeneration · multiple sclerosis · posterior fossa tumour · paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (anti-Yo, associated with breast and gynaecological malignancy) · hypothyroidism · coeliac disease · vitamin E deficiency · Friedreich ataxia and the spinocerebellar ataxias · Wilson disease in a young patient · ataxia telangiectasia in a child with recurrent infections and telangiectasia.

cerebellar_ataxia.the_immediate_priorities: Exclude stroke and a posterior fossa mass with imaging where the onset is acute or there are other signs. Check glucose, drug levels, thiamine status and thyroid function. Give thiamine before glucose in anyone at risk.

warnings: A relative afferent pupillary defect is an objective sign of optic nerve disease and cannot be feigned. Perform the swinging light test.
Colour vision is lost out of proportion to acuity in optic neuritis — compare red saturation between eyes at the bedside.
A NORMAL fundus does not exclude optic neuritis — most adult cases are retrobulbar.
Bilateral, severe, painless or poorly recovering optic neuritis suggests NMOSD or MOGAD, not MS — and several MS drugs worsen NMOSD.
In anyone over 50 with visual loss, consider giant cell arteritis and treat on suspicion — the other eye is at risk.
Trigeminal neuralgia under 40, bilateral, with any sensory loss, or unresponsive to carbamazepine, is SECONDARY — image it.
Idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia has a NORMAL neurological examination. Any deficit changes the diagnosis.
Opioids are largely ineffective in trigeminal neuralgia — carbamazepine is first line.
Carbamazepine causes hyponatraemia and is a potent enzyme inducer that reduces contraceptive efficacy.
Cerebellar signs are IPSILATERAL to the lesion.
Romberg tests PROPRIOCEPTION, not the cerebellum. It is negative in pure cerebellar ataxia.
A cerebellar stroke can mimic peripheral vertigo — inability to walk, or any other neurological sign, means image it.
Uhthoff phenomenon is heat-related worsening, not a relapse — do not treat it as one.
limitations: Antibody testing availability, imaging protocols and drug regimens are service-specific. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: How do you elicit a RAPD?
flashcards.a: Swinging light test — both pupils dilate when the light swings to the affected eye.

flashcards.q: Why is colour vision testing useful in optic neuritis?
flashcards.a: Colour, especially red, is lost out of proportion to acuity.

flashcards.q: Does a normal disc exclude optic neuritis?
flashcards.a: No — most adult cases are retrobulbar, so the disc looks normal.

flashcards.q: Which optic neuritis features suggest NMOSD rather than MS?
flashcards.a: Bilateral, severe, poor recovery, painless, or in a child.

flashcards.q: What is Uhthoff phenomenon?
flashcards.a: Transient worsening with a rise in body temperature — not a relapse.

flashcards.q: Red flags for secondary trigeminal neuralgia?
flashcards.a: Under 40, bilateral, any sensory loss, V1 alone, poor carbamazepine response.

flashcards.q: Recite DANISH.
flashcards.a: Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Slurred speech, Hypotonia.

flashcards.q: Which side are cerebellar signs on?
flashcards.a: Ipsilateral to the lesion.

flashcards.q: What does Romberg actually test?
flashcards.a: Proprioception. It is negative in pure cerebellar ataxia.

flashcards.q: Which stroke mimics peripheral vertigo?
flashcards.a: Cerebellar stroke — inability to walk or any other sign means image.

checkboxes: Neurological examination documented in trigeminal neuralgia

entries.title: Intracranial Bleeds and the Named Brain Imaging Signs
entries.summary: Extradural is LENTIFORM and does NOT cross sutures; subdural is CRESCENTIC and DOES. That single shape difference tells you which vessel bled and how fast — and the lucid interval belongs to the extradural.

terms: intracranial bleeds and the named brain imaging signs

extradural_epidural.shape: BICONVEX / LENTIFORM (lens-shaped). It does NOT cross SUTURE lines, because the dura is firmly attached there — but it CAN cross the midline and dural reflections.
extradural_epidural.vessel: Usually arterial — the MIDDLE MENINGEAL ARTERY, torn by a fracture at the PTERION, the thinnest part of the skull where four bones meet.
extradural_epidural.the_classic_history: Head injury with brief loss of consciousness, then a LUCID INTERVAL of apparent recovery lasting minutes to hours, then rapid deterioration as arterial blood accumulates. The lucid interval is what makes it dangerous — the patient looks well and is sent home or left unobserved.
extradural_epidural.who: Typically YOUNGER patients, because the dura is less adherent to the skull than in the elderly.
extradural_epidural.why_it_is_a_surgical_emergency: Arterial bleeding expands fast. Prompt evacuation gives excellent outcomes; delay is catastrophic. This is one of the highest-return neurosurgical operations there is.

subdural.shape: CRESCENTIC, concave against the brain surface. It DOES cross suture lines — because it lies inside the dura — but it does NOT cross the midline (the falx stops it).
subdural.vessel: Venous — the BRIDGING VEINS crossing from cortex to dural sinus.
subdural.who_and_why: ELDERLY, ALCOHOL-dependent, and ANTICOAGULATED patients, and infants. Cerebral atrophy stretches the bridging veins and gives the blood space to accumulate, so a trivial or entirely forgotten injury can cause it — and the presentation may be weeks later.
subdural.chronic_subdural: Presents insidiously with confusion, headache, personality change, gait disturbance, drowsiness or fluctuating consciousness — very frequently misdiagnosed as dementia, delirium, stroke or depression. Any older person with unexplained cognitive or gait decline deserves consideration of a chronic subdural, because it is treatable. Density changes over time: acute is hyperdense (white), subacute becomes ISODENSE to brain around 1–3 weeks (and can therefore be nearly INVISIBLE on CT — look for effacement of sulci, midline shift or asymmetry rather than for obvious blood), and chronic becomes hypodense (dark).
subdural.in_infants: Subdural haemorrhage with retinal haemorrhages and encephalopathy raises abusive head trauma — see the safeguarding entry.

the_four_compartments.subarachnoid: Blood in the CSF spaces — sulci, basal cisterns, Sylvian fissures. Usually aneurysmal or traumatic. Covered in its own entry.
the_four_compartments.intracerebral: Within the brain parenchyma. Hypertensive bleeds occur in the deep structures — basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum — from Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms. Lobar bleeds in the elderly suggest CEREBRAL AMYLOID ANGIOPATHY. Also consider tumour, arteriovenous malformation, venous infarction and coagulopathy.

the_named_signs_worth_knowing.hyperdense_mca_sign: A bright, dense middle cerebral artery on NON-contrast CT — thrombus within the vessel. It is one of the EARLIEST signs of ischaemic stroke, visible before any parenchymal change, and it identifies a large-vessel occlusion that may be amenable to thrombectomy. Compare with the opposite side; asymmetry is the clue.
the_named_signs_worth_knowing.insular_ribbon_sign: Loss of the normal grey-white distinction at the insular cortex — an early sign of MCA territory infarction, and one of the first areas to change because it is a watershed region.
the_named_signs_worth_knowing.loss_of_grey_white_differentiation_and_s: Early ischaemic change generally. Subtle and easily missed within the first hours, which is why comparing sides systematically matters.
the_named_signs_worth_knowing.dense_triangle_and_empty_delta: Signs of CEREBRAL VENOUS SINUS THROMBOSIS. The DENSE TRIANGLE is fresh thrombus in the superior sagittal sinus on non-contrast CT; the EMPTY DELTA is the enhancing sinus wall surrounding a non-enhancing central clot on contrast imaging. Suspect venous thrombosis with headache plus seizures, papilloedema, or an infarct that does not respect an arterial territory — particularly in pregnancy, the puerperium, on oestrogen-containing contraception, in dehydration or in thrombophilia.
the_named_signs_worth_knowing.swirl_sign: An area of lower density within an acute haematoma, indicating ACTIVE, ONGOING bleeding with unclotted fresh blood. It predicts expansion and worse outcome — an urgent finding, not a curiosity.
the_named_signs_worth_knowing.cord_sign: A dense cortical vein — another sign of venous thrombosis.
the_named_signs_worth_knowing.midline_shift_and_herniation: Quantify midline shift at the septum pellucidum. Watch for effacement of the basal cisterns, which indicates raised pressure and impending herniation. UNCAL herniation compresses the third nerve, giving an IPSILATERAL fixed dilated pupil, and then the midbrain — a fixed dilated pupil in a head-injured patient is a neurosurgical emergency, not a sign to observe.

the_practical_rules: A patient on ANTICOAGULANTS with any head injury, however trivial, needs imaging and a period of observation — bleeding may be delayed.
A LUCID INTERVAL means an extradural until proven otherwise. Do not let apparent recovery reassure you.
A normal early CT does not exclude an evolving bleed — repeat if the patient deteriorates.
An ISODENSE subacute subdural can look almost normal. Look for sulcal effacement, ventricular compression and midline shift rather than for visible blood.
Correct coagulopathy urgently and discuss anticoagulation reversal in any intracranial bleed.
Any older person with unexplained cognitive decline, gait disturbance or fluctuating consciousness deserves consideration of chronic subdural haematoma — it is treatable and it is missed.

warnings: A LUCID INTERVAL after head injury means extradural haematoma until proven otherwise.
Extradural is lentiform and does NOT cross sutures; subdural is crescentic and DOES cross sutures but not the midline.
Any head injury in an anticoagulated patient needs imaging and observation, however trivial the mechanism.
A subacute subdural becomes ISODENSE at 1 to 3 weeks and can be nearly invisible — look for effacement and shift.
Chronic subdural masquerades as dementia, delirium, stroke or depression in older people. It is treatable.
A fixed dilated pupil in a head-injured patient indicates uncal herniation — a neurosurgical emergency.
The SWIRL SIGN indicates active ongoing bleeding and predicts haematoma expansion.
