Suspect venous sinus thrombosis with headache plus seizures or papilloedema, or an infarct not respecting an arterial territory — especially in pregnancy, puerperium or on oestrogen.
A normal early CT does not exclude an evolving bleed. Repeat it if the patient deteriorates.
Lobar haemorrhage in an elderly patient suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy.
limitations: Imaging selection, reversal protocols and neurosurgical thresholds are protocol-specific. Radiological interpretation requires appropriate training and reporting.

flashcards.q: Extradural shape and suture rule?
flashcards.a: Lentiform/biconvex; does NOT cross sutures but can cross the midline.

flashcards.q: Subdural shape and suture rule?
flashcards.a: Crescentic; DOES cross sutures but not the midline.

flashcards.q: Which vessel bleeds in each?
flashcards.a: Extradural: middle meningeal artery at the pterion. Subdural: bridging veins.

flashcards.q: What is the lucid interval and what does it mean?
flashcards.a: Apparent recovery before deterioration — classic for extradural haematoma.

flashcards.q: Why is a subacute subdural hard to see?
flashcards.a: It becomes isodense to brain at 1 to 3 weeks — look for effacement and shift.

flashcards.q: What is the hyperdense MCA sign?
flashcards.a: Thrombus in the middle cerebral artery — an early sign of large-vessel ischaemic stroke.

flashcards.q: What are the dense triangle and empty delta signs?
flashcards.a: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — clot on non-contrast, and enhancing wall around non-enhancing clot on contrast.

flashcards.q: What does the swirl sign indicate?
flashcards.a: Active ongoing bleeding within a haematoma — predicts expansion.

flashcards.q: What does a fixed dilated pupil after head injury mean?
flashcards.a: Uncal herniation compressing the third nerve — neurosurgical emergency.

checkboxes: Sutures and midline used to classify the collection
Basal cisterns and midline shift assessed
Chronic subdural considered in unexplained cognitive or gait decline

entries.title: Cell Injury and Death — Necrosis Versus Apoptosis
entries.summary: Necrosis is an accident and it INFLAMES; apoptosis is a programme and it does NOT. That single difference explains why an infarct hurts and swells while the daily death of billions of cells is silent — and it is the foundation of the rest of pathology.

terms: cell injury and death — necrosis versus apoptosis

the_sequence_of_injury.reversible: Reduced oxygen means less ATP. The Na/K ATPase fails, so sodium and water enter — CELLULAR SWELLING, the earliest change. Ribosomes detach and protein synthesis falls; the cell switches to anaerobic glycolysis, producing LACTATE and intracellular acidosis. Fatty change appears in metabolically active organs. All of this is REVERSIBLE if perfusion returns.
the_sequence_of_injury.the_point_of_no_return: Two events mark irreversibility: severe MEMBRANE damage (plasma, lysosomal and mitochondrial) and massive CALCIUM INFLUX. Calcium activates phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases and ATPases, which digest the cell from within. Lysosomal rupture completes it.
the_sequence_of_injury.how_we_detect_it_clinically: Membrane failure releases intracellular contents into the blood — which is precisely what troponin, CK, ALT and LDH measure. Enzyme leak IS membrane failure, and that is why those tests work.
the_sequence_of_injury.reperfusion_injury: Restoring blood flow can paradoxically WORSEN damage, through a burst of free radicals, calcium overload, complement activation and neutrophil influx. It is the reason reperfusion strategies carry their own risk and why antioxidant and controlled-reperfusion approaches have been studied.

necrosis_versus_apoptosis.necrosis: UNREGULATED death from external injury. The cell SWELLS and RUPTURES, spilling contents into the tissue, which triggers ACUTE INFLAMMATION. It always affects GROUPS of cells. It is pathological.
necrosis_versus_apoptosis.apoptosis: REGULATED, energy-DEPENDENT programmed death. The cell SHRINKS, chromatin condenses, and it fragments into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed intact — so NO inflammation occurs. It affects SINGLE cells. It is physiological as well as pathological.
necrosis_versus_apoptosis.why_the_distinction_matters_clinically: Inflammation is the difference. It explains the pain, swelling, fever and raised inflammatory markers of an infarct, and their absence in the vast physiological turnover of cells. It also explains why apoptosis is the target of cancer therapy — most chemotherapy and radiotherapy work by pushing damaged cells into apoptosis, and cancers that have disabled apoptosis (for example through p53 loss) are correspondingly resistant.
necrosis_versus_apoptosis.apoptosis_pathways: INTRINSIC (mitochondrial) — DNA damage or loss of survival signals, mediated by p53 and the BCL-2 family, releasing cytochrome c. EXTRINSIC (death receptor) — Fas and TNF receptor ligation. Both converge on CASPASES.
necrosis_versus_apoptosis.when_apoptosis_goes_wrong: TOO LITTLE gives cancer and autoimmunity (autoreactive lymphocytes that should have been deleted survive). TOO MUCH contributes to neurodegeneration, and to the lymphocyte depletion of HIV.

the_patterns_of_necrosis_and_what_each_t.coagulative: Architecture is PRESERVED as a "ghost outline" because denatured enzymes cannot digest the tissue. Typical of ISCHAEMIC infarction in ALL organs EXCEPT the brain. Firm and pale.
the_patterns_of_necrosis_and_what_each_t.liquefactive: Tissue DIGESTED to a liquid. Occurs in the BRAIN (which is rich in lipid and low in supportive stroma, so an infarct liquefies and leaves a fluid-filled cavity) and in ABSCESSES, where neutrophil enzymes do the digesting. That the brain is the exception to coagulative necrosis is a classic and useful fact.
the_patterns_of_necrosis_and_what_each_t.caseous: A "cheese-like", crumbly, white appearance — a combination of coagulative and liquefactive with granulomatous inflammation. Characteristic of TUBERCULOSIS, and also of some fungal infections. Finding caseation on histology is a strong pointer to TB.
the_patterns_of_necrosis_and_what_each_t.fat_necrosis: Enzymatic (acute pancreatitis, where released lipase digests peritoneal fat and the freed fatty acids bind calcium to form chalky white SAPONIFICATION — which is also why acute pancreatitis causes HYPOCALCAEMIA), or traumatic (classically the breast, where it forms a hard lump that mimics carcinoma).
the_patterns_of_necrosis_and_what_each_t.fibrinoid: A bright pink, structureless deposit in vessel walls — immune complexes and fibrin. Seen in VASCULITIS, malignant hypertension and rheumatic conditions.
the_patterns_of_necrosis_and_what_each_t.gangrene: A clinical term, not a distinct mechanism. DRY gangrene is coagulative necrosis from ischaemia with a clear demarcation line. WET gangrene has superimposed bacterial infection with liquefaction, and it is the one that becomes rapidly life-threatening. GAS gangrene is clostridial with crepitus.

body.the_cellular_adaptations_that_precede_in: HYPERTROPHY (bigger cells) · HYPERPLASIA (more cells) · ATROPHY (smaller or fewer) · METAPLASIA (one mature type replaced by another better suited to the stress) · and then DYSPLASIA and NEOPLASIA when adaptation becomes disordered. Adaptation is the tissue succeeding; injury is adaptation failing.

warnings: Enzyme leak into blood (troponin, CK, ALT, LDH) IS membrane failure — that is what those tests detect.
The BRAIN is the exception: it undergoes liquefactive, not coagulative, necrosis after infarction.
Caseous necrosis strongly suggests tuberculosis.
Fat necrosis in acute pancreatitis binds calcium as soap — this is a mechanism of the hypocalcaemia.
Breast fat necrosis mimics carcinoma clinically and radiologically. Biopsy it.
Wet gangrene is infected and rapidly life-threatening; dry gangrene is not.
Reperfusion can worsen injury through free radicals and neutrophil influx.
Cancers that disable apoptosis (for example p53 loss) resist chemotherapy and radiotherapy, which work by inducing it.
limitations: A mechanistic overview; histological diagnosis requires a pathologist.

flashcards.q: Necrosis vs apoptosis in one word?
flashcards.a: Inflammation — necrosis causes it, apoptosis does not.

flashcards.q: What are the two markers of irreversible injury?
flashcards.a: Severe membrane damage and massive calcium influx.

flashcards.q: Why do we measure troponin and CK?
flashcards.a: They leak out when membranes fail — enzyme leak is membrane failure.

flashcards.q: Which organ shows liquefactive rather than coagulative necrosis?
flashcards.a: The brain.

flashcards.q: What does caseous necrosis suggest?
flashcards.a: Tuberculosis.

flashcards.q: Why does acute pancreatitis cause hypocalcaemia?
flashcards.a: Freed fatty acids bind calcium as soaps — saponification.

flashcards.q: Dry vs wet gangrene?
flashcards.a: Dry is ischaemic coagulative necrosis; wet has bacterial infection and liquefaction and is life-threatening.

flashcards.q: Why does p53 loss cause chemoresistance?
flashcards.a: Chemotherapy kills by inducing apoptosis, which p53 mediates.

checkboxes: Pattern of necrosis matched to likely cause
Wet gangrene recognised as a surgical emergency

entries.title: Inflammation, Healing and the Systemic Consequences
entries.summary: Acute inflammation is vascular and neutrophilic and resolves; chronic inflammation is cellular and fibrotic and does not. Whether a wound REGENERATES or SCARS depends on one thing — whether the tissue framework survived.

terms: inflammation, healing and the systemic consequences

the_five_cardinal_signs_and_their_mechan.rubor_redness: VASODILATATION increasing blood flow — mediated by histamine, prostaglandins and nitric oxide.
the_five_cardinal_signs_and_their_mechan.calor_heat: The same increased blood flow bringing core-temperature blood to the surface.
the_five_cardinal_signs_and_their_mechan.tumor_swelling: Increased vascular PERMEABILITY letting protein-rich fluid into the tissue — an EXUDATE. This is what distinguishes inflammatory fluid (high protein, high LDH) from a TRANSUDATE (low protein, from pressure imbalance as in heart failure), and it is the basis of Light criteria in pleural fluid.
the_five_cardinal_signs_and_their_mechan.dolor_pain: BRADYKININ and PROSTAGLANDINS sensitising nociceptors. NSAIDs work by blocking prostaglandin synthesis, which is why they treat pain AND swelling AND fever together — all three come from the same molecule.
the_five_cardinal_signs_and_their_mechan.functio_laesa: Loss of function, from pain, swelling and tissue damage.

acute_versus_chronic.acute: Onset over minutes to hours. Dominated by NEUTROPHILS and vascular change. Outcomes: complete RESOLUTION, ABSCESS, HEALING BY FIBROSIS, or progression to chronic.
acute_versus_chronic.chronic: Persists over weeks to years. Dominated by MACROPHAGES, LYMPHOCYTES and PLASMA CELLS, with simultaneous tissue destruction and attempted repair — which is why chronic inflammation produces FIBROSIS. It arises from persistent infection, prolonged exposure to a toxic agent, or autoimmunity.
acute_versus_chronic.the_useful_bedside_correlate: Neutrophils dominate early bacterial infection; lymphocytes dominate viral and chronic processes. That is why the differential white count is informative.

granulomatous_inflammation.what_a_granuloma_is: An organised collection of activated MACROPHAGES (epithelioid cells), often with multinucleate GIANT CELLS, surrounded by lymphocytes. It forms when the immune system cannot eliminate an agent and instead WALLS IT OFF.
granulomatous_inflammation.caseating: With central necrosis — TUBERCULOSIS above all, and some fungal infections. Always send tissue for MICROBIOLOGY and stains as well as histology; treating a caseating granuloma as sarcoidosis with steroids while it is TB is a serious and recurrent error.
granulomatous_inflammation.non_caseating: SARCOIDOSIS, Crohn disease, foreign body reaction, berylliosis, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
granulomatous_inflammation.why_it_matters: Granulomas explain why TB can be contained for decades and then REACTIVATE when immunity falls — with HIV, anti-TNF therapy, steroids, malnutrition or age. Anyone about to start anti-TNF therapy must be screened for latent TB for exactly this reason.

healing_and_repair.the_governing_principle: Whether a tissue REGENERATES (restoring normal structure) or REPAIRS by SCAR depends on the cell type AND on whether the connective tissue FRAMEWORK survived. If the scaffold is intact, cells can repopulate it correctly. If it is destroyed, fibrosis fills the gap.

cell_types.labile: Continuously dividing — epidermis, gut mucosa, bone marrow. Regenerate well, and are also the tissues most damaged by chemotherapy and radiotherapy, which is why mucositis, marrow suppression and hair loss are the predictable toxicities.
cell_types.stable: Normally quiescent but able to divide when needed — LIVER (the classic, capable of remarkable regeneration if the architecture survives), kidney tubules, fibroblasts, endothelium.
cell_types.permanent: Cannot divide — NEURONES, cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle (largely). Damage here is repaired by SCAR, not regeneration. This is exactly why a myocardial infarct leaves fibrous scar rather than new myocardium, and why cerebral infarction leaves permanent deficit.

healing_and_repair.the_liver_example: Liver regenerates well after acute injury with an intact framework. In CIRRHOSIS the framework is destroyed and replaced by fibrous septa, so regeneration becomes disorganised nodules — architecture is lost, portal pressure rises, and the process is largely irreversible. Same organ, same cells, completely different outcome depending on the scaffold.

wound_healing.primary_intention: Clean, apposed wound edges — minimal tissue loss, rapid, minimal scar.
wound_healing.secondary_intention: A large defect with separated edges — heals by granulation tissue filling from the base up, with WOUND CONTRACTION and a larger scar. Slower and more prone to contracture.
wound_healing.the_phases: HAEMOSTASIS (clot) → INFLAMMATION (neutrophils then macrophages) → PROLIFERATION (granulation tissue: new capillaries plus fibroblasts laying down type III collagen, with re-epithelialisation) → REMODELLING (type III collagen replaced by stronger type I over months). A wound regains only about 70–80% of original tensile strength, and never reaches 100%.
wound_healing.what_impairs_healing: Poor blood supply and hypoxia · INFECTION · foreign body · movement · diabetes · malnutrition, particularly PROTEIN, VITAMIN C (required for collagen hydroxylation — its deficiency in scurvy causes wounds to break down and old scars to reopen) and ZINC · CORTICOSTEROIDS (which impair every phase) · smoking · advanced age · radiotherapy · and chemotherapy.

abnormal_scarring.hypertrophic_scar: Raised but stays WITHIN the boundaries of the original wound, and often improves over time.
abnormal_scarring.keloid: Extends BEYOND the original wound boundary, does not regress, and frequently recurs after excision. It is markedly commoner in people with darker skin, and commonest on the sternum, shoulders and earlobes. It matters practically: elective incisions in high-risk sites and patients should be planned with this in mind, and patients should be counselled BEFORE surgery, including before ear piercing.
abnormal_scarring.contracture: Excessive wound contraction across a joint or orifice, limiting movement. A major cause of long-term disability after BURNS, and largely preventable with early physiotherapy, splinting and pressure garments.

the_systemic_consequences.acute_phase_response: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF drive fever, leucocytosis, and hepatic synthesis of CRP, fibrinogen, ferritin and hepcidin, while ALBUMIN and transferrin FALL (negative acute phase reactants). This explains a great deal of routine biochemistry: why albumin drops in any illness, why ferritin rises regardless of iron stores, and why ESR rises with fibrinogen.
the_systemic_consequences.anaemia_of_chronic_disease: HEPCIDIN, driven by IL-6, blocks iron release from macrophages and absorption from the gut. Iron is present but LOCKED AWAY. This is why iron supplementation fails in active inflammation and why ferritin is normal or high while the patient is functionally iron-deficient.
the_systemic_consequences.secondary_amyloidosis: Chronic inflammation drives sustained production of serum amyloid A, which deposits as AA amyloid — classically in kidney (causing nephrotic syndrome), liver, spleen and gut. It is a long-term consequence of untreated chronic inflammatory disease: rheumatoid arthritis, chronic infection, bronchiectasis, tuberculosis, osteomyelitis and inflammatory bowel disease. It is a reason that controlling chronic inflammation matters beyond symptoms.
the_systemic_consequences.the_others: Cachexia from TNF, reactive thrombocytosis, a pro-thrombotic state, and — over years — accelerated ATHEROSCLEROSIS, which is why chronic inflammatory diseases carry excess cardiovascular mortality.

warnings: Send tissue for microbiology as well as histology when a granuloma is found — treating TB as sarcoidosis with steroids is a serious and recurrent error.
Screen for latent TB before starting anti-TNF therapy — granulomas contain, they do not cure.
Permanent cells (neurones, cardiac muscle) heal by SCAR, not regeneration.
Liver regeneration depends on an intact framework — once cirrhosis destroys it, the process is largely irreversible.
Vitamin C deficiency causes wound breakdown and reopening of old scars, because collagen cannot be hydroxylated.
Corticosteroids impair every phase of wound healing.
Keloid extends BEYOND the wound, recurs after excision, and is commoner in darker skin — counsel before elective incisions and piercings.
Burn contractures cause major long-term disability and are largely preventable with early physiotherapy and splinting.
Iron supplementation fails in active inflammation because hepcidin locks iron away — a normal ferritin can coexist with functional iron deficiency.
Albumin falls in any inflammation — it is a negative acute phase reactant, not a nutrition marker.
Uncontrolled chronic inflammation causes secondary AA amyloidosis and accelerated atherosclerosis.
A healed wound never regains full tensile strength — about 70 to 80 per cent at best.
limitations: A mechanistic overview; it does not replace histopathological or microbiological diagnosis.

flashcards.q: Which mediator links pain, swelling and fever, and what blocks it?
flashcards.a: Prostaglandins — blocked by NSAIDs, which is why they treat all three.

flashcards.q: Exudate vs transudate?
flashcards.a: Exudate is protein-rich from increased permeability (inflammation); transudate is low protein from pressure imbalance.

flashcards.q: What is a granuloma and why does the body make one?
flashcards.a: Organised activated macrophages walling off something the immune system cannot eliminate.

flashcards.q: Caseating vs non-caseating granuloma?
flashcards.a: Caseating suggests TB and fungi; non-caseating suggests sarcoid, Crohn, foreign body.

flashcards.q: Which cell types cannot regenerate?
flashcards.a: Permanent cells — neurones and cardiac muscle. They scar.

flashcards.q: Why does cirrhosis not regenerate normally?
flashcards.a: The connective tissue framework is destroyed, so regeneration is disorganised into nodules.

flashcards.q: Hypertrophic scar vs keloid?
flashcards.a: Hypertrophic stays within the wound and may improve; keloid extends beyond and recurs.

flashcards.q: Why does iron therapy fail in chronic inflammation?
flashcards.a: Hepcidin blocks iron release and absorption — iron is present but locked away.

flashcards.q: What is secondary amyloidosis?
flashcards.a: AA amyloid from chronic serum amyloid A production in long-standing inflammation — often presenting with nephrotic syndrome.

checkboxes: Microbiology sent alongside histology for granulomas
Wound healing factors reviewed (nutrition, steroids, perfusion, infection)
Keloid risk discussed before elective incision
Physiotherapy and splinting arranged after burns
Inflammation considered before interpreting ferritin or albumin

entries.title: The Clinical Rules of N — Threes, Nines, Tens and the Rest
entries.summary: Numbered rules are memory aids, not evidence. Each one here is given with its actual meaning and, where relevant, the caveat that makes it safe to use — because several of them are routinely quoted in a form that is wrong.

terms: the clinical rules of n — threes, nines, tens and the rest

body.how_to_use_these: They compress a lot into a memorable form, and every one of them oversimplifies. Use them to PROMPT a thought, never to settle a decision — and know the caveat attached to each.

the_rule_of_nines_burns.what: Estimating total body surface area burned in ADULTS: head and neck 9% · each arm 9% · each leg 18% · anterior trunk 18% · posterior trunk 18% · perineum 1%.
the_rule_of_nines_burns.the_palm_rule: The patient own PALM INCLUDING THE FINGERS is approximately 1% of their body surface area — useful for scattered or irregular burns.
the_caveats_that_matter: It is INVALID IN CHILDREN, because a child head is proportionally much larger and the legs smaller. Use the LUND AND BROWDER chart, which is age-adjusted. Applying the adult rule of nines to a child systematically under-estimates the burn and therefore under-resuscitates.
Do NOT include SUPERFICIAL (erythema only) burns in the total used for fluid calculation — only partial and full thickness.
It is an ESTIMATE, and it is consistently over-estimated by inexperienced assessors, leading to over-resuscitation, which causes its own harm.

the_rule_of_tens_phaeochromocytoma.what: 10% bilateral · 10% extra-adrenal · 10% malignant · 10% in children · 10% not hypertensive · (some versions add 10% familial).
the_rule_of_tens_phaeochromocytoma.the_correction: The FAMILIAL figure is now known to be substantially WRONG — modern series find up to 40% are hereditary. Genetic testing is offered widely rather than to a selected 10%. Keep the mnemonic for the other features; discard the familial figure.

the_rule_of_twos_meckel_diverticulum.what: Present in about 2% of the population · about 2 inches long · about 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve · frequently symptomatic before age 2 · twice as common in males · and may contain 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric and pancreatic).
the_rule_of_twos_meckel_diverticulum.why_it_is_clinically_useful: The ectopic GASTRIC mucosa secretes acid and causes painless massive rectal bleeding in a child — and it is what makes the technetium pertechnetate "Meckel scan" work, because the tracer is taken up by gastric mucosa.

the_rule_of_threes.infant_colic: Crying for more than 3 hours a day, more than 3 days a week, for more than 3 weeks, in an otherwise thriving infant. Its value is that it defines a threshold for a benign diagnosis — and equally, it reminds you that crying which does not fit this pattern, or occurs in an infant who is not thriving, needs a cause found.
the_rule_of_threes.the_survival_rule: Roughly 3 minutes without oxygen, 3 days without water, 3 weeks without food. A crude but useful triage-of-priorities aid.
the_rule_of_threes.aortic_aneurysm_note: Various "rule of threes" are quoted for aneurysm surveillance intervals and thresholds — these differ between national programmes and must be taken from your local protocol rather than a mnemonic.

the_other_numbered_rules_worth_knowing.rule_of_15_hypoglycaemia: For a conscious patient able to swallow: 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then give a longer-acting carbohydrate. Follow your local protocol for the exact quantities.
the_other_numbered_rules_worth_knowing.rule_of_100_hyperkalaemia_note: Various "rule of 100" aids exist across specialties (for example in ventilation and in acid-base). They are institution-specific and should not be carried between contexts.
the_other_numbered_rules_worth_knowing.the_6_second_rule_ecg: Count the QRS complexes in 6 seconds (30 large squares at 25 mm/s) and multiply by 10 to estimate rate. It is the reliable method in an IRREGULAR rhythm, where the 300-divided-by-large-squares method fails.
the_other_numbered_rules_worth_knowing.the_300_150_100_75_60_50_sequence: Rate estimation for a REGULAR rhythm by counting large squares between R waves.
the_other_numbered_rules_worth_knowing.rule_of_9s_for_the_hand: Not to be confused with burns — various hand surface estimates exist; use the palm rule instead.
the_other_numbered_rules_worth_knowing.light_criteria_note: Not a rule of N, but frequently grouped with them: pleural fluid is an EXUDATE if fluid:serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, fluid:serum LDH exceeds 0.6, or fluid LDH exceeds two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Any ONE criterion makes it an exudate.
the_other_numbered_rules_worth_knowing.the_rule_of_10_for_surgery_in_phaeochrom: Not a real rule — see the alpha-before-beta rule instead, which is the one that matters.

body.the_honest_caveat: Numbered rules persist because they are memorable, not because they are accurate. Several have been superseded by evidence while continuing to be taught. Where a rule conflicts with a current guideline or with the patient in front of you, the rule loses.

warnings: The rule of nines is INVALID IN CHILDREN — use Lund and Browder, or you will under-estimate and under-resuscitate.
Do not include superficial erythema in the burn area used for fluid calculation.
The "10% familial" figure for phaeochromocytoma is wrong — up to 40% are hereditary and genetic testing is offered widely.
Burn area is consistently over-estimated by inexperienced assessors, causing harmful over-resuscitation.
Use the 6-second method to estimate rate in an irregular rhythm; the large-square method only works if regular.
Any ONE Light criterion makes a pleural effusion an exudate.
Numbered rules prompt thought; they never settle a decision. Where a rule conflicts with current guidance, the rule loses.
limitations: Several of these rules vary between institutions and national guidelines. Confirm the version your service uses.

flashcards.q: Rule of nines in an adult?
flashcards.a: Head 9, each arm 9, each leg 18, front trunk 18, back trunk 18, perineum 1.

flashcards.q: Why is it invalid in children?
flashcards.a: A child head is proportionally larger and legs smaller — use Lund and Browder.

flashcards.q: What is the palm rule?
flashcards.a: The patient palm including fingers is about 1% of body surface area.

flashcards.q: Which part of the phaeochromocytoma rule of tens is wrong?
flashcards.a: The familial figure — up to 40% are hereditary, not 10%.

flashcards.q: Recite the rule of twos for Meckel.
flashcards.a: 2% of people, 2 inches long, 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, symptomatic before 2, twice as common in males, 2 ectopic tissue types.

flashcards.q: Why does the Meckel scan work?
flashcards.a: Technetium pertechnetate is taken up by the ectopic gastric mucosa.

flashcards.q: Rule of threes for infant colic?
flashcards.a: Over 3 hours a day, over 3 days a week, over 3 weeks, in a thriving infant.

flashcards.q: How do you estimate rate in an irregular rhythm?
flashcards.a: Count QRS complexes in 6 seconds and multiply by 10.

flashcards.q: How many Light criteria make an exudate?
flashcards.a: Any one.

checkboxes: Superficial burn excluded from the calculation
Genetic testing offered in phaeochromocytoma regardless of the old 10% figure
Rate method matched to rhythm regularity
Local protocol confirmed where a rule varies

entries.title: Digoxin Effect Versus Digoxin Toxicity — Two Different Things
entries.summary: The scooped ST depression of DIGOXIN EFFECT is an EXPECTED finding in a correctly dosed patient and means nothing is wrong. DIGOXIN TOXICITY is a different entity with different ECG findings, and the level does not decide which one you are looking at.

terms: digoxin effect versus digoxin toxicity — two different things

the_distinction_that_matters.the_error: A scooped ST segment on the ECG of a patient taking digoxin is repeatedly reported as "digoxin toxicity". It is not. It is DIGOXIN EFFECT — the expected electrophysiological signature of the drug being present. Treating it as poisoning leads to stopping a drug that is working; ignoring genuine toxicity because "the level is in range" leads to death. The two are separate questions.
the_distinction_that_matters.the_rule: DIGOXIN EFFECT is about the ST SEGMENT and is benign. DIGOXIN TOXICITY is about RHYTHM plus SYSTEMIC symptoms, and it is a clinical diagnosis.

digoxin_effect.what_it_is: The normal repolarisation change caused by therapeutic digoxin. It indicates the drug is present. It does NOT indicate the dose is right, and it does not indicate the dose is wrong.

the_ecg.st_segment: DOWNSLOPING ST depression with a distinctive concave, "SCOOPED" shape — described as the REVERSE TICK sign (like a tick mark drawn backwards) or as "SALVADOR DALÍ sagging", after the drooping clocks. It is most obvious in the lateral leads (V5, V6, I, aVL) where the R waves are tallest.
the_ecg.t_wave: FLATTENED, biphasic or INVERTED T waves.
the_ecg.qt_interval: SHORTENED QT — a useful discriminator, because most causes of ST-T change either lengthen the QT or leave it alone. Shortening points at digoxin.
the_ecg.pr_interval: Mildly PROLONGED, from the drug's vagal effect slowing AV nodal conduction.

digoxin_effect.why_it_gets_confused_with_ischaemia: Downsloping ST depression also occurs in ischaemia and in left ventricular strain. The discriminators are the SCOOPED shape rather than a straight or upsloping line, the SHORT QT rather than a normal or long one, and the clinical context. When genuinely uncertain, treat the patient: digoxin effect does not cause chest pain.
digoxin_effect.what_to_do: Nothing. Record it, and do not order a digoxin level because of it alone.

digoxin_toxicity.what_it_is: Poisoning. A clinical diagnosis based on symptoms, rhythm and electrolytes — NOT on the serum level alone. Toxicity occurs at "therapeutic" levels when potassium, magnesium or renal function are wrong, and a high level in an asymptomatic patient with a normal rhythm may not need treatment.

the_ecg_findings.the_unifying_mechanism: Digoxin causes INCREASED AUTOMATICITY with DEPRESSED CONDUCTION. That combination is the signature: fast, ectopic activity happening at the same time as block. Almost any arrhythmia can occur, but the ones that should raise digoxin immediately are:
the_ecg_findings.the_near_specific_one: BIDIRECTIONAL VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA — a broad complex tachycardia in which the QRS axis alternates beat to beat. It is rare and highly suggestive; the other main cause is catecholaminergic polymorphic VT.
the_ecg_findings.the_classic_combination: ATRIAL TACHYCARDIA WITH AV BLOCK — a fast atrium with a blocked conduction system in the same tracing. This is the increased-automaticity-plus-depressed-conduction pattern made visible, and it is close to a fingerprint.
the_ecg_findings.the_others: Frequent ventricular ectopy and bigeminy, any degree of AV block, junctional rhythms, severe bradycardia, and — a specific pattern worth knowing — REGULARISED atrial fibrillation, where a previously irregular AF becomes regular because of complete AV block with a junctional escape. A regular rhythm in a patient known to be in AF is a red flag, not reassurance.

the_systemic_features.gastrointestinal: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain — usually the EARLIEST symptoms, and routinely attributed to something else in an elderly patient.
the_systemic_features.neurological: Confusion, drowsiness, weakness, headache, and in older patients a delirium that gets blamed on age or infection.
the_systemic_features.visual: The distinctive one — XANTHOPSIA: a yellow-green tinge to vision, with HALOES around lights. Also blurring and altered colour perception. Ask about it directly; patients rarely volunteer "things look yellow" as a drug side effect.

the_electrolytes_that_drive_it.hypokalaemia: The commonest precipitant of CHRONIC toxicity. Digoxin and potassium COMPETE for the same binding site on the Na/K-ATPase, so a LOW potassium means MORE digoxin binds and toxicity occurs at an ordinary level. Diuretics therefore cause digoxin toxicity indirectly and constantly. Also correct MAGNESIUM — hypomagnesaemia both causes refractory hypokalaemia and independently worsens toxicity.
the_electrolytes_that_drive_it.hyperkalaemia_in_acute_overdose: The opposite direction, and it is a SEVERITY MARKER rather than a cause. In acute overdose the pump is massively inhibited, so potassium leaks out of cells and the serum potassium RISES. A high potassium in acute digoxin overdose predicts mortality and is an indication for antidote.
the_electrolytes_that_drive_it.the_trap: Do NOT reflexively give intravenous CALCIUM for hyperkalaemia if digoxin toxicity is the cause. The traditional teaching is that it precipitates an inexcitable "stone heart"; the modern evidence for that is weaker than once believed, but the safe course remains to treat the digoxin with the antidote rather than reach for calcium first. Follow your local toxicology advice.
the_electrolytes_that_drive_it.other_precipitants: RENAL IMPAIRMENT (digoxin is renally cleared — an AKI turns a stable dose into an overdose), hypercalcaemia, hypothyroidism, age, low body weight, and DRUG INTERACTIONS: amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine, macrolides, itraconazole and spironolactone all raise digoxin levels.

management_principles: Continuous cardiac monitoring, and correct potassium and magnesium carefully.
Treat bradyarrhythmia with atropine; pacing may be needed, though it carries risk in a hyper-excitable myocardium.
DIGOXIN IMMUNE FAB is the antidote and is indicated for life-threatening arrhythmia, significant hyperkalaemia in acute overdose, haemodynamic instability or a very large ingestion. It works fast.
Digoxin is NOT removed by dialysis — the volume of distribution is far too large. This is asked constantly and got wrong constantly.
Avoid class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics; discuss with toxicology.

body.the_bedside_summary: Scooped ST with a short QT in a well patient = EFFECT, leave it alone. Any new arrhythmia, nausea, confusion or yellow vision in someone on digoxin = TOXICITY until proven otherwise, whatever the level says.

warnings: Digoxin EFFECT is not toxicity. Scooped ST depression with a short QT is expected and needs no action.
Toxicity is a CLINICAL diagnosis. It occurs at therapeutic levels, and a high level without symptoms or arrhythmia may not need treatment.
HYPOkalaemia precipitates chronic toxicity because potassium and digoxin compete for the same binding site. Diuretics are the usual route in.
HYPERkalaemia in ACUTE overdose is a severity marker and an indication for antidote.
Do not reach for intravenous calcium first in digoxin-associated hyperkalaemia — treat the digoxin. Follow local toxicology advice.
Bidirectional VT, and atrial tachycardia with AV block, should make you think digoxin immediately.
A previously irregular AF that becomes REGULAR suggests complete AV block with a junctional escape — a red flag, not improvement.
Ask directly about yellow-green vision and haloes. Patients do not volunteer it.
Digoxin is NOT dialysable — the volume of distribution is far too large.
Any AKI turns a stable digoxin dose into an overdose. Recheck renal function whenever the patient is unwell.
Amiodarone, verapamil, macrolides and spironolactone all raise digoxin levels.
limitations: Levels, antidote dosing and arrhythmia management are protocol- and toxicology-directed. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: What is the reverse tick sign?
flashcards.a: The scooped downsloping ST depression of digoxin EFFECT — expected, not toxicity.

flashcards.q: Which interval helps separate digoxin effect from ischaemia?
flashcards.a: The QT — digoxin SHORTENS it, most other causes do not.

flashcards.q: Is digoxin toxicity diagnosed on the level?
flashcards.a: No — it is clinical. It occurs at therapeutic levels and a high level may not need treating.

flashcards.q: Why does hypokalaemia cause toxicity?
flashcards.a: Potassium and digoxin compete for the same site on the Na/K-ATPase, so less potassium means more digoxin bound.

flashcards.q: What does hyperkalaemia mean in acute overdose?
flashcards.a: A severity marker predicting mortality — an indication for digoxin immune Fab.

flashcards.q: Which arrhythmia is near-specific?
flashcards.a: Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia; also atrial tachycardia with AV block.

flashcards.q: What does a regular rhythm in known AF suggest?
flashcards.a: Complete AV block with junctional escape — digoxin toxicity.

flashcards.q: What is xanthopsia?
flashcards.a: Yellow-green vision with haloes around lights.

flashcards.q: Can dialysis remove digoxin?
flashcards.a: No — the volume of distribution is far too large.

checkboxes: ST shape and QT assessed before calling it toxicity
Potassium, magnesium and renal function checked
Visual and GI symptoms asked about directly
Rhythm strip examined for block with ectopy

entries.title: Heart Failure by Ejection Fraction — HFrEF, HFmrEF, HFpEF and Recovered
entries.summary: The ejection fraction decides which treatments apply. HFrEF has four drugs that change survival; HFpEF is a stiff ventricle where most of those drugs have never worked, and the treatment is the comorbidities plus an SGLT2 inhibitor.

terms: heart failure by ejection fraction — hfref, hfmref, hfpef and recovered

what_the_number_means.definition: EJECTION FRACTION is the proportion of the blood in the left ventricle at the end of filling that is ejected with each beat — stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume. Normal is roughly 50–70%.
what_the_number_means.the_thing_to_understand: It is a RATIO, not a measure of how much blood is pumped. A small, stiff ventricle can eject 60% of a tiny volume and still deliver an inadequate cardiac output — which is exactly what happens in HFpEF. A normal ejection fraction therefore does NOT mean a normal heart or an adequate output.
what_the_number_means.how_it_is_measured: Usually echocardiography, which is operator-dependent with meaningful inter-observer variation — so a change of a few points between scans may be measurement, not disease. Cardiac MRI is the reference standard.

hfref.the_problem: The ventricle cannot CONTRACT adequately. It is typically dilated with thin walls — eccentric remodelling.
hfref.causes: Ischaemic heart disease (the commonest), previous myocardial infarction, dilated cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, myocarditis, alcohol, chemotherapy (anthracyclines, trastuzumab), peripartum, tachycardia-induced, and thyroid disease.
hfref.why_this_category_matters_most: It is the ONLY category with a large body of evidence for drugs that reduce MORTALITY. The four pillars — an ARNI or ACE inhibitor/ARB, a beta-blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and an SGLT2 inhibitor — each independently improve survival and should be started early and titrated, not sequenced slowly one at a time. Device therapy (ICD, CRT) applies here too.

hfmref.formerly: Mid-range ejection fraction — deliberately renamed to MILDLY REDUCED, because "mid-range" implied a benign middle ground and this group behaves much more like HFrEF than like HFpEF.
hfmref.the_practical_position: Evidence is weaker because these patients were often excluded from trials, but subgroup and pooled data support using HFrEF therapies. Treat it as HFrEF unless there is a reason not to. Importantly, this group is UNSTABLE as a label — many are moving in one direction or the other, so repeat the echo.

hfpef.the_problem: The ventricle contracts normally but is STIFF and cannot RELAX and FILL. Filling pressures rise, and that pressure is transmitted back to the lungs — which is why the patient is breathless despite a "normal" heart on a report.
hfpef.who: Older patients, more often women, with HYPERTENSION (the dominant driver), obesity, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease and sleep apnoea. It now accounts for around half of all heart failure and the proportion is rising.
hfpef.the_diagnostic_difficulty: The echo can look near-normal, so the diagnosis rests on symptoms and signs of heart failure PLUS evidence of raised filling pressures — natriuretic peptides, diastolic indices, left atrial enlargement, or a stress test. It is frequently misattributed to obesity, deconditioning or lung disease for years. Note that natriuretic peptides are LOWER in obesity, so a normal BNP in a very obese breathless patient does not exclude HFpEF.
hfpef.the_treatment_reality: Be honest about this: the drugs that transformed HFrEF have largely FAILED to show mortality benefit in HFpEF. What is established is SGLT2 INHIBITORS, which reduce hospitalisation and cardiovascular death and are now first-line. Beyond that: diuretics for congestion (symptom relief only), and aggressive treatment of the CAUSES — blood pressure, weight, atrial fibrillation, sleep apnoea, diabetes. Mineralocorticoid antagonists have a role in selected patients. Exercise training genuinely helps.
hfpef.the_mimics_that_must_be_excluded: Before settling on HFpEF, exclude the specific and treatable causes of a stiff ventricle: CARDIAC AMYLOIDOSIS (suspect it with a thick ventricle and LOW ECG voltages, carpal tunnel syndrome, or intolerance of standard heart failure drugs), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, constrictive pericarditis, and significant valve disease. Amyloidosis in particular is now treatable and is routinely missed.

hfrecef.ef: Previously 40% or below, now improved to above 40% — often 50% or more
hfrecef.what_it_means: HEART FAILURE WITH RECOVERED (or improved) ejection fraction. The ventricle has remodelled favourably on treatment, or the cause was reversible — tachycardia-induced, peripartum, alcohol, myocarditis, thyroid.
hfrecef.the_critical_point: RECOVERED IS NOT CURED. Withdrawing heart failure therapy in these patients causes RELAPSE in a substantial proportion, and the TRED-HF trial demonstrated exactly that. The improvement is the treatment working, not the disease being gone. Continue the medication and continue follow-up unless there is a specific reason and specialist oversight.

the_two_axes_people_conflate.ejection_fraction: Classifies the PHENOTYPE and decides which drugs apply. It changes slowly.
the_two_axes_people_conflate.nyha_class: Classifies current SYMPTOM severity — I no limitation, II slight, III marked, IV symptoms at rest. It changes week to week and can be III today and II next month on the same ejection fraction.
the_two_axes_people_conflate.the_point: They are independent. A patient can have an ejection fraction of 25% and be NYHA I. Quote both, and never substitute one for the other.

body.the_universal_principle: Heart failure is a SYNDROME, not a diagnosis. Whatever the ejection fraction, the question "what caused this?" must still be answered — ischaemia, valve disease, arrhythmia, thyroid, alcohol, infiltration, hypertension — because several of those causes are treatable in their own right and the label alone treats nobody.

warnings: A normal ejection fraction does not mean a normal heart. It is a ratio — a small stiff ventricle can eject 60% of too little.
RECOVERED is not cured. Withdrawing therapy causes relapse in a substantial proportion — continue treatment and follow-up.
Do not sequence the four pillars slowly one at a time in HFrEF; all four independently improve survival and should be started early and titrated.
In HFpEF, most HFrEF drugs have not shown mortality benefit. SGLT2 inhibitors are the established therapy; the rest is treating the causes.
Natriuretic peptides are LOWER in obesity — a normal BNP does not exclude HFpEF in a very obese breathless patient.
Exclude cardiac amyloidosis before settling on HFpEF — thick ventricle with LOW ECG voltages, carpal tunnel, or intolerance of heart failure drugs.
Echo ejection fraction is operator-dependent. A few points of change between scans may be measurement, not disease.
HFmrEF behaves more like HFrEF than HFpEF — treat it as HFrEF unless there is a reason not to.
Ejection fraction and NYHA class are independent. Quote both.
Heart failure is a syndrome — always answer what caused it.
limitations: Cut-offs and drug recommendations follow the guideline your service uses and are periodically revised. No doses are given here.

flashcards.q: Give the four ejection fraction categories.
flashcards.a: HFrEF ≤40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥50%, and HFrecEF previously ≤40% now improved.

flashcards.q: Why can a normal ejection fraction still be heart failure?
flashcards.a: It is a ratio — a small stiff ventricle ejects a normal fraction of an inadequate volume.

flashcards.q: What are the four pillars, and for which category?
flashcards.a: ARNI/ACEi, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor — for HFrEF. All four improve survival.

flashcards.q: What is established treatment in HFpEF?
flashcards.a: SGLT2 inhibitors, diuretics for symptoms, and aggressive treatment of the causes.

flashcards.q: Why does obesity matter when interpreting BNP?
flashcards.a: Natriuretic peptides are lower in obesity — a normal value does not exclude HFpEF.

flashcards.q: Which treatable mimic of HFpEF is routinely missed?
flashcards.a: Cardiac amyloidosis — thick ventricle with low ECG voltages.

flashcards.q: Can heart failure drugs be stopped once EF recovers?
flashcards.a: No — TRED-HF showed relapse. Recovered is not cured.

flashcards.q: How do EF and NYHA class differ?
flashcards.a: EF is the phenotype and changes slowly; NYHA is current symptoms and changes week to week.

checkboxes: Ejection fraction documented with the measurement method
Category assigned and NYHA class recorded separately
Cause of the heart failure identified
Four pillars started and titrated if HFrEF
Amyloidosis considered before settling on HFpEF
Therapy continued if EF has recovered

entries.title: Every Transporter and Channel, One by One — What It Moves, What Blocks It, What Breaks It
entries.summary: Thirteen pumps and channels explained from scratch. Nearly every diuretic, several inherited diseases and a good share of electrolyte medicine come down to one of these, and once you can picture what each one moves, the drug effects and the derangements stop needing memorisation.

terms: every transporter and channel, one by one — what it moves, what blocks it, what breaks it

the_three_kinds.pump: Burns ATP to move something AGAINST its gradient — uphill. Slow, but it can build a gradient from nothing. Named "-ATPase".
the_three_kinds.exchanger_or_cotransporter: Spends NO energy directly. It rides the gradient a pump already built, carrying a second substance along for the ride (symport, same direction) or in exchange (antiport, opposite directions). This is "secondary active transport".
the_three_kinds.channel: A hole with a gate. Things move DOWNHILL through it, fast, when the gate opens. No energy used.

how_to_read_this.the_one_idea_that_ties_it_together: Almost every transporter in the body is ultimately powered by the SODIUM GRADIENT, and that gradient is built by ONE pump — the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Poison that pump and everything downstream fails. That is why it appears first, and why digoxin, which blocks it, has effects everywhere.

one_na_k_atpase.plain_english: The battery. It sits in the membrane of every cell in the body and constantly pushes sodium OUT and pulls potassium IN.
one_na_k_atpase.what_it_moves: 3 Na⁺ OUT, 2 K⁺ IN, for every 1 ATP. Because it moves three positives out and only two in, it makes the inside of the cell slightly NEGATIVE — it is electrogenic.
one_na_k_atpase.why_it_matters: It creates the low-sodium, high-potassium interior that every other transporter borrows. It maintains cell volume (stop it and cells swell and burst). It sets the resting membrane potential, which is why nerve and muscle can fire at all. It uses a very large share of the body's resting energy — a substantial fraction of basal metabolic rate.
one_na_k_atpase.the_drug: DIGOXIN blocks it at the potassium site. Less sodium leaves, so the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger (below) cannot expel calcium, calcium accumulates, and the heart contracts harder. That single chain is the whole mechanism of digoxin.
one_na_k_atpase.the_clinical_link: Potassium and digoxin COMPETE for the same site. Low potassium means more digoxin binds — which is why hypokalaemia causes digoxin toxicity at an ordinary dose.
one_na_k_atpase.when_it_fails: Ischaemia (no ATP) → sodium and water rush in → cellular swelling, the earliest visible change in cell injury. Continue and the cell dies.

two_ca_atpase_serca_and_pmca.plain_english: The calcium vacuum cleaners. Calcium is a signal, and a signal only works if it can be switched OFF. These pumps clear it away.
two_ca_atpase_serca_and_pmca.serca: Sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase — pumps calcium from the cytoplasm back INTO the internal store, ready to be released again. It is what makes a muscle RELAX.
two_ca_atpase_serca_and_pmca.pmca: Plasma membrane Ca²⁺-ATPase — pumps calcium out of the cell entirely. Low capacity but high affinity, so it handles the fine trimming.
two_ca_atpase_serca_and_pmca.why_it_matters: Relaxation is an ACTIVE, energy-requiring process. This is not obvious and it explains a lot: rigor mortis occurs because ATP runs out and SERCA stops, so calcium stays high and the muscle cannot let go.
two_ca_atpase_serca_and_pmca.the_disease: Reduced SERCA activity is a feature of failing heart muscle and contributes to impaired relaxation — one mechanical reason a failing ventricle fills poorly.

three_na_ca_exchanger_ncx.plain_english: A swap door. It lets sodium fall inwards down its gradient and uses that energy to throw calcium out.
three_na_ca_exchanger_ncx.what_it_moves: 3 Na⁺ IN, 1 Ca²⁺ OUT, normally. No ATP — it spends the gradient the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase built.
three_na_ca_exchanger_ncx.the_critical_property: It is REVERSIBLE. If intracellular sodium rises (digoxin, ischaemia), the exchanger runs BACKWARDS and brings calcium IN. That reversal is the therapeutic effect of digoxin and, taken too far, is also part of how ischaemic cells kill themselves with calcium overload.

four_na_h_exchanger_nhe.plain_english: The acid bailer. It throws hydrogen ions out of the cell, again riding the sodium gradient inwards.
four_na_h_exchanger_nhe.why_it_matters: It defends intracellular pH, and in the kidney proximal tubule it is the main route for reabsorbing bicarbonate — so it is central to acid-base balance.
four_na_h_exchanger_nhe.the_drug_link: ACETAZOLAMIDE does not block NHE itself but blocks carbonic anhydrase, which supplies it — the net effect is bicarbonate loss and a metabolic acidosis, which is exactly why it is used in altitude sickness and glaucoma.

five_nkcc2_the_loop_diuretic_target.plain_english: A minibus that only leaves when all four seats are full. In the thick ascending limb it carries sodium, potassium and two chlorides in together.
five_nkcc2_the_loop_diuretic_target.what_it_moves: 1 Na⁺, 1 K⁺, 2 Cl⁻ — all INTO the cell from the tubular fluid.
five_nkcc2_the_loop_diuretic_target.why_it_matters_enormously: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs a large share of filtered sodium and, critically, builds the CONCENTRATED MEDULLARY INTERSTITIUM. That gradient is what lets the body concentrate urine at all. Block it and you lose both the sodium and the ability to concentrate — which is why loop diuretics are so powerful.
five_nkcc2_the_loop_diuretic_target.the_side_effects_all_follow_from_the_mec: Potassium recycling through ROMK creates a positive charge in the lumen that drives CALCIUM and MAGNESIUM reabsorption. Block NKCC2 and that driving force disappears — so loop diuretics waste calcium AND magnesium as well as potassium. Hypocalcaemia here is a feature, not a surprise, and it is why loops are used in hypercalcaemia.
five_nkcc2_the_loop_diuretic_target.the_inherited_version: BARTTER SYNDROME — a genetic loss of NKCC2 function. It looks exactly like being permanently on a loop diuretic: salt wasting, hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypercalciuria with a risk of nephrocalcinosis, and normal or low blood pressure. Presents in childhood.

six_ncc_the_thiazide_target.plain_english: The same idea, smaller vehicle, further down. In the distal convoluted tubule it carries sodium and chloride in together.
six_ncc_the_thiazide_target.the_drug: THIAZIDES — bendroflumethiazide, hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide, and chlortalidone.
six_ncc_the_thiazide_target.the_calcium_difference_that_confuses_eve: Loop diuretics LOSE calcium; thiazides RETAIN it. Blocking NCC lowers intracellular sodium, which makes the basolateral Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger work harder, pulling MORE calcium out of the tubular fluid. So thiazides RAISE serum calcium and reduce urinary calcium — which is why they are used to prevent calcium kidney stones, and why an unexplained hypercalcaemia should prompt a look at the drug chart before a parathyroid workup.
six_ncc_the_thiazide_target.the_other_effects: Hyponatraemia (thiazides are a leading drug cause, especially in thin older women), hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricaemia and gout, hyperglycaemia and hyperlipidaemia.
six_ncc_the_thiazide_target.the_inherited_version: GITELMAN SYNDROME — genetic loss of NCC. Like permanent thiazide: hypokalaemia, alkalosis, HYPOcalciuria and — distinctively — marked HYPOMAGNESAEMIA with muscle cramps and tetany. Presents later and more mildly than Bartter. Remember it as "Gitelman = thiazide, Bartter = loop", and the calcium goes the same way as the drug.

seven_enac_the_amiloride_target.plain_english: The final sodium door, in the collecting duct. Whatever sodium is left, this is the last chance to take it back.
seven_enac_the_amiloride_target.what_it_moves: Na⁺ IN, through a channel — no partner, no ATP.
seven_enac_the_amiloride_target.the_control: ALDOSTERONE increases the number of these channels. So aldosterone → more sodium reabsorbed → water follows → blood pressure rises. Sodium entering leaves the lumen negative, which drives POTASSIUM and HYDROGEN out into the urine — which is why aldosterone excess causes hypokalaemia AND alkalosis together.
seven_enac_the_amiloride_target.the_drugs: AMILORIDE and triamterene block the channel directly. SPIRONOLACTONE and eplerenone block the aldosterone receptor upstream. Both are potassium-SPARING for the same reason: less sodium in means less potassium out.
seven_enac_the_amiloride_target.the_inherited_version: LIDDLE SYNDROME — a gain-of-function mutation leaving ENaC permanently open. Severe early hypertension with hypokalaemia and alkalosis, but LOW aldosterone and low renin, because the channel is stuck on without needing the hormone. It looks like Conn syndrome and is treated with amiloride, not spironolactone — spironolactone cannot work because the problem is downstream of the receptor. That distinction is the whole point of knowing it exists.

eight_romk.plain_english: The potassium exit. A channel that lets potassium leak back out into the tubule.
eight_romk.why_it_matters: In the thick ascending limb it RECYCLES potassium back into the lumen so NKCC2 keeps working, and creates the positive lumen charge that drives calcium and magnesium reabsorption. In the collecting duct it is the main route by which potassium is actually excreted.
eight_romk.the_link: Loss-of-function causes a form of Bartter syndrome. It also explains why potassium excretion depends on sodium delivery and aldosterone together.

nine_cftr.plain_english: A chloride door that is gated by the cell's internal signalling. Where chloride goes, water follows — so this channel decides whether secretions are watery or thick.
nine_cftr.what_it_moves: Cl⁻ OUT of epithelial cells (and it regulates other channels, including inhibiting ENaC).
nine_cftr.the_disease: CYSTIC FIBROSIS — autosomal recessive loss of CFTR. Chloride cannot leave, so water does not follow, so every exocrine secretion becomes THICK and STICKY. That one defect explains the whole disease: recurrent chest infection and bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency with steatorrhoea and malnutrition, meconium ileus at birth, biliary disease, and infertility from congenital absence of the vas deferens.
nine_cftr.the_diagnostic_test_and_why_it_works: The SWEAT TEST. In a normal sweat duct CFTR REABSORBS chloride from sweat before it reaches the skin. Without CFTR that reabsorption fails, so the sweat stays SALTY — the basis of the test, and of the old saying that a baby who tastes salty when kissed will not thrive.
nine_cftr.the_flip_side: CHOLERA toxin locks CFTR permanently OPEN. Chloride and water pour into the gut lumen — that is the profuse watery "rice water" diarrhoea. Same channel, opposite fault, opposite disease.

ten_voltage_gated_na_k_ca_channels.plain_english: Gates that open in response to a change in voltage rather than a chemical. They are how electrical signals travel.
ten_voltage_gated_na_k_ca_channels.the_sequence_of_an_action_potential: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → sodium floods in → the cell depolarises rapidly (the upstroke). They then INACTIVATE. Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open → potassium leaves → the cell repolarises. Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels let calcium in, which is what actually triggers muscle contraction and neurotransmitter release.
ten_voltage_gated_na_k_ca_channels.the_drugs: LOCAL ANAESTHETICS block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels from inside the axon — no upstroke, no signal, no pain. Class I ANTIARRHYTHMICS block cardiac Na⁺ channels. PHENYTOIN and carbamazepine stabilise them in the inactivated state, which is how they stop seizures. CALCIUM CHANNEL BLOCKERS act on the L-type calcium channel — dihydropyridines mainly on vessels, verapamil and diltiazem more on the heart.
ten_voltage_gated_na_k_ca_channels.the_electrolyte_link: This is why potassium and calcium disturbances are dangerous: they shift the resting potential and the threshold, so the heart becomes either unexcitable or too excitable. It is also why calcium is given in hyperkalaemia — it does not lower potassium, it restores the gap between resting potential and threshold and stabilises the membrane.
ten_voltage_gated_na_k_ca_channels.the_channelopathies: Long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, malignant hyperthermia (ryanodine receptor), and the periodic paralyses — all faults in these channels.

eleven_aquaporins.plain_english: Dedicated water pipes. Water can seep slowly through a membrane on its own; aquaporins let it pour.
eleven_aquaporins.the_one_that_matters_clinically: AQUAPORIN-2 in the collecting duct. ADH (vasopressin) makes the cell insert AQP2 into the membrane. More channels → more water reabsorbed → concentrated urine. No ADH → no channels → dilute urine.

the_diseases.central_diabetes_insipidus: The pituitary does not MAKE ADH. Responds to desmopressin.
the_diseases.nephrogenic_diabetes_insipidus: The kidney does not RESPOND to ADH — the AQP2 machinery fails. Does NOT respond to desmopressin, which is the test that separates the two. Causes: LITHIUM (the commonest acquired cause by far), hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, and inherited receptor defects.
the_diseases.siadh: Too much ADH — too many channels — water retained — dilutional HYPONATRAEMIA with concentrated urine in a euvolaemic patient.

eleven_aquaporins.the_other_one: AQUAPORIN-4 in astrocytes is the antigen in NMOSD — the same molecule, an entirely different disease, and the reason aquaporin-4 antibody must be tested before starting MS therapy.

twelve_sglt1_and_sglt2.plain_english: Glucose hitchhikers. They cannot move glucose on their own, so they bind sodium and let sodium's inward rush drag glucose along with it.
twelve_sglt1_and_sglt2.sglt2: In the early proximal tubule. Reabsorbs the large majority of filtered glucose — high capacity, low affinity.
twelve_sglt1_and_sglt2.sglt1: Further along the tubule, and in the SMALL INTESTINE, where it absorbs dietary glucose.
twelve_sglt1_and_sglt2.the_drug: SGLT2 INHIBITORS (the "-gliflozins"). Blocking reabsorption makes the patient pass glucose in the urine, lowering blood glucose in a way that does not depend on insulin. Their benefits in HEART FAILURE and CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE turned out to be larger and partly independent of glucose lowering, which is why they are now used in patients without diabetes.
twelve_sglt1_and_sglt2.the_harms_that_follow_from_the_mechanism: Sugar in the urine and the genital area causes GENITAL MYCOTIC INFECTION and, rarely, Fournier gangrene. Osmotic diuresis causes volume depletion. And EUGLYCAEMIC DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS — ketoacidosis with a near-normal glucose, because the glucose is being excreted. That is a genuine trap: a patient can be in DKA with a glucose that looks reassuring, so check KETONES, not just sugar, in any unwell patient on a gliflozin.
twelve_sglt1_and_sglt2.the_beautiful_bit: SGLT1 in the gut is why ORAL REHYDRATION SOLUTION works. Cholera destroys chloride handling but leaves SGLT1 intact, so giving glucose WITH salt drags sodium — and therefore water — across the gut wall. Glucose alone would not do it; salt alone would not do it. That is why the recipe has both, and it is one of the highest-impact applications of a single transporter in medicine.

thirteen_glut_transporters.plain_english: Revolving doors for glucose. Unlike SGLT they need no sodium and no energy — glucose simply moves down its gradient, but far faster than it could alone. This is FACILITATED DIFFUSION.

the_ones_worth_knowing.glut1: Red cells and the blood-brain barrier — constant, baseline supply. Deficiency causes a treatable childhood epilepsy that responds to a ketogenic diet.
the_ones_worth_knowing.glut2: Liver, pancreatic beta cell, kidney, gut basolateral membrane. Low affinity and high capacity, so it senses HIGH glucose — which is exactly what a glucose SENSOR in the beta cell needs to do.
the_ones_worth_knowing.glut3: Neurons. High affinity, so the brain takes glucose even when the supply is low. The brain is protected first.
the_ones_worth_knowing.glut4: Muscle and fat, and the only one that is INSULIN-DEPENDENT. Insulin makes the cell move GLUT4 to the surface. No insulin, or resistance to it, means glucose cannot get into muscle and fat — which is a large part of what diabetes IS.

thirteen_glut_transporters.the_thing_worth_understanding: EXERCISE also recruits GLUT4 to the membrane, by a pathway that does NOT need insulin. That is why exercise lowers blood glucose in type 2 diabetes, why it can cause hypoglycaemia in someone on insulin, and why it is a genuine treatment rather than general advice.

the_summary_table_worth_memorising.loop_diuretic: NKCC2 · thick ascending limb · loses K, Ca, Mg · Bartter is the inherited copy
the_summary_table_worth_memorising.thiazide: NCC · distal convoluted tubule · loses K and Mg, KEEPS Ca · Gitelman is the inherited copy
the_summary_table_worth_memorising.potassium_sparing: ENaC or the aldosterone receptor · collecting duct · keeps K · Liddle is the inherited opposite
the_summary_table_worth_memorising.digoxin: Na/K-ATPase · everywhere · raises intracellular Ca via the Na/Ca exchanger
the_summary_table_worth_memorising.gliflozin: SGLT2 · proximal tubule · glucose out in the urine
the_summary_table_worth_memorising.local_anaesthetic: Voltage-gated Na channel · from inside the axon
the_summary_table_worth_memorising.cystic_fibrosis: CFTR · thick secretions everywhere · salty sweat

warnings: Loop diuretics LOSE calcium; thiazides RETAIN it. An unexplained hypercalcaemia should prompt a look at the drug chart before a parathyroid workup.
Bartter looks like a permanent loop diuretic; Gitelman like a permanent thiazide. The calcium goes the same way as the corresponding drug.
Liddle syndrome does NOT respond to spironolactone — the fault is downstream of the receptor. Use amiloride.
Hypokalaemia causes digoxin toxicity because potassium and digoxin compete for the same site on the Na/K-ATPase.
Calcium in hyperkalaemia does not lower potassium — it stabilises the membrane by restoring the gap between resting potential and threshold.
Lithium is the commonest acquired cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. It does not respond to desmopressin.
SGLT2 inhibitors cause EUGLYCAEMIC ketoacidosis. Check ketones, not just glucose, in any unwell patient on a gliflozin.
Oral rehydration needs BOTH glucose and salt — SGLT1 requires the pair. Sugar alone or salt alone does not work.
Muscle relaxation is active and requires ATP through SERCA. Loss of ATP is why rigor mortis occurs.
Aquaporin-4 is the NMOSD antigen — the same protein family, a completely different disease from diabetes insipidus.
limitations: A mechanistic reference. Drug choice, doses and monitoring are protocol-specific and are not given here.

flashcards.q: What does the Na/K-ATPase move, and at what cost?
flashcards.a: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, per ATP — and it is electrogenic, making the inside negative.

flashcards.q: How does digoxin actually strengthen contraction?
flashcards.a: Blocks Na/K-ATPase → intracellular Na rises → Na/Ca exchanger reverses → calcium accumulates.

flashcards.q: Which transporter do loop diuretics block, and what else is lost?
flashcards.a: NKCC2 — and with it calcium and magnesium, because the lumen-positive charge disappears.

flashcards.q: Why do thiazides raise calcium?
flashcards.a: Blocking NCC lowers intracellular sodium, so the Na/Ca exchanger pulls more calcium out of the tubule.

flashcards.q: Bartter vs Gitelman?
flashcards.a: Bartter = NKCC2 = loop-like, hypercalciuria. Gitelman = NCC = thiazide-like, hypocalciuria with marked hypomagnesaemia.

flashcards.q: Why does Liddle syndrome not respond to spironolactone?
flashcards.a: ENaC is stuck open independently of aldosterone — the fault is downstream of the receptor. Use amiloride.

flashcards.q: Why is sweat salty in cystic fibrosis?
flashcards.a: CFTR normally reabsorbs chloride from sweat; without it the chloride stays in.

flashcards.q: How does cholera toxin act on CFTR?
flashcards.a: Locks it permanently open — chloride and water pour into the gut.

flashcards.q: Which aquaporin does ADH control, and what fails with lithium?
flashcards.a: Aquaporin-2 — lithium blocks the response, causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

flashcards.q: Why does oral rehydration need both glucose and salt?
flashcards.a: SGLT1 co-transports them — glucose drags sodium and water across. Neither works alone.

flashcards.q: Which GLUT is insulin-dependent, and what else recruits it?
flashcards.a: GLUT4 — and exercise recruits it without insulin, which is why exercise lowers glucose.

flashcards.q: What is euglycaemic DKA?
flashcards.a: Ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose on an SGLT2 inhibitor — check ketones, not sugar.

checkboxes: Diuretic class matched to the expected electrolyte pattern
Drug chart reviewed before investigating a calcium abnormality
Ketones checked in any unwell patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor
Potassium corrected before blaming digoxin level alone
